1–2. *Pubbaṅgamā* means "preceding" or "going before. Ignorance (*avijjā*), characterized by lack of knowledge, occurs toward an object in the mode of delusion;
thus, because the associated states conform to that same mode, ignorance becomes a condition for them as well.

For instance, although phenomena have the intrinsic nature of being impermanent, foul, suffering, and non-self, they are apprehended by it as permanent and so forth. This is its "precedence" over them by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*). Furthermore, that which [is grasped] through delusion...

Overpowered by evil deeds and failing to see their danger, one kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, and practices various other forms of immorality;

this constitutes its "preceding state" both by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). "For the attainment" means for the attainment of that state, that is, for the arrival at unwholesomeness (*akusala*).
“For the sake of obtaining its own nature” means for the sake of its own arising; thus he said, “for its production.
The connection is that this aforementioned ignorance arises as the precursor to unwholesome states.

“That which” refers to that *ahirika* (shamelessness), which, due to a lack of disgust with evil, is established in the mode of having no shame regarding evil, and *anottappa* (fearlessness of wrongdoing), which, due to a lack of dread of evil, is established in the mode of having no fear regarding evil.
And lack of moral dread (*anottappa*); these two follow immediately after. Here, by the word *anu*, *etaṃ* (this) is used in the accusative case.
The meaning of *anudeva* is "together with" or "as one. In this context, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained for ignorance (*avijjā*) and by way of its opposite.
However, this is the distinction: there, in the case of the occurrence [of unwholesome states] by way of the unwholesome courses of action (*akusala-kammapatha*),...

Just as ignorance has primacy [in the unwholesome], so too should the primacy of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) in the course of existence—by way of the wholesome courses of action and the bases for meritorious deeds—be stated.
Furthermore, its primacy should be understood by way of its predominance in a process of existence governed by the influence of inquiry (*vīmaṃsā*), and by way of its mode of sovereignty.
The restriction "only by these two" is used because the mode of sovereignty must be included within the category of the co-nascent.

“Established in the mode of shame” means established in the mode of loathing evil. “Established in the mode of fear” means established in the mode of being terrified. Regarding the word “here,” it refers to *hiri* (shame) and *ottappa* (fear of wrongdoing).

It is called *vijjā* (true knowledge) because one knows (*vidati*) or finds (*vindati*). And since “one who sees clearly” (*viddasu*) is a synonym for one possessed of wisdom, he said, “‘Viddasuno’ means ‘of those who see clearly.
“One whose view is according to reality” means an unperverted view; it is a view that leads to liberation from defilement.
Regarding the phrase "right view arises," here that "clear knowledge" (vijjā) should be understood as right view.

All [the factors] are not obtained simultaneously because the prior formative volitions (pubbābhisaṅkhāra) for right speech, right action, and right livelihood are of various kinds. At the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained simultaneously;
for although their functions are distinct, they are not distinct in their essential nature there. Indeed, the abstention is one and the same.

At the moment of the path, it occurs accomplishing the function of all three abstinences, just as a single right view occurs accomplishing a fourfold function by way of full understanding and so forth.
And the construction is that all these eight are found in the path belonging to the first jhāna. "Belonging to the first jhāna" means possessing the first jhāna.

“Of one who has become such” means of one who possesses the Noble Path. Since it is stated in the *Mahā-Ṣaḷāyatana Sutta* that “by way of only five factors, namely right view and the rest,” the supramundane path therefore consists of five factors.
For the statement “but previously indeed” indicates the absence of the abstinences at the moment of the path; therefore, in sense-sphere consciousnesses—

The intention is that in supramundane consciousnesses, the abstinences (*virati*) are not fixed. "Showing the state of being pure" means for the purpose of showing the state of having pure virtue (*sīla*).
This meaning is illustrated; it does not mean that there is an absence of abstinences in the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
If this is so, why is the section on the fivefold path found in the *Abhidhamma*’s *Maggavibhaṅga*? To this he says: "As for what is [stated] in the Abhidhamma," and so forth.
Regarding the statement, “There is a five-factored path,” it is said that this was spoken “to show another function.
To demonstrate that, the passage beginning with “For at whatever time” was stated. “At whatever time” refers to the mundane time.
By this, the phrase “another function” indicates the function of the eightfold path. Through the arising of the abstinences, [the person] abandons wrong speech and so forth.
They are called the "five factors of action" (pañca kārakaṅgāni) because they cause [the path] to abandon [defilements] during the moment of the path, beginning with right view.

For right speech and so forth are indeed abstentions (virati), and these [factors] cause that [abstention] to be performed. "By way of abstention" (virativasena) means by way of the act of refraining, in the sense of being the instigator (kārāpaka-bhāva) or the agent (kattubhāva);
alternatively, the reading is "by way of the threefold abstention" (viratittayavasena).

"Right action is fulfilled" means that by means of these factors beginning with right view, the function of right action is fulfilled, because through those [factors] such as energy, that purpose is accomplished.
With reference to this, it was said, "in order to show another function.
To show this other function, even at the moment of the supramundane path, these same five [factors] [fulfill] the triad of abstinences beginning with right speech.

This is said in order to show that the factors of the path are produced simultaneously. As it was stated: "At that time, there is a five-factored path. At the moment of the mundane path, there are only five factors;
however, the abstinences (virati) are not fixed [as present], which is why it is called "five-factored" rather than "six-factored.
This is according to the teaching on the five-factored path in the Abhidhamma.
In order to show that while this is the path of praising the causes, the Noble Path consists of eight factors, he said, “And which, bhikkhus,” and so forth; that is indeed easy to understand.
In the Mahācattārīsakasutta, there are twenty factors on the side of the unwholesome: ten beginning with wrong view and ten unwholesome states conditioned by them;
and twenty factors on the side of the wholesome: ten beginning with right view and ten wholesome states conditioned by them.
It has been stated. "The Great Forty" is its name. It is spoken of as a mixture because supramundane factors are also obtainable here.

For in the *Kosalasaṃyutta* and here as well, after the Elder [Ānanda] had said, "Venerable sir, this is only half of the holy life," and so forth, and [the Buddha] had rejected it with the words, "Do not say so, Ānanda," and so forth, the Blessed One [affirmed it] with the words, "This, Ānanda, is the whole of it," and so forth.

The discourse that was taught has been handed down. Its meaning has already been explained in the commentary on the *Kosalasaṃyutta*; therefore, it is said: “Its meaning is exactly as stated in the *Kosalasaṃyutta*.
The commentary on the *Avijjāsutta*, etc., is concluded.
3. Commentary on the *Sāriputtasutta*.
3. Disciple-enlightenment (*sāvakabodhi*) consists of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiyo*); the knowledge included therein is "disciple-perfection-knowledge" (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*).
That, moreover, has reached its supreme pinnacle especially in the two chief disciples, and among them, specifically in the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), but not in others;
thus he says: "Because of the non-attainment... [of the state] of a disciple... Therefore, regarding the attainment of its pinnacle within the holy life of the path (*maggabrahmacariya*),...
Of that which succeeds, only a portion succeeds here, not the whole. For there is no such thing as a "half-holy life" (*addhabrahmacariya*);

therefore it was said, “Even the whole... is obtained. However, the storekeeper did not know this because his knowledge was limited even within the domain of a disciple, whereas the Dhamma-Senāpati’s knowledge was comprehensive in that regard.
"He understood. Therefore he said: "The Elder Ānanda... [omitted] ...understood. He spoke thus: "All this, venerable sir," and so he said.
The commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Brāhmaṇa Sutta.
4. Regarding the phrase "a chariot yoked with four mares," he says "by a chariot yoked with four mares" because the sound of a mare (*vaḷavā*) is a synonym for a mare itself.

A "war-chariot" (*yodharatha*) is a chariot that is to be mounted for the purpose of fighting with warriors. An "ornamented chariot" (*alaṅkāraratha*) is a chariot to be mounted on auspicious days by those who have dressed in their finest attire.
"Enveloped in fine cloth" (*ghanadukulena parivārito*) means covered with white fine cloth having the color of a silver band.
For here the word *parivāra* has the sense of "concealment. It is for the purpose of producing whiteness, being well-surrounded by silver-plated pipes.
The genitive case in the phrase *chaṇṇaṃ chaṇṇaṃ māsānaṃ* is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
"He circumambulates the city once" refers to the conduct that must be performed while standing in that particular position. "Not departed from the city" means [not having left] from the city.
They did not go outside. Those engaged in auspicious speech are *maṅgalikā*; those engaged in words of blessing (*suvatthi*) are *sovatthikā*.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes the *thuti*, *māgadha*, *vandika*, and *ācariyaka* [reciters]. They are like parrot wings in color. "Color-song" (*vaṇṇagīta*) means a song of praise (*thutigīta*).
"The vehicle that has become sublime" (*brahmabhūta-yāna*) means the vehicle that has become supreme among those who have become sublime.
Or, "vehicles" refers to the Brahma-vehicle. It is so called because it has conquered and, in particular, because it has triumphed.
"Bringing lust to its conclusion" means that it leads all lust away by means of its eradication and discipline, and thus brings its own task to completion.
For it is by the very completion of its task that it itself reaches its own conclusion and fulfillment. Therefore he said: "It goes to its conclusion; it is brought to fruition."

The word *dhuranti* is used in the sense of the locative case; thus he said, "yoked to the pair of equanimity" (*tatramajjhattatāyuge yuttā*). The *īsa* (pole) is the pair of wooden shafts that supports the yoke.

Just as it supports the external yoke, and only when it is firmly established is its function accomplished, so too does it—by virtue of the strength acquired through its functional activity—firmly support the pair of equanimity. By means of these very factors, the Noble Path-chariot is set in motion.
And here, by the inclusion of *hiri* (moral shame), *ottappa* (moral dread) is also included by virtue of its association with it. Therefore he said, "together with oneself," and so forth.
It is called *mano* because it measures the object, just as a man measuring with a nāḷi-measure;
thus, it is the mind. But which mind is that? And how is it similar to a cord? To this he said, "the vipassanā-consciousness," and so forth. By that [consciousness], it is like a cord...
He shows what "that which binds" is. The connection is: "The mundane insight-consciousness makes more than fifty wholesome states bound together and unified.
These, moreover, are to be understood according to the method given in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* by way of the mental factors (cittanga), as follows: "There is contact... pe... there is non-distraction.
By "supramundane insight-consciousness," he means the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*). "More than sixty" refers to...

These very [factors], together with right action and right livelihood, and along with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) and the rest, constitute more than fifty-six wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*).

"Bound to a single object" (*ekābaddha*) means bound to one and the same object. "In a single group" (*ekasaṅgaha*) means he brings them into a single group by way of the function of insight (*vipassanā-kicca*).
He is called the "charioteer of protection" (*ārakkhasārathī*) because he maintains watchfulness through his state of being the forerunner. For, as it is said:

Having said, “…of the chariot… [and] the charioteer,” he spoke the word “yogga” (the team) in order to demonstrate that. He causes the burden to be carried by the team; he yokes the team for the sake of proceeding evenly.
He lubricates the axle for the purpose of easy movement. He impels the chariot by means of urging the team.
He makes it free from defects by directing it onto the path of travel. They are manifested as protection.
It establishes protection because its nature is non-forgetfulness. "Courses" (*gatiyo*) means processes of occurrence or attainments.
"He investigates" (*samanvesati*) means he searches for.
It is like a chariot (*ratha*) because it brings a noble person (*ariyapuggala*) face-to-face with Nibbāna. It "adorns" (*parikaroti*) means it embellishes.
Requisites and adornments—virtue serves as the adornment for the Noble Path. Therefore it is said: “the ornament of the fourfold purification of virtue,” meaning the decoration of virtue.
“Associated with insight” means associated with both mundane and supramundane insight.
It is called *vīriya* (energy) because it must be impelled and set in motion according to the proper method; it is right effort (*sammāvāyāma*). Equally and rightly...

It is called *samādhi* because it concentrates (*dhiyati*). It is a *dhura-samādhi* because it is both a burden (*dhura*) and that concentration (*samādhi*). Since equanimity (*upekkhā*) has this *dhura-samādhi* as its burden, it is "equanimity-burden-concentration" (*upekkhā-dhura-samādhi*).
The meaning is that the Noble Path is the *dhura-samādhi* designated as equanimity.

However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), without taking the phrasing literally, it is stated that the terms *dhura* and *samādhi* have different grammatical bases (*bhinnādhikaraṇatā*). [The phrase] "in the neutrality of application" (*payogamajjhatte*)...
By the evenness of energy. "Non-desire" is the opposite of desire; therefore, he said, "consisting of non-greed.
"Encompassing" means a surrounding, that is to say, a covering.

"Loving-kindness" refers to the liberation of mind through loving-kindness; likewise for compassion. "The preliminary stage" refers to the access concentration of both. Both are also physical and mental seclusion.
[These terms] are stated by way of the preceding factors. "In the noble chariot of the path" means in the chariot consisting of the perfectly pure path.

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood through the method of *ekasesa* (single remainder) as "the noble chariot of the path and the chariot of the path," hence "the noble chariot of the path.
Therefore he said: "Standing in this mundane and supramundane chariot of the path. "Clad in armor" refers to the practitioner (*yogāvacara*).
"Clad in hide": "They do not pierce it" means that the paths of speech do not pierce it. It does not break by way of the destruction of the Dhamma;
the meaning is that there is no intermediate breaking of that chariot of the Noble Path when it is properly yoked.

Because it is obtained by relying on one's own human effort (*purisakāra*), the intention is that it belongs to one's own continuity (*santāna*). "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) means devoid of anything superior.

For that very reason, it is the supreme vehicle; because it has no equal, it is "without equal" (*asadisa*). Because they are endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*), the wise—the learned men—emerge from and proceed beyond the world.
Regarding the verse "Victory! Victory!", he says "conquering, conquering" because it is expressed through a permutation of words (*vacanavipallāsa*).
The commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Brāhmaṇa Sutta is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the Kimatthiya Sutta and others:
“Niyamattha” means the sense of restriction. By that restriction—that is, by that limitation—he rejects any other path.

Because there is no other path leading to liberation besides this one. Since it was stated, "for the full understanding of suffering," the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is what is meant.
When the Noble Path is taken up, its preliminary stage is necessarily included within insight (*vipassanā*); therefore, it is said that "the mixed path" is described.
This is self-evident, as there is nothing new [to be added]. However, this distinction is made by means of the terms "the destruction of lust" (*rāgakkhayo*), and so forth.
Even though Nibbāna has been mentioned, the holy life (brahmacariya) is likewise [the goal], just as Arahantship is.
Therefore, it is Nibbāna itself that is called "this is the culmination of the holy life.
The commentary on the Kimatthiyasutta and others is finished.
7. Commentary on the Second Discourse on a Certain Bhikkhu:
By such phrases as "the removal of lust," both Nibbāna and Arahantship may be expressed.
Since that bhikkhu’s understanding was fixed upon both of these, the Blessed One, in accordance with his inclination, said: "This, indeed, is for the element of Nibbāna," and so forth.
Having set forth the element of Nibbāna, he further said: "The destruction of the taints (āsava) is what is meant by that.

Because the Noble Path leads away from lust and the other defilements by means of their total eradication and exhausts the taints in every respect, it is for that reason called both Nibbāna and Arahantship;
therefore, it is stated that both of these have the names "the removal of lust" and so forth. This is due to skill in the connection [of the text].
By the phrase "asking this, he said," it is shown that "a connection by way of inquiry (pucchānusandhi) is found here";
however, it should be understood that a connection by way of intention (ajjhāsayānusandhi) is also found here.
The commentary on the second sutta concerning a certain bhikkhu is finished.
8. Commentary on the Vibhaṅgasutta:

"Having analyzed the Noble Eightfold Path by way of a single method" means that after showing the Noble Eightfold Path through its divisions by way of a single method beginning with "Right View," [the Buddha says] "And what, bhikkhus, is Right View? and so forth.

Desiring to analyze by another method as well, he stated, "by way of hearing, comprehension, penetration, and reviewing," because even the knowledges of learning, retention, and mastery are included within the knowledge of hearing.
"Adherence to the meditation subject" means the practice of the meditation subject. The connection is: "having learned the first two truths."
"Desirable, lovely, and agreeable" indicates a state of inclination toward cessation and the path, not a state of delight;

and that very state of inclination should be understood as the performance of the function [of penetration] therein. Because the truths have the single characteristic of being penetrated by one and the same mode, that very state of facing them is their convergence;
thus, there is a single breakthrough (*ekābhisamaya*).
"Assa" means of knowledge or of the practitioner. And here, some say: "Even mundane knowledge is penetration (*paṭivedha*), because it possesses the quality of awakening to things as they truly are.
[Objection: Is it not the case that penetration through learning (*uggaha*) and so forth is indeed penetration, yet it is not supramundane?

[Response: That is not so, because the term "penetration" by itself cannot denote penetration through learning and the rest; or rather, because it is designated as such by way of learning and so forth due to being the cause of penetration.
Knowledge occurring in the prior stage regarding suffering and the other truths is called "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) by way of designation, not because it is actually penetration;
however, knowledge that has become penetration itself deserves to be called "direct penetration. "By way of function" means by way of the functions of full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth.

"Penetration of the object" refers to penetration by realization (*sacchikiriyā*). "By way of function" refers to penetration by non-delusion. "Comprehension" (*pariggaha*) is the grasping of the truth through learning and the other stages.

“Difficult to see” means that because it cannot be seen according to its actual nature and characteristic by one who has not attained knowledge, it is not manifest even from the moment of its arising.
Therefore he said, “The truth of suffering,” and so forth. “Both” refers to the preceding two truths. “Exertion” (payoga) means activity or effort.
He shows by way of similes that this [effort] must be sought on a grander scale and is more difficult to accomplish.

By the phrase “for the purpose of grasping the peak of existence,” and so forth: just as the first two truths were described as fourfold—namely, “knowledge regarding suffering” and so on—by way of grasping the distinctions in their occurrence during the prior stage through the processes of learning and so forth due to being extremely profound and obscure in some manner, [the third truth] is likewise treated.
Yet that knowledge is actually one, because it occurs by way of a single realization (*ekābhisamaya*).

"By way of being the direct opposite of sensual desires" means by way of being the immediate antithesis to sensual desires. "By way of having escaped from sensual desires" means by way of being dissociated from sensual desires.
"For one who comprehends sensual desires" means for one who comprehends both types of sensual desire as impermanent and so forth.
"A basis" (*pada*) is that by which something proceeds or occurs; thus, "the basis of sensual desire" (*kāmapada*) refers to the cause for the arising of sensual desire.

*Ghāta* means eradication; it is the eradication of the basis for sensual desire. Therefore, he said, "the subsiding of sensual desire" (*kāmavūpasama*). That which is secluded from sensual desires is "secluded from sensual desires" (*kāmavivitta*).

Since that very state is their end—namely, seclusion through total eradication—it is said to have "arisen at the end of seclusion from sensual desires" (*kāmavivittante uppanno*) when that end is to be accomplished.
It departs from sensual desire, thus it is *nekkhamma*; that itself is the "intention of renunciation" (*nekkhammasaṅkappa*).
And within this analysis of the literal meaning of the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*), the specific determination of its meaning—
such as its being the opposite of sensual desire (*kāma*) as previously stated— is included.

By the phrase "this same method," [it is shown that] for the thoughts of non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) and non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*), there is [the inclusion of their respective opposites], such as their being the opposite of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and the opposite of cruelty (*vihiṃsā*).

He extends [the method] by analogy to the procedure for extracting the meaning (*atthuddhāraṇavidhi*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "renunciation-intention and so forth," he includes precisely the intentions of non-ill-will and non-cruelty.
"Perceptions of renunciation, etc. refers to the perceptions of renunciation and so on that are associated with the abstinence from sensual thought (*kāma-vitakka*) and the rest.
"Diversity" (*nānatta*) is due to their occurring at different moments. "In three instances" means in three types of causes. "Of that which has arisen" means of that which is fit to arise.
What is intended here is that which has arisen from having acquired the plane (*bhūmi*). This same method applies to what follows as well.
"From the cutting off of the footing" means from the cutting off of the cause. For "footing" (*pada*) is said to be the cause of arising; this is the meaning.

"By way of accomplishing non-arising" means by way of accomplishing such that the wholesome intention (*saṅkappa*) does not arise in the future, just as right view [prevents unwholesome states]. Only a single wholesome intention arises.
"In four instances" means in the four instances of transgression, such as deception and so forth.

Since "wrong livelihood for those who have gone forth" is characterized by food, he said, "for the sake of hard food, soft food, and so on. Right livelihood is the total abandonment of improper search;
thus he said, "by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. This is by way of those [factors] that have reached the level of courses of kamma.

"It is said, 'in seven instances. For when he resorts to a wrong means of livelihood that has reached the level of a course of unwholesome action (*akammapatha*), he indeed commits that "striking of the foot.
Or, "in such an object" means in whatever object these defilements have not previously arisen; it is precisely in that [object].
"Of those not yet arisen" means of those not yet arisen even by way of aspiration for their non-arising. "Zeal for energy" refers to energy.
It is the desire characterized by the wish to produce [wholesome states]. Some say it is "energy associated with desire.

However, energy itself is described by way of the term "desire" because it possesses the quality of desire found in the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and because it exerts effort in its task.
For indeed, energy is defined as "not relinquishing desire and not relinquishing one's burden. By preventing one from falling into the side of indolence—
He makes the mind exerted. "Exertion" (*padhāna*) means energy that has become exertion.
"By way of continuous production" means by way of causing [the state] to arise without interruption.

"By way of accomplishing the function in four places" means by way of performing the function of exertion in the four aforementioned places, through the non-arising [of unwholesome states] and so forth.

"By way of accomplishing what is to be done" means by way of shattering the grasping at beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, and by way of accomplishing foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.

"This" refers to the aforementioned distinction between similarity and dissimilarity. "Of this" refers to the path. "How is it here? means if [it is compared] to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere.

From the first stage up to the peak of all existence (*sabbabhavagga*), there is a similarity among the factors of jhāna, the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*), and the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). This being so, one might ask:
"In this context, how should the meaning of the statement 'in the formless realms (*ārūpa*), the fourfold and fivefold jhāna arises, and that is supramundane (*lokuttara*)' be understood?
To this he says: "Even here," and so forth. "Consisting of that jhāna" (*taṃjhānikā*) means whichever jhāna among the first jhāna and the others is the basis for the attainment of the path.
That which serves as the basis consists of the jhānas; for one who possesses those jhānas, there are also the three higher noble paths. "In this way" means by the manner thus described.
It is the foundational jhāna itself that is determined in the arising of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in the formless realm.

"The aggregates that have become the object of insight" refers to the aggregates that have been comprehended through contemplation (*sammasita*). The individual's inclination determines the relationship between the foundational jhāna and the comprehended jhānas.
Regarding the distinction: because the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*) alone determines the specific factors of the Noble Path,

such as the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*), therefore— in all three positions— the insight itself [is the path], since the knowledge of equanimity towards formations arising from the second or subsequent foundational jhānas lacks the desire to attain the factors that transcend the foundational jhāna due to its state of dispassion (*virāga*), whereas the other [knowledge] lacks that state.

It should be understood that [the path] is determined; therefore, even in the first statement, because of the determination of insight (vipassanā-niyama), the paths based on access concentration (apādaka-jjhāna) and so forth are also associated with the first jhāna. And by means of the other supporting jhānas and determinations of insight, they are associated with their respective jhānas.
In this way, the determination of insight should be applied to the remaining statements as far as possible. In the second statement, there is association with their respective jhānas.

It occurs through the fixed sequence of insight into conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-vipassanā*) and the fixed sequence [of jhāna]. For in that context, insight must be developed as the cultivation of specific dispassion (*virāga-bhāvanā*);
it does not, by being accompanied by joy or equanimity, establish the fixed sequence of the path factors such as those of jhāna.

Thus, the fixed sequence of insight should be understood according to the method already stated. And in this position, when there is the presence of the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) of the foundational jhāna attained through comprehension, [the path arises].
Regarding the statement, "The underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) is absolute," it is said that "they say the person’s disposition determines [the path].
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, because this commentary is included within the same compilation as the *Visuddhimagga*, it says, "Their discussion of the doctrine...
should be understood. "In the prior stage" (*pubbabhāge*) means at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*).
The commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Sūka Sutta:
"Sūka" refers to the awn of rice, barley, and so forth. For it is like a harrow; when the hand is directed toward it, [it catches hold].

Or it breaks a foot; therefore, it is said that what is placed upright is called "rightly directed," while what is placed otherwise is called "wrongly directed. Regarding the phrase "by one wrongly directed":
this refers to the wrong placement of the wisdom of the ownership of kamma—that is, [the view]: "These beings experience pleasure and pain by way of kamma, yet..."
The false attribution [of causality] such as, "Brahmā creates by means of the power of the Lord's (issara) will," and so forth.
Some, however, say that it is the occurrence [of views] in the manner of "there is no giving" and so on, or the non-occurrence of that knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "by the cultivation of the path": here too, the wrong placement is either the occurrence of the wrong path or the non-occurrence of the noble path (ariyamagga).
Therefore he said, "Because of its non-occurrence. "He will break through ignorance" means he will utterly eradicate ignorance.

Having made it dependent on the path and having placed it within the path itself—this is because that knowledge is the root cause of the path, since when the path is established, the function of that [knowledge] reaches its culmination.
"By means of right-directed view and right-directed development of the path."

Because it has been stated thus, the mixed path is explained. Herein, the breaking of ignorance should be regarded as similar to the breaking of skin, and the state of the supramundane path as similar to the emergence of blood.
The commentary on the *Sūkasutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the Nandiyasutta:
The wanderer Channa is one who covers himself with robes; he is not a naked wanderer.
The commentary on the Chapter on Ignorance (*Avijjāvagga*) is finished.
2. Vihāravagga 1.
Commentary on the First Vihāra Sutta 11.
"For half a month" (*aḍḍhamāsaṃ*) is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration. "To dwell in seclusion" (*paṭisallīyituṃ*) refers to that aforementioned period of time.
Day after day, the mind should settle into meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and reflection on the Dhamma.

"Should be disciplined" means it should be disciplined by the discipline of total eradication (*samuccheda-vinaya*), such that the Noble Path (*ariya-magga*) is attained. "That" refers to following the example of others' views (*diṭṭhānugati*). "Of him" refers to the populace.
"Departs" means he goes away from the presence of the Teacher. "Su" is a mere particle used for emphasis.
“By way of parts” means by way of a portion. “Together with parts” means *sapadeso*.

Since this *sapadeso* appears in the Canon specifically by way of feeling (*vedanā*), therefore, within the categories of ultimate phenomena (*paramattha-dhamma*), feeling is obtained without remainder;
taking those [feelings] into account, he says, “the part of the aggregates,” and so forth. “All that” refers to all of it, beginning with the part of the aggregates. “Comprehending” means...
He said "reviewing" by way of showing the meaning of the word. Here, "reviewing" (paccavekkhaṇā) is called "comprehension" (sammasana), not insight (vipassanā).
For the Blessed One’s own comprehension through insight was accomplished only on the full moon of Visākha;
therefore, even though the feelings of the Blessed One belong to one plane, they arise as incompatible with beings belonging to other planes.
It is said: "Pleasant feeling that occurs as far as the peak of existence. "In every aspect" means in every way:
by way of its specific nature (*sarūpato*), its origin, its passing away, and its gratification and so forth. "Grasping" and "examining" [it] means comprehending it.

"Without exception" means entirely and without remainder. The section on the faculties and the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) is easy to understand; thus, it is not redundant. "Assa" means...
Of the Blessed One. "In those instances" means in each respective occasion consisting of what is to be reviewed.

"Each respective dwelling-attainment" refers to the attainment of jhāna and the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), which have been entered into gradually after having grasped and comprehended feeling alone—which constitutes a portion of those [states]—as they occur by way of the aggregates and by way of the bases, etc. The attainment of fruition...

For although these attainments are not different in meaning because they are repeatedly entered into after having been thus comprehended, they are spoken of as if they were different due to the distinction between the constituent factors that serve as their basis;
hence, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that there are twenty-four hundred thousand billion varieties of attainments occurring daily.
While it is true that they arise by way of other factors as well, here the emphasis is placed on them by way of feeling (*vedanā*).
They were born through the influence of the experience of feeling (*vedanā*). Why were they born in this way? Because of the internal divisions within the range of the Buddhas' knowledge.

For the Blessed One practiced comprehension (*sammasana*) by means of feeling alone for an entire fortnight, and in accordance with that, he attained those meditative dwellings and attainments (*vihārasamāpatti*). Announcing this marvel, which is not shared by others, to the monks:
The Teacher said, "By which [feeling] I say... and so forth.

"Unwholesome" means that there is only unwholesome feeling by way of the ten unwholesome courses of action—namely, killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, idle chatter, covetousness, and ill will—as well as by way of various wrong views.
Having arisen in the Brahma-world and so forth, there...
"One should connect [the phrase] ‘relying on such a view’ with the thought, ‘We shall become permanent and stable.

In temples and similar places, they plant flowering shrubs for the purpose of worshipping deities or for the enjoyment of all people. By the word ‘etcetera’ in the phrase ‘killing, imprisonment, etc.,’ the inclusion of taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, idle chatter, and so forth, should be understood.
Because the ripening of the result in the present life is neither frequent nor manifest, it is said, ‘for those who have gone to another existence.’"
Regarding the phrase *iti ne saṃti*: here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*).
By this, just as in the case of harsh speech, so too for other unwholesome kamma, the occurrence of unwholesome feeling conditioned by wrong view should be formulated accordingly;
this is the same method. Thus, [the text continues] with the conditions of wrong view and right view.

And just as wholesome and unwholesome resultant feelings have been shown by way of the "simultaneous" condition and the "decisive support" condition as appropriate, so too they should be shown by way of the "wrong intention" condition and others as appropriate; this is what is indicated here.
In the phrase "conditioned by desire," it is the desire for the wish to act, accompanied by craving-desire, that is intended.
He said: "In the phrases beginning with 'conditioned by desire' (*chandapaccayā*), however, the feeling associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed should be understood.

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by applied thought" (*vitakkapaccayā*), it is stated that only applied thought that has reached absorption (*appanā*) is intended; thus it says, "feeling of the first jhāna conditioned by applied thought.
Because the feeling of the first jhāna conditioned by applied thought is included, [the text says] "excluding..."
"First jhāna. Above are the three fine-material-sphere [jhānas], and below are the three immaterial-sphere [jhānas]; thus are the remaining six perceptions, attainments, and feelings.
"Of the three" refers to zeal, applied thought, and perception. "In the non-quiescence" means in that which has not been stilled by its opposite. For of those three...
The conditionality by way of coexistence exists only in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed (*lobha*). Regarding that, what ought to be said has already been stated.

"Of mere desire" refers to mere desire among those three [factors]. In the case of tranquility, only the feeling of the first jhāna is intended, because it is the state attained at the level of absorption (*appanā*).
In the case of the subsiding of desire and applied thought (*vitakka*), the feelings of the second jhāna and so forth are intended, because perception (*saññā*) has not yet subsided.
For by the inclusion of the feeling of the second jhāna and so forth, all perceptions and attainments are indeed included.
By the phrase "the subsiding of even these three," the feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is intended,
because perception reaching the peak of existence subsides through the attainment of an extreme subtlety in desire and thought.
Below, in the phrase “conditioned by right view,” the inclusion of “right view” already encompasses the right view of the lower paths;
thus he says: “For the attainment of what has not been attained” means for the sake of attaining the fruit of arahantship.
Alternatively, since there is no highest path without the realization of the lower paths, the realization of the lower paths is implicitly included.
Having said this, it is stated: "for the sake of attaining the fruit of arahantship. It is called *āyāma* because by means of this one is mixed with the fruit;
thus he says, "there is *āyāma*, there is energy (*vīriya*)," meaning right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).
"Of that undertaking of energy" refers to right effort as the cause for the attainment of higher knowledge (*aññā*). In the Canon, the word *ṭhāna* is a synonym for cause.

He said: "In the cause for the fruit of arahantship. Regarding the phrase "on account of that" (*tappaccayā*), he said "on account of the condition of the state of arahantship" (*arahattassa ṭhānapaccayā*), because here the word "that" (*taṃ*) refers back to the very cause mentioned by the word "state" (*ṭhāne*).

By the expression "co-nascent with the four paths," he clarifies that in the phrase "for the attainment of the fruit of arahantship," the lower paths are included by way of implication (*atthāpatti*). Some...
However, they say: "Having stated 'co-nascent with the four paths,' the phrase 'supramundane feeling that has arisen' is a descriptive qualification.
The term 'supramundane feeling that has arisen' should be considered first, and 'co-nascent with the four paths' afterwards.
The commentary on the First Abiding Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Abiding (Dutiyavihārasutta-vaṇṇanā) 12.
"The subsiding of wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhivūpasama*) means that by means of this, wrong view is completely pacified and entirely abandoned. Regarding the statement:
"'The subsiding of wrong view' is right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*). Thinking that what arises in another existence is too distant, one does not take up the experience of its result (*vipākavedanā*')."

It is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). Although the meaning was indicated by referring back [to a previous section] with the words "by this method," in order to make that matter even clearer, he spoke the passage beginning with "for whichever...
and so forth. Having thus stated the general principle, he said "due to the subsiding of desire" and so on, in order to show the same meaning in its specific form regarding the final three sections;
that is indeed easy to understand. The meaning has already been explained in the immediately preceding sutta.
The commentary on the Second Abiding Sutta is finished.
3–7. Commentary on the Sekkha Sutta and others. 13–17.
One whose virtue consists in training in all three trainings is "one of a training nature" (*sikkhanasīlo*). Alternatively, one who trains is [also so called].
Or it is one who is in training (*sekkha*). For this has been said: "Monks, because he trains, therefore he is called 'one in training.
And what does he train in? He trains in higher virtue," and so forth. It is below the three fruits. That [training] includes the training that has arisen together with the fourth path.
For at the moment of the path, the task of training is not yet finished because it is still in progress; however, at the moment of the fruit—
But this [section] is concluded. Since the meaning is obvious, it follows the method already explained below.
The commentary on the Sekkhasutta and the following is finished.
The commentary on the Vihāravagga is finished.
3. Commentary on the Chapter on Wrongness (Micchattavagga) 21–30.

"Wrong nature" means a nature that is not according to reality, a nature that does not lead to liberation. "Right nature" means a nature that is according to reality, a nature that leads to liberation.
Regarding the phrase "the cause for the basis of wrong practice," he said that here the prefix *adhi-* is devoid of meaning.
—“Because they are the causes for practicing wrong conduct. It is called *ñāya* because it goes toward Nibbāna by way of being penetrated.

That very [path] is called *dhamma* in the sense of supporting those who possess it from falling into the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*); thus he said: “*Ñāya-dhamma* means the Dhamma of the Noble Path.
Since there is no such thing as a false intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) for knowledge, it is consciousness itself here that functions by way of reviewing.
Because it is said that what is occurring is called "knowledge" by way of the word *ñāṇa*, he says, "one of wrong consciousness.
"Wrong reflection" means that after having done some evil, one reflects wrongly, thinking, "Oh, what a good deed I have done!

"Wrong liberation" refers to one who grasps at the fulfillment of the cow-virtues (*gosīla*) and ox-virtues (*govata*) as being liberation. The "turning away from the round" (*vaṭṭavivaṭṭa*) occurs through wrong practice and so forth.
It has been explained. And it is concluded by the statement, “This, monks, is called an untrue person,” and so forth.
Although it is the person alone who is specified by the words, “He holds wrong view,” and so on, nevertheless, this teaching of the Dhamma is given under the heading of the person;
thus he says, “The Dhamma is analyzed. For that very reason he says, “The person is shown by means of the Dhamma. By means of the Dhamma—
By means of states such as wrong view and so forth. From the stage of the virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) onwards, all are called "true persons" (*sappurisa*);
one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is a "truer person. "Well-functioning" (*suppavattaniya*) means capable of being set in motion with ease. "Runs" (*dhāvati*) means goes.

It is a "basis" (*upanisā*) because one must approach and rely upon it by way of what arises through conditions; it is a condition (*paccaya*), [the difference being] that one *sa*-sound has been elided.
Having omitted [the word], he says: "together with its proximate cause (saupanisaṃ) and its condition (sapaccayaṃ). Because it is that which surrounds, it is an "accessory" (parikkhāra);

because it is a retinue, he says: "with its accessories (saparikkhāraṃ) and its retinue (saparivāraṃ). Its state of having a condition (sapaccayatā) should be understood by way of co-nascence and decisive support;

and its state of having a retinue (saparivāratā) should be understood as entering into the state of assistance in the accomplishment of a function, in the production [of a result], and in the performance of a task.
The commentary on the Chapter on Wrongness is finished.
4. Commentary on the Chapter on Practice (Paṭipattivagga): 31–40.

"Practice that is not according to reality" (*ayāthāvapaṭipatti*), or "practice that is not as it should be" (*na yathāpaṭipatti*), because it establishes things incorrectly regarding both causes and fruits.
One sutta is spoken by way of the Dhamma and by way of practice; one sutta is spoken by way of the person and by way of the practitioner.
Because it is the further shore of the great flood of saṃsāra, that which one reaches is called "the further shore" (pāra), namely Nibbāna.
Because there is no further shore here due to its opposite nature, it is called "this shore" (apāra), namely saṃsāra. Thus it is said.

—“‘The far shore and the near shore’ refers to Nibbāna as being beyond the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). ‘Those who have gone to the far shore’ refers to those beyond training (*asekha*). ‘Those who are going there’ refers to those in training (*sekha*).
‘And those who will go there’ refers to virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*). Regarding the phrase ‘those who go to the far shore,’ the word *kita* here denotes the three times;
thus it is said. ‘The shore’ refers to this side of the river. Therefore it is said: ‘He merely runs along the round of existence. This is because the mind is entirely dark.”
It is said that "the dark" refers to unwholesome states because they cause the mind to become dull and because they are the cause for a dark rebirth.
It is said that "the bright" refers to wholesome states because they cause the purification of the mind, make it luminous, and are the cause for a bright rebirth.
It is called "a home" (*oka*) because it is the place where the Māra of defilements, the Māra of volitional formations, and the Māra of death prevail.

The cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is so called; because it is the opposite of that, Nibbāna is "the non-abode" (*anoka*). Thus he said: "From the abode to the non-abode: from the cycle of existence comes Nibbāna.
In the ultimate sense, the Noble Ones (*ariya*) are called "ascetics" (*samaṇa*); the state of being an ascetic is "asceticism" (*sāmañña*), which is the Noble Path.
Because it is to be sought after and approached by means of that, Nibbāna is the "goal of asceticism" (*sāmaññattha*). Thus he said: "Nibbāna is the goal of asceticism, for it... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the goal of brahminhood" (*brahmaññattha*), the meaning here should also be understood according to this same method. By "brahminhood," it means by the noble path (*ariyamagga*).

In the expression "the destruction of lust" (*rāgakkhaya*), the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth. By that, it includes the two phrases "the destruction of hatred" (*dosakkhaya*) and "the destruction of delusion" (*mohakkhaya*).
They say, "It is indeed appropriate [to say] 'the destruction of lust,'" because, in a figurative sense, the state of arahantship is what is being described.
The commentary on the *Paṭipattivagga* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Aññatitthiyapeyyālavagga*, sections 41–48:
For one who turns back again and again, being endowed with the proper conduct, through the very thorough comprehension of the extent of *saṃsāra*, [there arises] *nibbāna*.
Because it is something to be attained, it is said: “Having attained Nibbāna, it is called ‘fully understood’ (pariññāta). “Having attained Nibbāna” means by reason of attaining Nibbāna.
For this particle *tvā* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in: “Having drunk the ghee, strength arises; having seen the lion, fear arises.
Therefore, because the attainment of Nibbāna through the function of fully understanding what is to be fully understood establishes the full understanding of the path (*addhānapariññā*).

It is known; therefore, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), Nibbāna is called "full understanding of the course" (*addhānapariññā*), just as one says, "the sun rises over the snowy mountains.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of realizing the fruit of true knowledge and liberation" (*vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyattha*): here, "true knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of the supreme path.
"Liberation" (*vimutti*) is intended to mean the concentration of the supreme path. Their fruit is "final knowledge" (*aññā*); thus he said: "by the fruit of true knowledge and liberation."
"Arahantship has been declared. Because it is known according to reality and seen directly, it is called "knowledge and vision";
here, the reflection upon the fruit and Nibbāna is intended, thus he said: "Reflection by means of knowledge and vision has been declared.

By the remaining terms: the fading away of lust, the abandoning of the fetters, the uprooting of the underlying tendencies, full understanding of the course [of existence], the destruction of the taints, clear knowledge, liberation, the realization of the fruit, knowledge and vision, and final Nibbāna without clinging.
The commentary on the Aññatitthiyapeyyālavagga is finished.
6. Commentary on the Sūriyapeyyālavagga (49–62):
Just as the appearance of dawn is the certain precursor to the rising of the sun, so too is spiritual friendship.

Regarding "the manifestation of the Noble Path": the simile for this is similar to the dawn. Here, "good friend" (kalyāṇamitta) should be understood as either the Noble One or the Noble Path itself, because—like the appearance of the sun—it dispels the darkness that is to be shaken off.
"The desire to act skillfully" is the perfection of desire, owing to its being perfected compared to other forms of desire. Regarding "the diligence that causes [action] to be performed":
[It is] of that which effects the penetration of truth. Thus, in all instances, the word "accomplishment" (sampadā) is to be understood as the cause for the attainment of distinction.
"By another aspect" means by an aspect other than "dependent on seclusion," etc., namely, by an aspect such as "culminating in the removal of lust," and so forth.
The commentary on the Sūriyapeyyāla-vagga is finished.
7. Commentary on the Section on the Series of Single Dhammas (Ekadhammapeyyālavagga), etc., [Verses 63–138].

These were spoken according to the inclinations of those who would understand when they were taught in such and such a way; therefore, one should not raise the objection: "The meaning has already been stated, why was it stated again?
The commentary on the Section on the Series of Single Dhammas, etc., is concluded.
8. The Chapter on the Summary of Heedfulness (Appamādapeyyālavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Tathāgata (Tathāgatasuttavaṇṇanā) 139.
What is called "heedfulness as an instigator" is: "These unwholesome states are to be abandoned; these wholesome states are to be aroused."

Diligence (*appamāda*) is that which proceeds by way of avoiding what has been stated as avoidable and accomplishing what has been stated as to be accomplished. "This" refers to diligence. It is mundane (*lokiya*) only;
it is not supramundane (*lokuttara*). By the words "this" and "that," he speaks of diligence alone. "Of these" refers to the phenomena (*dhamma*) belonging to the four planes.
"In the sense of causing the acquisition" means in the sense of bringing about the attainment.
The commentary on the *Tathāgata Sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Pada Sutta* 140.
“Of those from the wilderness” (*jaṅgalānaṃ*) means of those who dwell in the wilderness. Here, the word *jaṅgala* is a designation for the earth by way of its common characteristic of being solid.
It does not denote a distant place that is not present. Therefore he said: “of those dwelling on the surface of the earth.
Because the words are being spoken, it is stated with the qualification “of footed beings. “Samodhānaṃ” means the state of being included within; therefore he said:
“the placing together,” meaning that which should be cast in after having been brought near.
The commentary on the Padasutta is finished.
3–10. Commentary on the Kūṭasutta and following suttas, 141–148.
*Vassika* refers to the flower of the *vassikā* plant, just as the fruit of the *āmalakī* is called "āmalaka. "On the great floor" (*mahātalasmiṃ*).
In the phrase "uparipāsāde," the words "yāni kānici" are suitable to be in grammatical apposition with the others;
thus, stating that "the genitive case is used in the sense of identity (paccatte sāmivacanaṃ)," the change of case ending was made accordingly.

Regarding the word "tantāvutānaṃ," since it is a genitive used for specification (niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ), the phrase "atha vā" and so forth was stated in order to show the meaning by supplying the word "vatthāni" as the remainder of the sense.
The commentary on the Kūṭasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Appamādavagga is finished.
9. Balakaraṇīyavagga.

1. Commentary on the *Balasutta* (Sutta 149) “Kammantas” means simply “kamma,” just as “suttantas” means simply “suttas. Regarding the phrase “the Noble Eightfold Path,” it is stated that “accompanied by insight” (*sahavipassana*) because insight is indeed included here due to its inseparable connection [with the path].
2. Commentary on the *Bījasutta* (Sutta 150)

150. The fivefold collection is called "seed-planting" (*bījagāma*) in the sense of a mass. "That very thing" refers to the root-seeds and so forth. "Well-grown" means possessing roots that have developed together with the plant. "Starting from the state of being blue" means starting from the attainment of the state of being blue.

3. Commentary on the *Nāga Sutta* 151. "Exerting their strength" means they exert the physical strength of their own bodies. Furthermore, that is precisely what constitutes the attainment of strength for the *nāgas*.
He said: "Seizing strength. "The opening of the confluence" means the mouth or entrance of the great rivers that have joined with the great ocean.

Because the Blessed One introduced the comparison by way of a simile—starting with "The nāgas increase their bodies," and so on—he correlates the simile with the text beginning "In the same way, indeed...
regarding the three phrases starting with "When they have arrived," which indicate a characteristic state through the state itself (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe*).
5. Commentary on the Kumbha Sutta (153).
“Does not vomit out water”: a jar that has been turned upside down vomits out its water; it does not take it back again through its mouth. Therefore he said, “It does not cause it to enter within.
7. Commentary on the Ākāsa Sutta.
155. "It is said that by this [it is meant]": by the success of that Noble Path, the success of all these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) is stated.
8–9–10. Commentary on the First *Megha Sutta*, etc. 156–158. "Dust and dirt" (*paṃsu-rajo-jalla*):
this refers to the impurity born together with the dust of the earth. "The simile of the merchant" (*vāṇijaka-upama*): this also refers to the first sutta, the *Vāṇijaka-upama*.
11–12. Commentary on the Āgantuka Sutta, etc. (159–160).

It is stated that through the successful development of the Noble Path accompanied by insight (vipassanā), there occurs the success of the higher knowledges (abhiññā) regarding the full understanding and so forth of those phenomena that are to be fully understood by higher knowledge;
this is because the discourse was prepared for one who is performing the duties of a khattiya and others, such as [ruling over] their respective domains.
The commentary on the Chapter on What is to be Done (Balakaraṇīyavagga) is finished.
10. The Chapter on Seeking (Esanāvagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Seeking (Esanāsutta).
161. "Sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) refers to both sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual defilements (*kilesakāma*).

For even a sensual defilement is to be sought after by means of the method imagined as "it is desirable" and by means of excessive lusts. "Existences" (*bhavā*) refers to the three realms of existence.
Because it serves as the basis for the holy life (*brahmacariya*) imagined by those who follow wrong views, wrong view itself is intended here by the term "holy life."
2–11. Commentary on the Section on Modes (Vidhāsuttādivaṇṇanā) 162–171.

They are called "modes" (*vidhā*) because they are held (*dhīyanti*) or established (*vidhīyanti*) through their respective divisions, such as "I am superior," and so forth; they are thus portions of conceit or the establishment of conceit. "They strike down" means they afflict.
The commentary on the Chapter on Searches (*Esanāvagga*) is finished.
11. The Chapter on the Floods (Oghavagga) 1–2. Commentary on the Discourses on the Floods, etc. (172–173).

They are called floods (ogha) because they sweep away and cause one to sink into the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). Regarding "in the realms of form and formlessness": this refers to the aggregates produced by karma pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres, which have craving for the fine-material and immaterial realms as their decisive support. It is called a bond (yoga) in the sense of binding.
3–4. Commentary on the *Upādānasutta*, etc. (174–175).
It is called *kāmupādāna* because one grasps by way of sensual desire (*kāma*). Therefore, he said: "the mention of sensual desire.
"Of the mental body" (*nāmakāyassa*) refers to the four immaterial aggregates, beginning with feeling. "The defilement that joins and binds" refers to the cause [producing] the fruit.

The defilement that brings about the connection—the linking together—of the process of action (kamma-vatta) with the process of result (vipāka-vatta), which is designated as the continuity of suffering.
The view of grasping at extremes is the adherence to eternalism or annihilationism.
The commentary on the Sutta on Grasping and so forth is finished.
5–10. Commentary on the *Anusaya-sutta* and others (176–181).
"In the sense of being firmly established" (*thāmagata*) means by way of attaining a state of stability within the continuum of a sentient being (*sattasantāna*).

Furthermore, "firmly established" should be understood as the unique, individual nature (*āveṇika-sabhāva*) of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and the other [latent tendencies], which is not shared with anything else. "Sensual lust" (*kāmarāgo*) refers to sensual lust.

Thus it is "not abandoned. Because it is liable to arise in the continuum when conditions are obtained, it is called an *anusaya* (latent tendency). "In the others as well" refers to the latent tendencies of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) and so forth.
The "lower part" is said to be the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it exists below the form and formless realms.
They are "belonging to the lower part" (*orambhāgiya*) because they serve as conditions for activity therein, just as one says "the milk-pail belongs to the basket. They "bind" (*saṃyojenti*).
Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the meaning should be stated as it was below. "The higher portion" means the sublime portion;
the intention is that the phrase "conducive to that" has not been stated here because it follows the same method already explained below.
The commentary on the *Anusaya-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the Oghavagga is finished.
The commentary on the Maggasaṃyutta is finished.
2. The Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta.
1. The Chapter on Mountains (Pabbatavagga) 1. Explanation of the Himavanta Sutta (Himavantasuttavaṇṇanā) 182.
It is called *bodha* because by means of it the noble disciple awakens to the Four Noble Truths; it is the harmony of the Dhamma (*dhammasāmaggī*). Furthermore, the noble disciple...

"Bodhi" means that which awakens to the Four Noble Truths. "Aṅga" means causes. The connection is with the phrase "by means of which harmony of states. Establishment is by way of craving; accumulation is by way of views.
Establishment is by way of the eternalist view; accumulation is by way of the annihilationist view. Establishment is by way of dullness; accumulation is by way of agitation.
Establishment is by way of devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure; [accumulation is by way of devotion to the pursuit of self-mortification].
Accumulation by way of devotion to self-mortification. In the commentary on the *Oghataraṇa Sutta*:
“Establishment by way of defilements, accumulation by way of formations; establishment by way of craving and views, accumulation by way of the remaining defilements and formations;
establishment by way of all unwholesome formations, accumulation by way of all mundane wholesome formations.”
This should be understood by way of those modes not mentioned here among those already stated.

By the phrase "he awakens from the sleep of the continuity of defilements," he shows that even mindfulness and the other factors accompanied by insight that has reached its culmination possess the nature of enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*).

By the phrase beginning with "four," etc., he shows [the nature of those factors] accompanied by the path and fruit. How is it that the penetration of the truths occurs through the seven enlightenment factors being cultivated?
The phrase "it should be known" is said with reference to the formal charge (codanā), beginning with "as it has been said.
By the expression "like the factors of jhāna and the factors of the path," he shows that the terms *bodhipakkhiya-dhamma* and *bojjhaṅga* have both collective and individual referents.

By the expression "like the components of an army and the components of a chariot," he shows that the designation of a person (*puggalapaññatti*) is a designation for what does not exist [independently].
"They conduce to enlightenment, therefore they are called *bojjhaṅga*"; thus it is said that "the word *aṅga* has the sense of a cause. That which awakens is *bodhi*;
since they are the factors of that very *bodhi*, they are called *bojjhaṅga*. Thus it is said: "They awaken, therefore they are *bojjhaṅga*.
They awaken correctly, directly, and without error, facing toward the causes such as insight (*vipassanā*) and toward the truths that are to be awakened to.

By the words "awakening" (*bodhi*) as stated in such passages as "they awaken by means of the higher paths that illuminate specific bases," it is said that [the term] "comprehensively includes" them through the commonality of the act of awakening (*bujjhanatā*).

And herein, the combination of the factors—investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*), energy (*vīriya*), rapture (*pīti*), and exertion (*padhāna*)—is the antidote to the adherence to dullness, the adherence to sensual pleasure (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*), and the dogmatic insistence on annihilationism (*ucchedābhinivesa*).

It is also the antidote to restlessness and agitation (*uddhacca-āyūhana*), the adherence to self-mortification (*attakilamathānuyoga*), and the dogmatic insistence on eternalism (*sassatābhinivesa*).
The combination of the factors of serenity, concentration, equanimity, and exertion is the antidote. Mindfulness, however, is required in both cases;
for it is said to be beneficial in all circumstances.
The prefix *sam-* signifies praise. Thus, he says, "the enlightenment factor is praised and excellent," meaning that its purpose is indeed beautiful.
“*Abhinibbattetīti*” means he produces [it] by way of a distinguished state; it expresses a state of excellence.
Having said, “Some explain thus,” the words beginning with “*Te hi*” were spoken in order to show two other kinds of seclusion (*viveka*) besides the three kinds of seclusion already mentioned there.
Among those, first at the moment of *jhāna*, it is based on the seclusion of suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*) by way of its function; at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*),...
“Depending on his inclination, he develops [the mind] based on the seclusion of subsided [defilements]. Therefore he said: “I shall enter and dwell in the unsurpassed liberation.
In this context, by the inclusion of the kasiṇa-jhānas, the non-arising [of defilements] should also be understood as being included, due to the certainty regarding each respective stage.
The commentary on the Himavanta Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Kāya Sutta 183.
"It stands by means of this" is *ṭhiti*, meaning a cause. The fourfold condition—known as kamma, temperature, consciousness, and nutriment—is the basis for its standing;
thus it is called *paccayaṭṭhitiko*. Indeed, the terms *āhāra* and *paccaya* have the same meaning. "Even beauty" refers to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
It is a condition; because it proceeds by way of the beautiful (*subha*) toward what is actually foul (*asubha*), it is called "the beautiful.

For that reason, because it serves as the sign (*nimitta*) for another sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) that proceeds [based on it], it is called "the sign of the beautiful" (*subhanimitta*). "Of the beautiful" means of the beautiful as previously described.
"The object too" means that even an object such as a visible form (*rūpa*), when apprehended by way of the beautiful or by way of the desirable, is the sign of the beautiful.
In the manner already stated. "Inappropriate attention" (*anupāya-manasikāra*) is attention that is not a means for the desired welfare and happiness;

for that very reason, it is "attention to a wrong path," which is unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). "In that" refers to both kinds of the sign of beauty (*subha-nimitta*)—namely, that which has been defined as consisting of sensual desire and that which serves as its object.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is simply stated as "in the beautiful object" (*subhārammaṇe*).

It is said: "There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is stated that the discourse showing the nutriment for the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is clear;
thus it is said: "In this way, the application should be understood for all the hindrances.

Hostility (*paṭigha*) is also the sign of hostility (*paṭighanimitta*), because it serves as the sign for what arises later based on what arose previously. It has hostility as its object (*paṭighārammaṇa*).
By name, there are nineteen conditioned states that serve as bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*). "Discontent" (*arati*) is the lack of delight in remote lodgings and the like.

"Weariness" (*ukkaṇṭhitā*) is the state of being weary. "In remote places" (*pantesu*) means in distant or secluded places. "In higher wholesome states" (*adhikusalesu*) refers to the phenomena of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

Discontent is the opposite of delight. "State of discontent" (*aratitā*) is the mode of not delighting. "Lack of delight" (*anabhirati*) is the state of lacking delight. "Non-delighting" (*anabhiramaṇā*)...
The aspect of non-delight (*anabhiramaṇākāra*). "Distress" (*ukkaṇṭhitā*) is the aspect of being distressed. "Agitation" (*paritassitā*) is the agitation that occurs by way of distress itself.
It is adventitious, not established by intrinsic nature. "Bodily languor" (*kāyālasiya*) is the state of laziness in the body.

However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated: "Lethargy (*tandī*) is natural laziness. "Declares" means [he declares] the occurrence of contraction due to conditions such as excessive cold and so forth.
[The text] demonstrates this. With reference to this, it was said in the *Kilesavatthuvibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Bases of Defilements):

"Languor" (*tandī*) is natural laziness. "Languor-ness" (*tandiyanā*) is the mode of being languid. "State of being overcome by languor" (*tandimanakatā*) is the state of the mind being overwhelmed by languor. The state of one who is lazy is "laziness" (*ālasya*). The mode of being lazy is "laziness-ness" (*ālasyāyanā*).
The state of one who has become lazy is "state of having become lazy" (*ālasyāyitattaṃ*). Thus, by all these [terms]...
By these terms, physical lethargy due to the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*) is described.
"Due to the influence of the defilements" means due to delusion (*sammoha*). "Bending of the body" (*kāyavinamana*) is the bending of the body into an unsightly posture.
"Stretching" (*jambhana*) is quivering. "Repeated stretching" is *vijambhanā*. "Bending forward" (*ānamanā*) is leaning forward; "bending backward" (*vinamanā*) is leaning backward.
*Bhamanā* means bending; *sannamanā* means bending all around.
*Paṇamanā* refers to raising the body upright, just as a weaver who has risen from his loom takes hold of whatever remains above and straightens his body.
*Byādhiyakaṃ* means the state of having an arisen illness. Thus, by all these terms, only the shaking of the body due to the defilements is described.

"Burning from food" (*bhattapariḷāha*) is the arising of a feverish distress due to food. "Having eaten" (*bhuttāvissa*) means one who has eaten. "Stupefaction from food" (*bhattamucchā*) is a sickness caused by food;
for through having eaten too much, one becomes as if fallen into a swoon. "Exhaustion from food" (*bhattakilamatha*) is a state of weariness caused by eating.
"Burning from food" (*bhattapariḷāha*) is the distress of food; for in one who has eaten until full, a burning distress arises.
One becomes as if with impaired faculties; the body grows weary. "Bodily sluggishness" (*kāyaduṭṭhulla*) refers to the body’s lack of functional efficiency due to the food one has eaten.

"The state of the mind’s sinking" (*cittassa līyanākāro*) is the occurrence of contraction in the mind regarding its object. "The mind’s lack of health" (*cittassa akalyatā*) is the state of illness of the mind.
One who is ill is called "unwell. Thus it is said: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. "Lack of functional efficiency" (*akammaññatā*)...
The state of unworkability, which is designated as "mental illness" (cittagelañña). "Sloth" (olīyanā) is the mode of sloth.
Even the mind engaged in the postures (iriyāpathika-citta), by virtue of which one is unable to maintain the posture and becomes sluggish, is referred to as "sloth" with reference to that mode.
The second term is augmented by a prefix. "Languid" (līna) means having reached a state of contraction due to a lack of expansion.
The other two are descriptions by way of aspect (*ākāra*). *Thinana* is non-exertion due to lack of expansion; it is the state of not being gathered or not being supported.
*Thiyanākāro* is the aspect of being lethargic (*thiyanā*). *Thiyitattaṃ* is the aspect of that which is lethargic; the meaning is "lack of expansion.
*Cetaso avūpasamo* is the lack of tranquility of the mind, its state of not being settled. Therefore he said: "the aspect of non-tranquility" (*avūpasantākāro*).

As for its meaning: this state of non-quiescence is, in fact, precisely restlessness-and-worry (uddhacca-kukkucca) in meaning, because its intrinsic nature is distraction and it is a cause of distraction.
As for the "phenomena that are the objects of doubt," these refer to the eight bases of doubt mentioned in such passages as "he is doubtful about the Buddha."

Phenomena (dhammā). Because doubt arises as a successive object-condition (*uggahaṇapaccaya*), just like ill-will and so forth, therefore only the object that serves as the basis for doubt is shown by the phrase "phenomena that are the objects of doubt.
Because a previously arisen doubt becomes a condition for a subsequent doubt, therefore doubt itself is also a phenomenon that serves as the basis for doubt.
[These] should be understood. Herein, this is the etymological analysis: they "stand" or "proceed" in these [objects], thus they are *ṭhānīyā*;

doubt itself is the standing-point, thus it is *vicikicchā-ṭhānīyā*. However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), taking into account that the object also serves as a specific condition therein, it is said:
"Sensual desire and doubt—these two states are spoken of by way of their objects. [This refers to] the sign of the beautiful (*subha-nimitta*).
For this was said with reference merely to the state of being a condition;

nevertheless, just as it is stated that "ill-will is mentioned by way of decisive support (upanissaya) by treating even aversion as the sign of aversion," so too can it be understood that sensual desire is mentioned by way of decisive support by treating the beautiful as the sign of the beautiful.
The remaining factors are sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and worry.
In this context, sloth and torpor are a condition for one another by way of co-nascence and so forth; likewise for restlessness and remorse.
Since there is nothing at all to be said regarding their status as conditions by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), he says: "by way of co-nascence and decisive support.
For mindfulness (*sati*) is defined by such passages as "the four foundations of mindfulness" as the act of recollecting various phenomena.
It occurs; therefore, those states are called "factors conducive to the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
And even with respect to supramundane states, it occurs in that same way by means of grasping them through hearsay and so forth.
Hence it is said: "by mindfulness," and so on. Skill is called wisdom (*paññā*); that which arises from that is "born of skill. "Having blameless happiness as their result" means they are blameless.
"Having been offered, they ripen into a pleasant result"—by these two phrases, he shows wholesome states (kusala-dhamma) in terms of their condition, intrinsic nature, function, and fruit.
This same method applies to the description of unwholesome states (akusala) as well. "Blameworthy" means censurable; "blameless" means not censurable.
"Inferior" means base; "exalted" means superior. "Black" means dark and impure; "white" means bright and pure. The word *paṭibhāga*...
In the first instance, the meaning should be understood as a similar category; in the second, as an opposing category; and in the third, as an opposing category that is to be restrained.
Because the energy that arises through the state of being an undertaking for wholesome action possesses the nature of fortitude (*dhiti*), it is called an "element" (*dhātu*);
thus he said, "The 'element of initiative' is the energy of the initial undertaking. Energy that has acquired practice, having reached the stage of power, [proceeds further].
It is said, "it disperses the opposites," because it has emerged from indolence; thus it is "the element of emergence (nikkamadhātu)," being more powerful than that.
It has reached a state of being sharp, sharper, and so forth, capable of dispersing opposing states that are themselves increasingly intense;
thus it is said, "it is the element of exertion (parakkamadhātu)" because it advances to ever higher stages, and is therefore even more powerful than that.

They are called *ṭhānīya* because they stand (*tiṭṭhati*) and proceed (*pavattati*) therein; that is, they are the objective phenomena (*ārammaṇadhammā*). Regarding the phrase "factors conducive to the joy factor of enlightenment" (*pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīya*), it means "the objective phenomena for joy.
Since joy itself may also be described in that way by virtue of its successive arising, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*: "That very thing is the name for joy itself."
"Tranquility of distress" (*darathapassaddhi*): "Distress" (*daratha*) is the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*); that by which this is calmed is "tranquility of distress.

Through tranquility of body, there is the calming of the material body just as there is the calming of the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling; through tranquility of mind, there is the calming of the mind alone.
For this very reason, the Blessed One has stated here that it is twofold, just as in the case of lightness and the other [qualities].
Likewise, when it is apprehended after having been observed in its concentrated aspect, serenity itself is the sign of serenity, as is the counterpart-sign which has become its object.
That which has various peaks is "byagga," meaning distraction; for it is said to have the essence of instability and to be manifested as wavering.
Because it is the opposite of what is distracted due to its state of one-pointedness, it is "abyagga," namely, concentration. It is that.
The phrase "the sign" (nimitta) should be explained as before. Therefore, he said:

"It is a synonym for that very [state]. Whether it be the neutral aspect to be grasped by not attending to the desirable or undesirable aspects of the object, or the neutral aspect that previously arose through the cultivation of the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga)—both these two kinds of neutrality are intended here as the objective phenomena (ārammaṇa-dhamma) of equanimity.
He said: "In terms of meaning, however, it should be understood that equanimity consists of those states which are the basis for equanimity.
They are described by way of their object because the object itself serves as their specific condition. The remaining four states are energy and so forth;
for in their case, a decisive support (upanissaya) alone is required as the predominant factor.
