The commentary on the Kāya-sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Sīla-sutta: 184.
The supramundane virtue (*lokuttara-sīla*) of one whose taints are destroyed consists of right speech, right action, and right livelihood as included within the paths and fruits.

The other factors, such as volition and so forth, have reached the characteristic of virtue (*sīla*). However, mundane virtue (*lokiya-sīla*) is comprised within functional-ineffective (*kiriya-abyākata*) consciousness;
it consists of the virtue of conduct (*cāritta-sīla*), for there is no possibility of the virtue of restraint (*vāritta-sīla*), because there is an absence of occurrence by way of abstention.
Some say: "Virtue belonging to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-sīla*) is mundane virtue."

"Vision by the eye" means seeing with the eyes. "Vision of the characteristic" means the vision of the individual characteristics (*paccattalakkhaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), through the full understanding of knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), and the vision of the general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) such as impermanence, through the full understanding by investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*).

For even one who abandons [defilements] is said to "see" them by way of their aspect as things to be abandoned. The "suchness-characteristic" (*tathalakkhaṇa*) of Nibbāna is [seen] by means of the Path and the Fruits.
"Seeing" refers to penetration; furthermore, seeing the earth-kasiṇa and so forth by means of jhāna, as well as seeing forms by means of the direct knowledges (abhiññā), is indeed "knowledge-seeing.
However, "eye-seeing" is what is intended here, because hearing and waiting upon are mentioned separately later on.
"Waiting upon for the sake of questions" means waiting upon by way of asking questions, as opposed to approaching for the purpose of some other task.
It is because they are illuminated by the mere act of approaching [the noble ones].

To show that what is called "recollection of the noble ones" (ariyānaṃ anussati) is by way of their qualities, and specifically that it is the recollection of qualities such as virtue (sīla) exactly as they are through the medium of attending to the instructions received from them, the phrase beginning with "jhāna-vipassanā" was stated.
"In the presence of others only" means in the presence of those belonging to the Teaching (sāsanika) who are other than the noble ones (ariya).

“Nearby. Therefore he said: “What is called ‘following after the going-forth’ (anupabbajjā). “Among others” means among those other than the members of the Dispensation, such as ascetics and wanderers.
For it is stated there that the going-forth of the Noble Ones is not called “following after the going-forth.
There were about one hundred thousand [monks] because of the Great Elder’s all-encompassing grace (samantapāsādikattā). “In the island of Laṅkā,” etc., refers to the head of the support (nissaya).
It is the observation of dependence. For the going forth was not obtained from the island, but rather from the teacher residing on the island.
[Mahinda]...pe... "They go forth" means they go forth as part of his retinue.
"He remembers" means he reflects upon and takes that Dhamma of advice and instruction into his mind. "He strikes with thought" means again and again...

By means of reflection (*parivitakka*), one brings that purpose to completion through the accomplishment of thought (*vitakka*). "Is undertaken" (*āraddha*) means it has been accomplished (*sampādita*).

Furthermore, since that accomplishment is itself fulfillment (*pāripūri*), he says, "it becomes fulfilled" (*paripuṇṇa*). "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the states (*dhamma*) as they have been described.

"By way of the movement of knowledge" (*ñāṇacāravasena*) means by way of the proceeding of knowledge. "Of those various states" (*tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ*) refers to each respective state of instruction (*ovāda*).
Of the material and immaterial phenomena that have arisen. "Characteristic" means both the specific characteristic (*visesalakkhaṇa*) and the general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).
"Investigates" means he arrives at an analysis such as, "This is material form; this much is material form," and so forth.

"And establishes knowledge" means he brings forth knowledge [regarding them] as "impermanent, moving, perishable, and subject to dissolution," and so forth. "He engages in inquiry... and so on... by way of the sequence of the sevenfold materiality and the sevenfold immateriality.
One arrives at *sammasana* (comprehension) by seeing impermanence and so forth as if through direct personal experience (*paccakkha*) of insight (*vipassanā*).

"Both of these" refers to the two points mentioned as the benefits of the fruit. They are identical in meaning because they are merely different modes of expression (*pariyāyasadda*). "Early on" (*paṭikacca*) means beforehand.
"At the time of death" (*maraṇakāle*) means near the time of death; for this locative case is used in the sense of proximity, as he says: "at the time close to death."
Thus, it is threefold according to whether the knowledge is sharp, medium, or dull. Therefore he said, "In [aeons] with a lifespan of a thousand kappas," and so forth.
One who attains *parinibbāna* after having struck (upahacca-parinibbāyī) is so called because they attain *parinibbāna* after having passed beyond the midpoint of their lifespan.

"In any [of these]" means in any one among the Aviha heavens and so forth. "By means of application" (*sappayogena*) means by means of the application consisting of the mental formations of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

The meaning is: "together with the practice of insight" (*vipassanāpayoga*). One whose stream of the Path flows only upwards within the plane of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsabhūmi*) is an "upward-streamer" (*uddhaṃsota*).
Because one goes to the Akaniṭṭha existence by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), one is an "Akaniṭṭha-goer" (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*).
Even while existing in the Aviha and other [Pure Abodes], a person who is destined exclusively for upward movement is indeed called an "Akaniṭṭha-goer."

It is said: “There are five [types], including the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm. The word *tesaṃ* (of them) is used in the genitive case for the purpose of specification (*niddhāraṇe*).

Although the noble plane is indeed produced even in the lower realms and so forth due to the state of being an “upstream-goer,” nevertheless, without taking the lifespan in those planes into account, his lifespan of sixteen thousand eons should be understood as being by way of the lifespan specifically in the Akaniṭṭha existence. “Seven...”
Because it is said, "The fruits are the benefits to be expected," it is stated that "the insight prior to the path of Arahatta is called the enlightenment factors.
Since their coexistence is found even among all seven, it is stated that "they are neither before nor after, but exist within a single moment of consciousness.
This is understood from the expression "at that time" (tasmiṃ samaye) which occurs here and there in the Pāḷi.
However, because the factors of enlightenment have diverse intrinsic natures, it is said that they "have diverse characteristics.
The commentary on the Sīla Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Vattha Sutta.
185. "The enlightenment factor of mindfulness"—if such a thought occurs to me, it means that the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is indeed the best, the highest, the most excellent;

therefore, thinking "I shall dwell having entered into the attainment of fruition under the heading of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness," if such a thought occurs to me in the prior stage—that is the meaning.
"It is immeasurable"—if such a thought occurs to me regarding this very enlightenment factor of mindfulness...

"It is 'immeasurable' because of the total absence of defilements that create limits and because it has immeasurable phenomena as its object"—thus does this occur to me through non-delusion within the attainment.

"It is 'perfectly complete' because it is well fulfilled by the completion of development"—thus does this occur to me through non-delusion within the attainment. "It 'persists'" refers to the attainment with its temporal limit.
The mindfulness enlightenment factor stands by way of its persistence through being included therein, acting as a support.

"Non-attention to arising" means by not attending to, that is, by not giving mental focus to, arising. And here, under the heading of "arising," it is the conditioned formations themselves that possess arising which are intended.
"Non-arising" refers to Nibbāna, because of the absence of arising in it and because it is free from those things that possess arising.

"Proceeding" refers to the proceeding of kamma-result (*vipākappavatta*). "Not proceeding" is *nibbāna*, by way of its being the opposite of that. "Sign" (*nimitta*) is the sign of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). "Signless" (*animitta*) is *nibbāna*.

By the term "conditioned" (*saṅkhāra*), there is the grasping of conditionality alone, through not specifying [the specific stages of] arising and so forth. "Unconditioned" (*visaṅkhāra*) is *nibbāna*.
Because it has been brought to mind, the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*) proceeds from the moment it was brought to mind, starting from that point.
"It remains. "In eight ways" means by eight causes. "He knows" means he understands at the time of emerging from the attainment (*samāpatti*).

"In eight ways" means that the Elder understands one who is passing away—both as one who passes away through non-abiding by way of attainment and as one who passes away by means of the eight ways mentioned, which are the opposites of the aforementioned modes, such as the advertence to arising (*uppādāvajjana*) and so forth, as well as the advertence to non-arising (*anuppādāvajjana*) and so forth.
"Factors of enlightenment pertaining to the fruit" (phalabojjhaṅgā) means the factors of enlightenment included within the attainment of the fruit. But do they arise separately?
To this he says, "When," and so forth. "Making it the head" means making it the primary or the best.
"Following that" means following after that, namely, following the mindfulness factor of enlightenment. And that is done by way of reviewing the Dhamma after having made it thus.
Some, however, say: "Having performed that reflection and so forth.
The commentary on the Vatthasutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Bhikkhusutta.

186. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of awakening" (*bodhāya*): here, "awakening" (*bodha*) means the act of waking up (*bujjhana*). Asking "Of what [is it]? or "By what?", he says, "For the sake of awakening to what?
Having stated this, he speaks the passage beginning with "by the path" (*maggena*) to demonstrate that. They lead to awakening to Nibbāna by means of the path;
they lead to awakening to the state of having accomplished the task through review. In the first alternative, it refers to the clear realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).

Since this has already been shown, he states the second alternative, "or by the path," for one who is not satisfied with that. By the phrases "dependent on seclusion" and "dependent on dispassion," all the functions of the path and its fruit are shown.
By the phrase "dependent on cessation," the realization of Nibbāna is indicated.

By the passage beginning with "the mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire," the abandoning of the defilements is shown. And by the phrase "when it is liberated, there is the knowledge 'it is liberated,'" the knowledge [of liberation] is shown.
By the words "it occurs," etc., reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*) is shown.
The commentary on the *Bhikkhu-sutta* is concluded.
6–7. Commentary on the *Kuṇḍaliya-sutta*, etc.
187–188. One whose habit is to sit in an ārāma because he dwells there regularly is an *ārāmanisādī*.
One who moves about having entered into an assembly is a *parisāvacaro*; thus he said, "But whoever," and so forth.

"In this way" means by this manner. "Seizing" (*gahaṇa*) means grasping. By that, he explains the meaning of the question. "Releasing" (*nibbeṭhana*) means releasing from the grasp. By that, [he explains] the answer.
It clarifies the meaning. By this method: with this, he shows the meaning of the word *iti* in the phrase "thus-spoken" (*itivāda*).

One speaks with the intention of reproaching by means of this; thus it is a "speech" (*vāda*), namely, a fault. "There is thus-spoken" means that in this way there is the attribution of a charge against him.
"The release from thus-spoken" means that in this way there is release from that. Thus [he explains] the benefit of the release from such speech by others.

Having shown [the previous point] by way of unraveling what was attributed [to the opponent], he now says, "This is the fault in the question," and so forth, in order to show it by way of pointing out the defect.
"This much of a section" refers to the extent from the beginning up to the words "the three types of good conduct. "This teaching" refers to this very instruction.
“This teaching proceeds in the manner beginning with ‘restraint of the faculties’ (indriyasaṃvara). ‘He does not covet’ means he does not long for with covetousness.

‘He does not exult’ means he does not rejoice excessively. ‘It stands firm within its own range’ means it stands, being well-established, by way of concentration upon the object of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Therefore he said ‘well-composed. ‘Well-composed’ means [it is] rightly so by way of non-distraction.”
It is established. "By way of liberation through the meditation subject" means by way of liberation from the hindrances, which are its opposites, through the practice of the meditation subject.
"Well-liberated" means thoroughly liberated. In the sight of that unpleasant form, he is not dejected or discolored;
that is, not dejected or discolored due to defilements or due to hatred. His mind is not stiff, his mind is not rigid; for it is through stiffness that the mind [becomes rigid].
It is rigid, not supple. "With a mind that is not dejected" means having a mind free from fault due to the absence of that state of dejection which arises through mental distress (*domanassa*).
"With a mind that is not putrid" means having a mind cooled by the absence of ill will (*byāpāda*).
In these six doors, there are eighteen types of misconduct (*duccarita*), each divided into bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct.

In order to show these by way of classification, the passage beginning with “How? was stated. Therein, the phrase “when a desirable object has come into the range [of the senses]” is merely an illustration;

by means of this, one should state the three kinds of misconduct by extending it to “one who arouses hatred when an undesirable object has come into the range,” and likewise “one who arouses delusion when a neutral object has come into the range,” and so forth. This is done by way of the general category of mental misconduct and the rest.
However, it should be understood that there are only three types of misconduct (*duccarita*).
"By way of formal designation" (*paññattivasena*) means by way of a mere collective summary, without referring to the specific underlying basis (*vatthu*), but solely by way of formal designation.

"In the reflective contemplation established through development" (*bhāvanāpaṭisaṅkhāne*) means in the reflective contemplation accomplished by development; the sense is "in the reflective contemplation by means of development."
"These" refers to the objects of the six doors as previously described. "Misconducts" refers to the causes of misconduct.

"For one who stands in non-reflection, having performed misconducts as if they were good conduct"—"transforms" means he turns them around; not producing misconducts therein, he brings about good conduct.
"In this way" means in the manner thus described. The restraint of the faculties... [and so on]... should be understood.
Because the three types of good conduct are accomplished by way of achieving restraint of the sense faculties. Therefore he said, "To this extent," and so forth.
"To this extent" means from the beginning up to the phrase "fulfilling the three types of good conduct.

Restraint of the sense faculties as morality that guards virtue means that the morality of restraint of the sense faculties is explained as that which guards the fourfold purity of morality (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
But how is it that this very thing becomes its protector? Because it serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for successive arising.
"The three kinds of virtue" refers to the virtues consisting of restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and dependence on the requisites.
"Mixed with the supramundane" means that they are both mundane and supramundane. "Of the seven factors of enlightenment" refers to the seven supramundane factors of enlightenment.
Regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*): the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) are their root and constitute the preliminary stage. With reference to these, it was said:
"Kundaliya, the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. "Those too" refers to the aforementioned foundations of mindfulness.
The statement that "the factors of enlightenment are rooted in the foundations of mindfulness" means specifically that the factors of enlightenment are rooted in mundane foundations of mindfulness.

Regarding the phrase *pubbabhāgā vā*: here some adopt the reading *pubbabhāgā ca* and explain the meaning as "both the supramundane (*lokuttara*) factors mentioned previously and those belonging to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).

As for the phrase *vijjāvimuttimūlakā*: the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) spoken of thus—"O Kuṇḍaliya, the seven enlightenment factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation (*vijjāvimutti*)"—are indeed supramundane, because they coexist with true knowledge and liberation.
The commentary on the Kuṇḍaliya-sutta and others is finished.
8. Commentary on the Upavāna-sutta: 189.
Regarding the term *paccattaṃ*, it is an instrumental designation; thus he says, "by himself. "Only while making" means while producing.

Thus. "Well-liberated through liberation from the meditation subject" means it is well-freed from the hindrances because they have been distanced by the attention directed toward the meditation subject.
"Having made it the goal" means having made the attention of development supreme, being one who desires [it] with the thought, "A great benefit has indeed arisen for me."
9. Commentary on the First Arising Sutta (Paṭhamauppannasutta-vaṇṇanā) 190.
By the passage beginning "At the manifestation of the Tathāgata," it is shown that the acquisition of the jewels of the factors of enlightenment occurs at the very time of the Buddha’s appearance.
The commentary on the Mountain Chapter (Pabbatavagga-vaṇṇanā) is concluded.
2. Gilānavagga 1–3.
Commentary on the *Pāṇasutta* and others, §§192–194.
“Of whom” means of those beings. “There are four postures” means they are obtained through the acquisition of the bodily parts conducive to them.

This refers to the statement: "They assume the four postures. Because of the statement beginning with "dependent on seclusion," it is said that these are the "path factors of enlightenment accompanied by insight" (*vipassanā*).
The second and third [sections] have their meaning explained in plain terms, as they follow the method already stated below.
4–10. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Sick, etc.
195–201. It became pure, as the disturbance of the discordant elements was stilled. Therefore he said: "As on a lotus leaf... having turned back, it went away.
This same method applies to the fourth [simile], since it is identical in both text and meaning to the fifth and sixth.
"By the contact of the wind from the poison-tree" means by the contact of the wind dependent upon the poison-tree. "Mandāsītajaro" (slightly cold and feverish).
"Easy to warm" means [one who] is cold-natured. "The rest" refers to what remains after what has been stated. "In all cases" refers to the four [cases], beginning with the seventh.
The commentary on the Gilānavagga is finished.
3. Udāyivagga.
1–2. Commentary on the *Bodhāya-sutta* and others. 202–203.
By what reason indeed are they called "factors for awakening" (*bujjhanaka-aṅga*), and how do they receive the designation of being "factors of a person who awakens"?
The mixed factors of awakening (*missaka-bojjhaṅga*) have been explained; [now] the path-factors of awakening together with insight (*sahavipassanā-magga-bojjhaṅga*).
"Having been told" means: the section on the Dhamma has been told because it was spoken by defining it merely by way of enumeration;
it is not a section defined by a change of subject matter, nor is it a section defined by insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and so forth.
3–5. Commentary on the *Ṭhāniyasutta* and others.
204–206. Because they are the objects where one becomes infatuated by sensual lust, they are called "objects of sensual lust";
thus he said, "of the objective phenomena. Since it was stated, "by frequenting mental attention," it is said that "it is spoken of solely in terms of the object.
By the phrase "the aforementioned limit," it is shown that the meaning here is obtained not only by way of the object, but also by way of the decisive support (upanissaya).
This is shown. For in the second sutta of the first chapter, the meaning is demonstrated by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) alone.
The mixed factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are spoken of because they are taught without distinction. "In non-decline" means leading to non-decline through the three trainings (*sikkhā*).
6–7. Commentary on the *Taṇhakkhaya-sutta* and others.
207–208. "He will ask me thus"—with this intention, the Blessed One concluded his teaching.
It is "expanded" because it has reached full development through its broad extension; it is "greatness" because it has attained magnitude by means of that very cultivation.
For that very reason, it possesses the measure of increase. Since it arises from the removal of the hindrances, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is thereby eliminated.
He said: "By means of the removal of the hindrances and the absence of ill-will. "Rooted in craving" means having craving as its condition.
For whatever is accompanied by craving, or even if not accompanied by it, yet is produced in dependence upon craving—all that is rooted in craving.
It is abandoned through abandonment by non-arising. This is due to the destruction of craving and the rest alone, not through the destruction of those formations. By these...
By means of the words "the destruction of craving" and so forth. 8. Commentary on the Discourse on Factors Conducive to Penetration (Nibbedhabhāgiya-sutta).
209. They penetrate, thus they are "penetrations" (*nibbedha*); the Dharma, the Vinaya, and so forth, possess the quality of penetration. Because they are included therein...
That which has reached the portion of penetration (*nibbedha-bhāga*) is "pertaining to penetration" (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*); thus he said, "belonging to the section of penetration.
By means of a mind established through cultivation. Having included the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*) as well, they are called "mixed path factors of enlightenment" (*magga-bojjhaṅgā*).

"By them" refers to the mind cultivated by those factors of enlightenment. Alternatively, the "mind established through cultivating those factors of enlightenment" is the resultant consciousness (*phala-citta*).

Therefore, it is exclusively the supramundane that has been produced. As for the phrase "that too," since even the fruition-consciousness is dependent on the path by virtue of its immediate succession to the path, it is appropriate to speak of it as being mixed, because it is said [in the Sutta] that "they lead to enlightenment.
9. Commentary on the Ekadhamma Sutta (The Discourse on the One Thing)

210. "Fetters" (vinibandhā) refers to the bonds known as the fetters of sensual lust and so forth. "Grasping by way of final determination" (pariniṭṭhapetvā gahaṇa) means grasping in the manner of having finalized [the object] as if swallowing it.
10. Commentary on the Udāyisutta: 211.

"Much done" (bahukata) is said to mean great service or great respect; that which has no such "much done" is "not much done" (abahukata), meaning one who has not performed great service or shown great respect.
It is said that the Dhamma, when arising, is as if turning upright, and when ceasing, is as if turning upside down; thus it is stated: "Upright refers to arising (udaya);
upside down refers to passing away (vaya). "Turning over" means [viewing things] as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self.
At the conclusion [of the discourse], it says: "For this path has been attained by you, Udāyi, which will lead you... to suchness."

In this context, the word of the Blessed One should be seen as the proof. "Dwelling in each respective mode" means dwelling in the mode of comprehension, that is, in the dwelling of insight (*vipassanā-vihāra*).
"For the sake of becoming such" refers to the reviewing of the state of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). Therefore he said:
"'Birth is destroyed'... [etc. ...showing this, he spoke thus."
The commentary on the Udāyivagga is finished.
4. The Nīvaraṇavagga: 3–4.
Commentary on the Upakkilesasutta and following.
214–215. “Neither radiant” means not possessing radiance. “Of a nature to break” refers to its state of being brittle when heated and struck.
“The remaining iron” refers to all types of iron mentioned as the remainder: natural iron (*jātiloha*), mixed iron (*vijātiloha*), and artificial iron (*kittimaloha*).
Regarding the phrase “by not allowing it to arise,” one might ask: does this not apply even to mundane wholesome consciousness?
Is it because they do not allow for the arising [of purity] in one who is already thoroughly purified that they are called "defilements"? This is true;
however, in whatever mental continuum the hindrances have gained a foothold, there is no possibility even for sublime wholesome states, let alone supramundane wholesome states.
Yet, limited wholesome states do arise according to their respective conditions. For when the hindrances have subsided within a continuum, [wholesome states] can arise.
It is unpurified; it is called "defiled" like a lamp whose oil and so forth remain in a lamp-stand that is unpurified.
Furthermore, showing that these are defilements precisely because they do not allow [the path] to arise in its true sense, he said, "At the moment when," and so forth.
Its state of being pulverized and scattered should be understood by way of its having reached a state of distraction regarding the object.
“They do not obstruct” means they do not obstruct by way of not permitting wholesome states to arise; rather, they exist for the sake of their arising.
“They do not conceal” means they do not bind. “Of the four-plane consciousness” refers to the wholesome consciousness of the fourth plane, because it is untainted by those [defilements].
8. Commentary on the Āvaraṇanīvaraṇa Sutta 219.
Wisdom is weak and not powerful because it is defiled by its opposites. Therefore, he said: "Dull and unrefined.
The five hindrances are distant because of the absence of obstruction. "That very joy" refers to that which has arisen upon hearing the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress].
Rapture (*pīti*). By not abandoning it through observing its mode of arising at that time, and by its repeated production, he said:
“Having suppressed the five hindrances. With reference to this, he meant: “Even for so many days they do not perish;
having obtained the requisite conditions, that Dhamma-rapture brings about distinction. It is with reference to this meaning that he said: “For him, the five...”
"It is said: 'At that time, the hindrances do not exist,' and so forth. 'Associated with rapture and gladness' means having rapture and gladness as their conditions.
'They vanish' means they vanish because they proceed by way of the condition of cessation. Although they may arise again by way of a similar condition...
it is so called because they proceed by way of accomplishing their function."
9. Commentary on the *Rukkhasutta* (The Tree Sutta) 220.
*Abhiruhanakā*: those that grow by overcoming nearby trees. *Aṭṭhikacchaka*: a thicket with many bones. It is named *kapitthana* because its fruit resembles the *kapittha* (wood-apple).
10. Commentary on the *Nīvaraṇasutta* (The Hindrances Sutta)
221. They cause blindness because they obstruct the eye of wisdom; for it is said of them, “They make one sightless and bring about the cessation of wisdom.
It is called *vighāta* (affliction) because it strikes down (*vi-hanati*) or oppresses (*vi-bādhati*); thus he says, “Belonging to affliction means belonging to suffering.
They do not lead to nibbāna, hence they are *anibbāna-saṃvattanikā*. Only mixed factors of enlightenment are mentioned here, because those pertaining to the preliminary stage have been discussed.
The commentary on the Chapter on Hindrances is finished.
5. The Chapter on Wheel-turning Monarchs. 1.
Commentary on the Sutta on Differentiation.

222. They are called *vidhā* because they are being arranged (*vidhīyanti*). Since they are portions or sections of pride and so forth, he says, "three sections of pride" (*tayo mānakoṭṭhāsā*). Because of burning or establishing oneself in such and such ways—namely, by burning or establishing oneself in various modes such as "I am superior," etc., or because of that which is to be established.
2. Commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta 223.

One who shines, glows, and is beautiful through the attainment of glory is a king (*rājā*). [He is so called] by means of what are known as generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.
By means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*). "He delights" means he causes them to rejoice. "Exalted" means having arisen, having been produced, because it travels here and there.
"He turns the wheel" means he sets in motion the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*). "A place for deities" means a place for deities worthy of worship.

"In the sense of being honored" means by way of its state of being worthy of worship. There is no price [to be set] because of the presence of treasures established through the power of merit accumulated over a long period of time.
"Than others" means than the treasures that have become the possession of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). "In the world" means in the human world;
by this, he excludes other worlds. By using the term "existing," he excludes the past and the future.
The intention is that Buddhas arise only occasionally and rarely, whereas wheel-turning monarchs mostly arise in that very same [world]. "Anoma" means not inferior.
[The word] *ukkaṭṭha* [refers to the wheel]. The remaining [items] are the jewels (*ratana*).
In that context, *tattha* is a particle used for introducing a statement, referring to that expression concerning manifestation.

Having said "it is improper," he spoke the passage beginning with "for it has arisen" while clarifying the intended meaning therein. This is because the term "wheel-turning monarch" (*cakkavatti*) depends upon the fixed order of those jewels.
"By necessity" means exclusively. It attains the status of being expressible through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) regarding what is yet to be, just as with what has already occurred; for example:

"The Buddha went to Rājagaha. "One who has acquired a name" refers to a distinguished person who is desirable and has acquired the conventional designation (*samaññā*) of "wheel-turning monarch" (*cakkavatti*) in the world.
"Because it is a term for original arising" refers to the first appearance of the phrase "with the manifestation of the wheel-turning monarch."
Also from the scriptural statement. Now, explaining that meaning, he says, "For whoever... and so forth.
For whoever is a Wheel-turning King (cakkavatti-rāja), because the Wheel-treasure arises with his arising, the name "Wheel-turner" arises for him in this way.
However, the phrase "he will turn the wheel" is stated according to the method of taking up the non-arising of the treasures, without regard for the fixed order (niyāma) of their appearance.
The perception arises: "He is a wheel-turning monarch. "One alone" means that the wheel-treasure alone appears first.

Since the designation "wheel-turning monarch" occurs for the king when that [wheel] has appeared, and subsequently the other treasures appear, this statement—"with the appearance of the wheel-turning monarch, there is the appearance of the treasures"—is spoken both on account of the appearance of many [treasures] and by way of the plural number.
This is the classification of meaning known as "causality. From "manifestation" (*pātubhāvā*) means "by way of manifestation.

It is stated that the equipment of merit (*puññasambhāra*), by virtue of its distinct continuity, is also, in a figurative sense, a decisive support cause (*upanissaya-hetu*) for the [Three] Jewels. This is indeed appropriate, because it is consistent with the reasoning already stated.
"Intention" (*adhippāya*) refers to that which possesses an intended meaning to be expressed; it is a designation for the meaning, [and thus] in brief, it is "intention."

This is the summary of the intended meaning. Because the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) is accomplished through the power of the wheel-treasure (cakraratna), it is said, "of one capable of giving.
Because it moves over an area measuring one *yojana*, it is called "darkness measuring one *yojana*. The ellipsis to be supplied is:
"of one who stands having avoided the sixfold defects, such as being excessively tall or excessively short."

It is "possessed of the body of Dhamma" (dhammakāyūpapanna) in the sense of being the foremost of all phenomena belonging to the four planes, because it functions by way of investigating the destinies of wholesome states;
and because it possesses the nature of a great phenomenon that cannot be abandoned even by Buddhas and others, it is pre-eminent within the body of Dhamma.
Furthermore, it is "exalted" (accuggata) in the sense of being situated above due to its nature as a palace of wisdom, and in the sense of being extensive.

"Vipulaṃ" means vast. "Mahantaṃ" means great due to its magnitude. Because it shatters the continuum of defilements cultivated since beginningless time in a single moment, the synonyms "sīgha," "lahu," and "java" are used.
For it is said, "because of being exclusively wholesome," since [the factors] are included within the categories of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga).
It is stated, "by way of associated [states]" and "by way of the state of light-shattering through joy," as expressed in the passage beginning with "sahajāta-paccayādi."

"The Section on the Dhamma Comprising All" refers to the section on the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga-dhamma), which is described as "comprising all" because it pertains to the four planes of existence.
4–10. Commentary on the *Duppañña-sutta* and others, 225–231.
"Eḷa" means fault; one who is like a mute due to such faults is called an "eḷamūga. Demonstrating this meaning, [the commentator] said: "With the mouth, speech," and so forth.
The commentary on the Cakkavattivagga is finished.
6. Sākacchavagga 1.
Commentary on the Āhārasutta.
232. "By the previous method" means by the method already stated, beginning with "of those states that are bases for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
"Thus" means in the manner now being described. Mindfulness and clear comprehension together constitute *satisampajañña*.

Alternatively, *satisampajañña* is the knowledge that grasps the state of being a teacher (the guide) regarding the "excellent" and so forth during the four postures; it brings about the state of acting with mindfulness in all circumstances.
It conduces to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor.
Just as the abandoning of contrary states and the teaching of corresponding states lead to the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen,

so too does the avoidance of persons devoid of mindfulness, the cultivation of persons who practice with mindfulness, and application and devotion to that [practice] lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor.
This meaning is shown by the passage beginning with “mindfulness and clear comprehension. Fulfillment occurs through the path of Arahantship;
for it is only the Arahant who is called “one who has attained perfection in mindfulness.

Investigation of phenomena (dhamma), or among phenomena—that itself is the enlightenment factor according to the method explained below; [this refers] to that enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.

“Being a questioner” means that, having attended upon a teacher and mastered the five Nikāyas together with their commentaries, one possesses the habit of questioning the meaning of the aggregates and so forth regarding whatever points of difficulty (gaṇṭhiṭṭhāna) occur therein, saying: “Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?
For this reason, he said: “The state of being abundant in [inquiring about] the aggregates... and so forth.”

Regarding "the act of purifying the basis" (*vatthuvisadakiriyā*): because it serves as the locus for the occurrence of mind and mental factors, the body and the robes and so forth associated with it are intended here by the term "basis. Making them such that they bring ease to the mind is the act of making them pure.
Therefore, it is said: "of the internal and external," and so forth. "Accumulated defilement" (*ussannadosa*)...
"With the humors such as wind (vāta) and so forth in excess" means: "smeared with sweat and with the bodily impurity known as filth (jallikā).
By the word "and" (ca), other things that bring affliction to both the body and the mind are included. "Or a lodging" (senāsanaṃ vā):
by the word "or" (vā), the inclusion of alms-bowls and so forth should be understood. Whether it be non-objective (avisaya) or objective (visayabhūta). How?
"Are those [objects] the domain for one devoted to meditation? This was said by way of the mental states that arise from time to time.

For those mental states, even though they are accomplished through one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*), lead to a state of impurity regarding the mind and mental factors (*citta-cetasika*) which serve as the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) and so forth.
The word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "knowledge also" (*ñāṇampi*) is used in a collective sense; by it, it is indicated that not only is that [object] the basis (*vatthu*), but...

Now, when that [object] is impure, knowledge is also impure; thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*), it demonstrates that the impurity of the objects entails the impurity of those who possess them, just as the impurity of the support entails the impurity of the supported.
"Equalizing" (*samabhāvakaraṇa*) means making things neither deficient nor excessive in their function. This occurs with respect to the object of faith according to its conditions.

Because the function of resolve (adhimokkha) is more acute while wisdom (paññā) is not yet clear, and because energy (vīriya) and the other factors are slackened due to their lack of supporting strength, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) becomes powerful.

Therefore he said, "the others are weak. Thus, because of the power of the faculty of faith and the weakness of the others, the associated mental states are prevented from falling into the side of indolence (kosajja).
“Exertion” (*paggaha*) means grasping and providing support; it should be connected with the phrase “unable to perform the function of exertion.
“Establishment” (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the act of approaching and remaining upon the object, or non-relinquishment; it is the opposite of distraction.
Alternatively, that by which associated states become undistracted is “non-distraction” (*avikkhepa*). Just as form is seen by the eye, that by which [the mind] perceives things as they truly are...
It sees the nature of the object, yet it is unable to perform that function of seeing because it is overwhelmed by the powerful faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).

For among co-nascent phenomena (*sahajātadhamma*), the accomplishment of their purpose occurs only through the state of having a single flavor (*ekarasa*) as they arise together while exercising lordship (*indaṭṭha*);
it is not otherwise. Therefore, he refers back to the aforementioned point by way of its causal basis.
That is the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).

Regarding "by reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena": for one in whom the faculty of faith has become powerful through the exceptional engagement of resolve (*adhimuccana*) toward the sublime qualities of an object worthy of faith, [this occurs] by way of the analysis of the conditions and the conditionally arisen, and so forth.

By investigating things as they truly are. For when one grasps things in this way through the method of their natural law (*evaṃdhammatā*), according to their own essential nature and intrinsic flavor, there is no expansive resolve (*savipphāro adhimokkho*)—because the activity of wisdom (*paññā*) is preeminent in the thought, "This is the essential nature of these phenomena.
Indeed, among the primary factors, just as when faith is strong there is a weakness of wisdom, so too [when wisdom is strong]... [wisdom is weak].
When there is strength, there is a deficiency of faith. Therefore it is said: "It should be diminished by reflecting on the specific nature of that phenomenon...

and so forth. Likewise, "by not attending" means by not engaging in the practice of meditation in the same manner in which the faculty of faith became strong for one who was devoted to meditation. Here, [the diminution] is twofold with respect to the faculty of faith.

The state of being strong [of the faith faculty] arises either because its own function exceeds that of the others due to a specific condition, or because the functions of energy and the rest are weak.
In this regard, the method for diminishing [the other faculties] is shown in the first alternative;

however, in the second alternative, just as the faith faculty becomes strong through attention while the functions of energy and the rest are weak, so too does it become strong through non-attention while the functions of energy and the rest are weak.
By means of attention that brings about a state of greater clarity, one should diminish the faculty of faith while bringing it to equality with those [other faculties].
In this same manner, the method for diminishing the remaining faculties should be understood.
Regarding the case of the Elder Vakkali: for that venerable one was devoted to faith and had performed his duties there, yet he longed to see the physical body of the Teacher.
While living as a mere lay follower, even though he was exhorted by the Teacher with words such as, "Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this foul body?
Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma sees me," and was directed toward his meditation subject, he did not apply himself to it.
Having been dismissed, he climbed to a precipice in order to cast himself down.
Then the Teacher, while remaining seated as he was, revealed himself by emitting a radiance and said:
“A bhikkhu full of gladness, with confidence in the Buddha’s teaching,
shall attain the state of peace, the bliss that is the stilling of all conditioned formations.”
Having spoken this verse, he said, “Come, Vakkali. At those words, as if sprinkled with the Deathless, he became joyful and elated and applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
However, because his faith was so predominant, he did not enter the path of insight.
Knowing this, the Blessed One purified a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for him to bring about the balancing of his faculties and gave it to him. Then, by the Teacher—
By means of the method of giving, he intensified his insight and attained arahantship through the successive stages of the path. Therefore it is said:

"The story of the Elder Vakkali is the illustration here. "Here" refers to the case where, when the faculty of faith is predominant, the remaining faculties fail to perform their respective functions.
"Distinction of other duties" means the specific duties such as attending upon [the teacher] and so forth.
Regarding "tranquility and so forth," by the word "and so forth," the inclusion of the concentration and equanimity enlightenment factors (sambojjhaṅga) should be understood.

"Should be diminished" means that just as the strength of the faith faculty is diminished by reflecting on the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), so too the excessiveness of the energy faculty is diminished by the cultivation of tranquility and the rest, because they belong to the side of concentration.

Of that [concentration]. For just as the development of energy and the other [faculties] protects the preponderance of the faculty of concentration from falling into indolence, so too does it protect the preponderance of the faculty of energy from falling into agitation; thus it causes [the latter] to be entirely abandoned.
Therefore it is said: "It is to be abandoned by the development of tranquility and the rest. The story of the Elder Soṇa refers to the Elder Sukumāra-Soṇa.
The Story: For that venerable one, having received a meditation subject from the presence of the Teacher and dwelling in the Sītavana forest, thought:
"My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness by means of mere ease; even by wearying the body, the duty of a recluse must be performed.
Thus, resolving upon standing and walking meditation alone, he applied himself to striving, even though blisters arose on the soles of his feet.
While maintaining equanimity toward feeling, he exerted firm energy, yet he was unable to bring about further distinction due to over-exertion of energy.

The Teacher went there, instructed him with the "Lute Simile," and having purified his meditation subject while demonstrating the method for applying balanced energy, He departed for Vulture Peak. The Elder, following the method given by the Teacher, [applied] the balance of energy.
Having performed the sacrifice, he developed insight and, having brought it to preeminence, he was established in Arahantship itself. Therefore it is said:
"The story of the Elder Soṇa should be cited. "In the remaining ones as well" means in the case of the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
"Balance" refers to the state of neither deficiency nor excess between faith and wisdom, and likewise between concentration and energy. Just as...
Indeed, because faith and wisdom are each a primary factor (dhuriyadhamma), it is especially desirable that they do not exceed one another in their respective functions.
For when these two are balanced, absorption (appanā) is achieved;
likewise, when concentration and energy—which belong to the sides of laxity and agitation—are balanced, the associated mental states are mutually supported.
"Because there is no falling into the two extremes, absorption succeeds perfectly.

The passage beginning with "one who has strong faith" is a corroboration, by way of contrast, of the very meaning already stated. Its meaning is as follows: one who possesses strong faith but lacks clear knowledge is one whose faith is superficial;
he is not one whose faith is based on penetration (*aveccappasanna*). For such a person places his confidence in what is not a proper ground, just as, for example...

The disciples of the sectarians. "The side of the kerāṭika" means he resorts to the side of deceit. Overreaching with a wisdom devoid of faith, deceived by mere semblances of reasons, he imagines such things as:
"Merit consisting in giving arises even by the mere arising of the thought, without the relinquishing of the object to be given.
Being thus, his mind ravaged by harsh reasoning, he [rejects] the word of the wise.
It does not take [the medicine], nor does it respond to the instruction. Therefore he said: "Like a disease arising from medicine, it becomes incurable.

And just as here the mutual balance of faith and wisdom brings about welfare while their imbalance brings about harm, so too the mutual balance of concentration and energy brings about welfare, whereas the other [imbalance] brings about harm; such is their state of balance.
It brings about non-distraction; the other brings about distraction. The intention is that it overcomes laziness, and by means of that, one does not fail to reach absorption (*appanā*).

This same method applies here as well regarding the phrase "it overcomes restlessness. "Both of those" refers to the pair consisting of faith and wisdom, and the pair consisting of concentration and energy.
"Should be made equal" means that equality should be established.
“Of one whose work is concentration” means of one whose meditation subject is serenity (*samatha*). “Thus” means this being so; the sense is: when faith has become somewhat strong.
“Having faith” means not thinking, “How can absorption arise by mere attention to ‘earth, earth’?
but rather having faith and generating faith, thinking, “Surely the method spoken by the Fully Enlightened One succeeds. “Having conviction” means...
Entering into the object as it were, by way of resolving upon it, he leaps forward.
Strong one-pointedness is required because concentration is the primary factor in jhāna. "Of both" refers to concentration and wisdom.
Since for one whose function is concentration, the excellence of concentration requires the excellence of wisdom as well, he says "by means of evenness," meaning by way of balance.

The meaning is as follows: "Absorption" (appanā) here refers to mundane absorption (*lokiya-appanā*). For he speaks with apprehension, saying, "It certainly occurs," whereas supramundane absorption (*lokuttara-appanā*) is desired by them precisely through the balancing of those [factors].
As it is said: "He develops serenity and insight coupled together.
If he desires the equality specifically of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy, how then can there be mindfulness?
He said: "But in all cases, it is appropriate that [the faculty] be strong. "In all cases" refers to the five faculties belonging to the side of lethargy (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*).
Taking one portion of those belonging to the side of agitation, he says, "faith, energy, and wisdom. Otherwise, joy (*pīti*) would also have to be included.
For it has been stated thus: "by means of concentration belonging to the side of indolence (*kosajja*)," and not...
“By means of serenity, concentration, and equanimity. *Sati* is mindfulness. One who is appointed to all royal duties is a “minister of all affairs” (*sabbakammika*).
For that reason—for which reason they are desired in every instance—it was said in the commentary. Those who are appointed in every instance are “universal” (*sabbatthika*);

or alternatively, they are to be sought after by means of every factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) belonging to the side of either laxity or agitation, thus they are “universally beneficial” (*sabbatthiya*).
"Beneficial in all respects" means beneficial everywhere. "Mind" refers to wholesome consciousness (*kusala-citta*).
For that, mindfulness is the refuge and the ultimate resort for the attainment of what has not been attained and for the realization of what has not been realized. Therefore he said:

"Manifested as protection," and so forth. "Of those whose wisdom has not penetrated the distinctions of the aggregates and so on" means those whose intellects are not established in the aggregates, sense bases, and other categories, even by way of extensive learning (*pariyatti-bāhusacca*).

For associating with those of great learning brings about knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*). Even one possessing nascent insight (*taruṇa-vipassanā*) is certainly called "wise" because of being established in knowledge consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa*);
thus he said: "Associating with persons... endowed with equal wisdom.
Because of the profundity of the phenomena to be known (*ñeyya-dhamma*), there is a grasping of the profundity of the knowledge that delimits them; thus he said: "In the profound..."

“...of the profound wisdom that occurs regarding the aggregates and so forth. For that object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) is called the "course of profound knowledge" because it must be traversed by such wisdom;
or, the "course of profound knowledge" is the occurrence of that wisdom there in its various modes.
Its "reviewing" is what is meant by the phrase "the reviewing of the distinctions of profound wisdom. Just as one who has attained perfection in mindfulness...
He is indeed an Arahant; thus, even when he has attained the fullness of wisdom, it is said: "The completion of development occurs through the path of Arahantship.
This same method applies to energy and the other factors as well.
Regarding the fivefold tortures of binding and penal servitude in hell, described by the passage beginning with "They thrust a red-hot iron stake into the hand," and so forth:
In such discourses as the *Devadūta-sutta*, it is said that [suffering] occurs first for a being who has been reborn;
because this is stated at the beginning of that [text], he says: "starting from the time of being subjected to the fivefold bond and punishment.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the time of carrying carts, etc.," he includes the times when one is harassed by other humans and animals. "One interval between Buddhas" (*ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ*).
This was stated with reference to beings who are reborn among the *petas* again and again;
or it was stated thus because some *petas*, like certain animals, may likewise possess such long lifespans. For instance, the Naga King Kāla was one who beheld the forms of four Buddhas.
Thus, regarding "one who sees the benefits": "The attainment of all mundane and supramundane distinctions depends solely upon energy. Thus [it is said].
For one whose nature is to see the benefits [of virtue]. "The path of travel" refers to the way leading to Nibbāna together with its preliminary stages.
It is the sequence of the Noble Path accompanied by insight, or the succession of the seven purifications;
for, since it is the way that must be traversed in order to emerge from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it is called the "path of travel."
“Abundant in bodily strength” means intent on nourishing the body. “Alms” refers to the alms-food of the country.
“Honoring the alms” (piṇḍāpacāyanā) is the act of honoring the alms-begging by making the gift-givers perceive the great fruitfulness of their own deed through one’s own proper conduct.
“Taking it out” means taking it out from the bowl-bag. “Hearing that sound” means hearing that [sound] of the female lay devotee...
They say that while standing at the door of the leaf-hut, he heard these words with his divine ear (*dibbasota*) due to his possession of the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhiññā*).
There are three kinds of success: human success, celestial success, and finally, the success of Nibbāna. "Smiling as it were" means:
at the conclusion of his reflection, "I have transcended the suffering of the round of existence without difficulty," he was smiling out of the joy (*pāmojja*) thus arisen.
Avoiding from afar those indolent persons who do not know even the mere name of meditation, who are intent on nourishing the body,
who eat as much as they desire and devote themselves to the pleasures of sleep and so forth, and who engage in worldly talk— this is the avoidance of lazy individuals.
[This is for those] who have initiated energy through the commencement of meditation according to the instruction, “By walking and sitting during the day,” and who possess firm perseverance.
Approaching from time to time and associating with persons who have initiated energy—this is what is meant by the phrase beginning with “having filled the belly.
However, in the *Visuddhimagga*, this pair—“reflection on the greatness of one’s birth” and “reflection on the greatness of one’s fellow celibates”—is not included;
rather, it is “the dispelling of sloth and torpor” and “reflection on the right exertions” that are taken.

Two things are included therein. Among them, the reflection on the right exertions is included specifically by way of seeing their benefits, because it consists in seeing that the attainment of the distinctions of both the mundane and the supramundane depends upon energy.

The dispelling of sloth and torpor is included by way of being intent upon that [dispelling], for the dispelling of sloth and torpor is, in its actual meaning, the state of one who is engaged and devoted to the arousing of energy.

This is indeed established. In this context, it should be understood that the dispelling of sloth and torpor— by means of avoiding indolent persons, associating with persons who have initiated energy,
being intent upon that [energy], and destroying opposing factors— and the reflection on the fear of the states of misery (apāya) and so forth,
are the conditions for the arising of the energy enlightenment factor (vīriyasambojjhaṅga) by way of providing encouragement.
Because access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) is the culmination of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), it is said: "as far as access.
"Pervading the entire body" means pervading the whole body with sublime forms produced by rapture (*pīti*). The construction is:

even for one who is recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) arises, pervading the entire body as far as access. The same applies to the remaining recollections.

And one should apply this also to the reviewing of the Suttantas that inspire confidence (*pasādanīya-suttanta*), because they too belong to that same category by virtue of being bases for liberation (*vimuttāyatana*).
"At such a time" refers to the times mentioned as those of fear from famine and so forth. The statement, "In the attainment...

they do not manifest," is said with reference to the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*); for while there is a partial pacification of formations (*saṅkhāra*), there is also a complete pacification [of them].
Because it proceeds there with wisdom, the attention of development (bhāvanā-manasikāra), being capable of suppressing the defilements, brings about access concentration (upacāra-samādhi);
thus, being endowed with such joy and mental happiness, it leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy (pīti-sambojjhaṅga).
Aridity (lūkhatā) is the state of the heart indicated by the absence of clarity and affection toward inspiring objects. And that...
In this context, it is understood through the failure to show respect and reverence; thus he said, "when a coarse nature is indicated by lack of careful performance.

Tranquility (*passaddhi*)—characterized by the subsiding of agitation in body and mind—is itself the tranquility factor of enlightenment (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*), which constitutes one of the aforementioned factors of enlightenment.
Regarding that factor of enlightenment: "the practice of refined food" means the practice of refined and suitable food.
It should be understood that by the mention of "grasping at comfort in postures," the appropriate postures are included.

For when all three types of posture are practiced appropriately, they bring about pliancy of mind by way of producing fitness in the body, and thus become the cause for both kinds of tranquility (*passaddhi*).
That pleasure and pain found among sentient beings are without cause—this is one extreme.

The view that there is an unequal cause such as a creator god (*issara*) and so forth is the second extreme. Not falling into either of these two extremes, but rather [holding that] "it comes about through one's own respective karma"—this is the middle way of practice.
One whose application is neutral is "one of neutral application" (*majjhattapayoga*);
the state of being such is "neutrality of application" (*majjhattapayogatā*). For this is the cause for the tranquility of the body, which consists in the abandoning of bodily restlessness.

It brings about the two kinds of tranquility (*passaddhi*). By this very fact, it should be understood that avoiding persons whose bodies are agitated and associating with persons whose bodies are tranquil are praised as bringing about those two.

The purification of the physical basis and the balancing of the faculties are said to "bring about wisdom" (*paññāvahā*). They also bring about serenity (*samatha*), and because they bring about serenity, they bring about wisdom; thus it is said: "The purification of the physical basis... [and so on]... should be understood."

Because skill in the means [of meditation] and skill in the development [of the jhānas] do not exist without the state of non-obstruction, and because skill in protection is rooted in them, it is said: "Skill in signs means skill in grasping the kasiṇa sign.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "excessive laxity of energy, etc.," one includes dullness in the application of wisdom and a deficiency in diligence. Its "exertion" is...
The uplifting of that sluggish mind is its raising from the state of sluggishness by means of arousing the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor and the others.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the mind is sluggish, at that time it is the right time for the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor."
It is the time for the development of the energy enlightenment factor; it is the time for the development of the rapture enlightenment factor.
Why is that? Because, monks, a sluggish mind is easily uplifted by these states.
Just as if, monks, a man wishing to kindle a small fire were to take dry...
“If one were to throw dry grass into it, throw dry cow dung into it, throw dry wood into it,
blow upon it with the breath of one’s mouth, and not sprinkle it with dust— would that man be capable of making the small fire blaze up? “Yes, venerable sir.”

And here, it should be understood that the development and arousing of the enlightenment factors beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena factor (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) occurs according to their respective nourishment; this has already been explained immediately above.
By the phrase "through over-exertion of energy, etc.," the word "etc. includes the application of wisdom and strength, as well as excessive elation and agitation.
"Its suppression" means the suppression of that agitated mind by means of arousing the concentration enlightenment factor (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) and the others.
The prevention of an arisen state of agitation. And this was said by the Blessed One:

"But at whatever time, monks, the mind is agitated, that is the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment, that is the time for the development of the concentration factor of enlightenment, that is the time for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment."
For what reason? Because, monks, an agitated mind is easily pacified by these qualities.

Just as if, monks, a man were desirous of extinguishing a great mass of fire and were to scatter upon it wet grass... [and so on] ... and dust, would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire?
"To extinguish. "Even so, Bhante.
Here too, it should be understood that the development and arousal of the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility occur by way of their respective nutriment.
Among those, the development of the enlightenment factor of tranquility has already been explained; [now follows] that of the enlightenment factor of concentration.
When being spoken to, she will speak immediately after the other. "Due to the weakness of the application of wisdom" means due to the lack of the activity of wisdom.
For just as giving has non-greed as its primary factor and virtue has non-hatred as its primary factor, so too does meditation have non-delusion as its primary factor.
In that regard, when wisdom is not strong, then meditation does not bring about a progressive distinction between what precedes and what follows.
Just as unprepared food does not arouse a man’s relish for it, so too, because it does not produce delight in the mind of the practitioner, that [meditation subject] becomes unpalatable.
Likewise, due to the absence of the correct progression of the path through development, one does not experience the bliss of tranquility;
for this reason also, the mind becomes unpalatable. Therefore it was said: "The application of wisdom... [etc. ...becomes unpalatable."
Showing that this [teaching] serves to arouse spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and to produce confidence (*pasāda*), he said, "The eight bases for spiritual urgency," and so forth.
Therein, since birth, aging, sickness, and death occur respectively in both the happy destinies (*sugati*) and the miserable destinies (*duggati*),
the suffering of the states of woe (*apāya*) must be understood as something distinct from those, caused by the fivefold bonds, hunger and thirst, mutual affliction, and so on.
All of that has been taken as pertaining to the present existence of various beings;
therefore, the sufferings rooted in the round (vaṭṭa) in the past and future times have been taken separately.

However, for those beings who subsist on nutriment and therein subsist on the fruits of their exertion, the suffering of livelihood—which is not shared with others—is the eighth basis of spiritual urgency (saṃvegavatthu).

"It has been grasped" is how it should be understood. "This is called encouragement at the proper time" means that this is the correct encouragement given at the time when one is to be encouraged, by way of generating a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and by way of producing confidence (*pasāda*), according to the method already stated;
the meaning is the gladdening of the mind of development through the production of confidence preceded by the generation of spiritual urgency.

"By resorting to right practice" means by resorting to the practice of development that is truly correct through the path of serenity (*samatha*), being free from both dullness (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*).

Regarding the terms "not dull" (*alīna*) and so forth: it is "not dull" because of the absence of excessive states belonging to the side of indolence; it is "not agitated" (*anuddhata*) because of the absence of excessive states belonging to the side of agitation;
and it is "not dissatisfied" (*anirassāda*) because of the perfection of wisdom-application and the attainment of the bliss of tranquility (*upasama-sukha*).
Therefore, it proceeds evenly upon the object and has entered the path of serenity (*samatha*).
In this state, it does not require further effort for encouragement through non-depression, for restraint through non-elation, or for gladdening through non-discontent.
Through non-depression and non-elation, it proceeds evenly upon the object; through non-discontent, it has entered the path of serenity; or, through even proceeding, [it remains so].
It should be understood as being neither sluggish nor restless, and not finding satisfaction in the course of serenity (*samatha*).

This is called "equanimity at the proper time" (*samaye ajjhupekkhanatā*); this refers to equanimity that overcomes the opposite tendency—consisting of the mind's engagement in exertion, restraint, and encouragement—at the time when it ought to be viewed with equanimity. This is the concentration enlightenment factor (*samādhi-bojjhaṅga*).

What has not yet arisen arises. By means of the path of Arahantship, there is the fulfillment of development; by this, he shows that even an Arahant who has attained the fullness of concentration does so precisely through this method.
Equanimity, which is the state of neutrality resulting from the abandonment of attraction and aversion, is the cause of the equanimity enlightenment factor (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*); in that regard—
Because it succeeds when there is [equanimity] and fails when there is not, and because that state of equanimity is twofold according to its object, he says:

"equanimity toward beings and equanimity toward formations. Since conflict arises due to both of these, and such conflict is removed precisely through the cultivation of the tranquility factor of enlightenment (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*), he says "equanimity toward beings" and so forth, showing the method for abandoning only that which is non-conforming.
For it is said that avoiding persons who dally with the conditioned phenomena of beings is the "cause for its arising.
Since greed is specifically the opposite of equanimity, equanimity is called the "path of purification" for a person abounding in greed.
"In two ways" means by these two: reflection on one's own karma as one's own property, and reflection on the emptiness of self.
For two reasons. The restriction "only for two" is intended to show the equality of the number when accompanied by the [corresponding] mental formations (*saṅkhāra*).
Here, it is only the number that is the same, not the things numbered, which are in every respect dissimilar. The state of being ownerless is the absence of self-ownership (*anattanīyatā*).
For if there were a self, the robe or anything else might be called "belonging to the self" by virtue of being its property; however, that...
The intention is that there is none at all. "Anaddhaniya" means not enduring for a journey;
it does not last long, but is brief and impermanent—this is the meaning. "Tāvakālika" is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Mamāyati" means one makes it one's own (possesses it). "Mama" means one remains having grasped it with craving. "Dhanāyanta" means [treating it as] wealth.
While performing the task: "Assa" means that the full development of the enlightenment factor of equanimity occurs through the path of Arahantship;
for it is only in the case of an Arahant that the sixfold equanimity is accomplished.

"Dhammā with the foul as their object" refers to those phenomena consisting of various aspects of the foul which have become the objects of foulness-jhāna. Granted, these may also be bound up with the sense faculties.
The hair and so forth are simply modes of the foul; however, specifically taking what is to be loathed as the cause for loathing, he said, "the ten.

The attention that proceeds in such a way that, when one attends to them, the perception of the foul becomes established there by way of their intrinsic nature and essence, is "attention as a means" (*upāya-manasikāra*). It is the grasping of the aspect of repulsiveness as foul within the foul, or rather, how it is therein...
The learning sign arises; such attention is the apprehension of the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*).
Application to the development of foulness (*asubhabhāvanā*) is the practice of the development of foulness that leads to access concentration and absorption.
When there is thorough restraint of the six sense faculties, including the mind, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), finding no opportunity, [does not arise].

It is indeed abandoned; likewise, for one who knows the proper measure in eating and consumes food in moderation, sensual desire is abandoned because it finds no opportunity due to the absence of being overcome by sloth and torpor.

Furthermore, one who correctly perceives food as repulsive—in its transformation, in its basis, and in the extreme loathsomeness of its state as undigested matter in the stomach—and understands that the body subsists on food, [abandons sensual desire].
One who knows this is specifically called "one who knows the proper measure in food" by virtue of knowing the measure in all respects regarding food.

For such a person, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is indeed abandoned. However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the phrase beginning with "of four [mouthfuls]" was stated merely to demonstrate moderation in eating.

Elder Tissa, the practitioner of the meditation on the foul (*asubha-kammika*), was one who saw teeth and bones. "Of what has been abandoned" refers to its abandonment by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
Of what has been abandoned. According to the method of the Abhidhamma, all greed is the hindrance of sensual desire;
thus it is said: "By means of the path of arahantship, there is non-arising in the future.
One who is affectionate, meaning one who is moistened by the spreading of benevolence, is a "friend" (mitta); [it refers to] a person seeking welfare. That which exists toward such a friend is...

It is "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) because it belongs to one who is loving; it is the desire for their welfare. That very thing, as liberation of the mind from its opposites, is "loving-kindness liberation of mind" (*mettā-cetovimutti*).
In this context, the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness is the arising and occurrence of the radiance of welfare toward sentient beings through the act of loving.
Therefore he said: "Designated," and so forth.

In this context, "specified" (*odissaka*) refers to [the practice] by way of oneself, a dear friend, a neutral person, or an enemy. "Unspecified" (*anodissaka*) is understood when the delimitation of boundaries has been broken down.

"Pervasion of directions" (*disāpharaṇa*) should be understood as the grasping of loving-kindness (*mettā*) by way of pervading one direction and so forth. This "grasping" (*uggaha*) should be seen as extending up to the stage of access concentration (*upacāra*).
Once grasped, its repeated cultivation is "development" (*bhāvanā*). [The objects of this are: all women, men, noble ones, non-noble ones, gods, and humans.
"Directed toward the fallen" (*vinipātika*) refers to sevenfold loving-kindness (*mettā*) that proceeds by way of the classes of beings, or twenty-eightfold;

tenfold loving-kindness that proceeds by way of the directions of space; and four hundred and eighty types that proceed by way of specific directions, each direction being divided into categories such as "beings," "women," and "enemies.
[The formula is: "All beings, all living things, all creatures, all persons..."

"Included within one's own person" (*attabhāvapariyāpannā*): by way of these, there are five kinds. Through the fourfold occurrence—thinking, "May each one be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness"—there are twenty types of non-specific pervasion (*anodhisopharaṇa-mettā*).

Referring to that, he said: "Even for one developing [loving-kindness] specifically... (*odhiso...pe... bhāventassapi*). "This belongs to you," etc., refers to the reflection on the fact that one is the owner of one's own karma (*kammassakatā-paccavekkhaṇa*).

[The text] shows this. "For one who stands in reflection" means for one who correctly understands through reflection both the aforementioned danger in anger and the benefit of non-anger, which is its opposite, namely, loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"For one who cultivates [it]" means for one who associates with it; ill-will (*byāpāda*) is abandoned.
"Grasping at the sign in over-eating" means that in eating more food than necessary, there is grasping at the sign of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), thinking: "In this much..."
The meaning is: grasping the causes and non-causes of sloth and torpor, such as thinking, "Sloth and torpor arise after eating; they do not arise to this extent.
Regarding "the daylight of the sun by day," the meaning here should be understood as: "even for one who attends to the daylight of the sun, which was perceived as a sign during the day.
It is said, "also by talk that is favorable and based on the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)," because the ascetic practices are dependent upon energy (vīriya).

Since remorse (*kukkucca*)—arising through the grieving over what has been done and what has not been done—possesses the same characteristic as restlessness (*uddhacca*) in that it brings about a lack of mental tranquility, the Blessed One said, “There is, bhikkhus, a calming of the mind,” and so forth, in order to show the means for abandoning both.
Therefore, to demonstrate that great learning and the like are the causes for its abandonment, he said: “Furthermore...”

He said, “Six things,” and so forth. In that context, for one who is learned and who investigates the Dhamma both in terms of the text and its meaning, distraction does not arise because of the possibility of attaining self-satisfaction and so on.

Since remorse finds no occasion when one has attained the practice as prescribed and the counteraction in accordance with the Dhamma, it is said: “By means of great learning... [and so on]... restlessness and remorse are abandoned.”

It should be understood that to the same extent that restlessness and remorse are abandoned by one who is well-versed in the scriptures and possessed of reflective discernment, they are also abandoned through frequent questioning and through understanding what is to be done according to the discipline (*vinaya*).

Furthermore, because associating with the elders brings about the adoption of their virtuous conduct, it is said to effect the abandonment of restlessness and remorse due to its quality of producing tranquility of mind;
however, this is stated without regard for the mere seniority of age, but rather by those who are experts in the discipline (*vinayadharā*).

"Those who dispel remorse are to be regarded as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta). Since distraction in monks is for the most part caused by remorse, "one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is unallowable," and so forth, are specified by way of the method of training itself.

In the phrase "when restlessness and remorse have been abandoned," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Because remorse is accompanied by mental distress (*domanassa*), [it is included].
The non-arising [of defilements] in the future has been stated by way of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*).
As for what ought to be said regarding "wholesome and unwholesome phenomena" and so forth, that has already been explained above.
Granted, even the doubt consisting of the eight bases is abandoned through great learning and thorough inquiry; nevertheless, all other forms of doubt are rooted in doubt concerning the Three Jewels.

Having said this, it was stated: “With reference to the Three Jewels,” and so forth. Furthermore, when there is proficiency in the Vinaya, doubt regarding the training (*sikkhā*) is simply impossible;
likewise, when there is an awakening to the qualities of the Triple Gem, uncertainty regarding the past and so on does not arise.
Thus he said: “In the Vinaya,” and so forth. Conviction that is capable of inspiring trust is a firm resolve that, as it were, enters into the object of faith itself.
