And that is precisely the generation of such resolve (*adhimokkha*). Resolve (*adhimutti*) is the state of being inclined, sloping, and leaning toward faith.
[The Buddha] reached the peak by means of Arahantship, because the teaching was concluded after expanding upon all seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
The commentary on the *Āhāra-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Pariyāyasutta 233.
They are called "many" because the designation "Saṅgha" does not apply [to fewer than four]. "More than that" means more than three persons;

for from four onwards, they attain the status of a formal act (*kamma*) by virtue of being a Saṅgha performing a Saṅgha-act such as one requiring a quorum of four. "They entered" refers to the entry that was yet to take place.
He says, "They have entered," because it is spoken by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) as if they were already [there], even though they have not yet become so.

For metaphorical designation is applied to what is yet to be (the future) as if it were already present (the past). Therefore he says, "But those," and so forth; the meaning is "but those monks. Again, "those" refers to the heretics and the disciples of the heretics.
"In this presentation" means in this manner of explaining the meaning, which proceeds in the form beginning with, "having abandoned the five hindrances," and so on.
It is called a *visesa* because it distinguishes (*visissati*) one thing from another by way of division;

thus, it is a distinction or a difference. Since this refers here to a state of being included within something additional, he asks: "What is the *visesa*? meaning "What is the additional [element]? The term *adhippāyo* means an additional application (*adhika-payuñjana*), that is, an additional effort.
It is called a *nānākaraṇa* because one is made different (*nānā karīyati*) by means of it; thus, it is a distinction. Therefore, he asks: "What is the diversity (*nānatta*)?"

"In the second phrase" means in this phrase: "or the instruction in the instruction. "The same method" means that just as the application of the meaning was done for the first phrase, it should be applied in the same way to the second phrase.
"Three stations" refers to the three stations of devas, Māras, and Brahmas, which are included within the world by the expression "in the world with its devas," and so forth.
“Of this generation with its recluses and brahmins, with its devas and humans”—this refers to two bases.

By including [the phrase] “of this generation” here, it is expressed by means of five terms. “Enumeration” (uddesa) means the state of being enumerated. “Numbering” (gaṇana) means that it is understood as “sensual desire is one.
“In one’s own hands, feet, and so forth” should be regarded as a mere illustration; for aversion arises with reference to a collection [of parts].
Because it arises from doubt regarding one's own aggregates, such as "Am I indeed?

Although all energy (*vīriya*) is purely mental, that energy which, by way of being based on bodily action and so forth, gives rise to a physical application when directed toward the mind, receives the designation "bodily" (*kāyika*);
therefore, to distinguish it from that and to show the intended second category, it is specified here as "mental" (*cetasika*).

Although it cannot be said that the energy proceeding by way of maintaining the postures as they have been arranged is a condition for the body proceeding in such a manner, nevertheless, there is no such bodily exertion occurring at that time;
thus it is said, "energy arisen without bodily exertion. By the phrase "similar to the enlightenment factor of mindfulness," [it refers to] the internal...
It extends by analogy the method beginning with "equanimity toward internal phenomena" to that which proceeds by way of looking on with equanimity toward volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
Having stated, "The mixed factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) have been explained," the passage beginning with "In these" was spoken in order to clarify that meaning.
It is said that "bodily energy not yet reached the path" because one is capable of attaining the Noble Path even while walking back and forth. Factors of enlightenment.

"They are not obtained" means that the actual (nippariyāya) factors of enlightenment are not obtained. The intention is that they "extract the factors of enlightenment" by way of a figurative expression (pariyāya).

The "rest" refers to, among external phenomena, mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, equanimity, mental energy, applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), zest (pīti), concentration (samādhi), and the two kinds of tranquility (passaddhi).
However, this method has been stated according to the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) based on their common occurrence.

However, according to the Theravāda, since the enlightenment factors of rapture and concentration— when devoid of both initial and sustained application (avitakka-avicāra)— also exist in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara),
one might have to say that there are ten mixed types by including those as well.
The commentary on the *Pariyāya-sutta* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Aggisutta 234.
*Loṇadhūpanaṃ*: salt and incense; thus, "salt-and-incense. *Yodhakammaṃ*:
work to be performed by a warrior-person. *Mantakammaṃ*: counsel regarding royal affairs. *Paṭihārakammaṃ*: [service] in the presence of the king.

Having reported the words of those who had arrived to the king, he then performed the work of repelling them. Therefore, because mindfulness is beneficial in all circumstances (*sabbatthika*), he spoke thus:

"And mindfulness indeed, I say," and so forth. The factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) pertaining to the preliminary stage of insight are mentioned here because they involve exertion, restraint, and removal.
The commentary on the *Agni-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Mettāsahagata-sutta*:
235. "What is its destination? means "of what destination," which is to say, "what is its ultimate end"? What kind of supreme state?
"What has this as its highest limit" means "what is its ultimate. "What kind of fruit, benefit, or arising does it have? means "what is its fruit.
The terms *saṃsaṭṭha* (conjoined) and *sampayutta* (associated) are merely explanations of the meaning of the word *sahagata* (accompanied by);

however, here, having made the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*) the basis, the factors of enlightenment belonging to the stage prior to insight (*vipassanā-pubbabhāga-bodhi-aṅga*) are expressed as "the mindfulness factor of enlightenment accompanied by loving-kindness," and so forth.
It should be understood that they are “stated. “In all instances” means in all the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and in all the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).

That which one feels aversion toward is “repulsive” (paṭikūla); it is undesirable. That which is not repulsive is “non-repulsive” (appaṭikūla); it is desirable. Therefore he said, “in a desirable object.
“Therein” means in a non-repulsive object. “Thus” means perceiving [it] as repulsive. [This refers to perceiving] beings who are non-repulsive as repulsive.

The pervasion by foulness (*asubhapharaṇa*) occurs when one brings to mind the reflection that formations (*saṅkhāra*), though not repulsive [to themselves], are impermanent. "By means of foulness" means by means of the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*).
"Or he applies it as impermanent" means he sets forth the mental attention that "they are impermanent.

To explain the meaning stated in brief with the words "In the same way," the passage beginning with "In those that are repulsive and non-repulsive" was spoken. "Six-factored equanimity" refers to the six...
Equanimity possessing six factors for one who has abandoned attachment toward sense objects in their arising.

"By means of loving-kindness" means by means of the cultivation of loving-kindness. The capacity to dwell with a desired state of mind regarding repulsive objects and so forth belongs to the Noble Ones (ariya) alone;
and since this succeeds only for the Arahant therein, it is called noble psychic power (ariyiddhi). And of that noble psychic power...
Because it has been shown, the teaching must be turned back and brought to its conclusion.
One is unable to reach Arahantship because the faculties are not yet matured and because attachment is difficult to eradicate. This teaching:

the teaching beginning with “he develops the enlightenment factor accompanied by loving-kindness” has thus been commenced. For he who, having made the jhāna of loving-kindness the basis, applies himself to contemplation...
Failing to reach Arahantship despite having begun the effort, he produces the fine-material-sphere jhāna known as a liberation within the pure color-kasiṇas;
with reference to this, the Blessed One said: "But he enters and dwells in the beautiful liberation."

“Having purity as its supreme limit” means having the liberation of the beautiful (*subhavimokkha*) as its supreme limit. Wisdom would exist right here in this world; therefore he said, “the meaning is ‘of mundane wisdom’.
Loving-kindness has only Arahantship as its supreme limit because it serves as the foundation for the path to Arahantship. The same method applies to compassion and the others as well:
by making the jhānas of compassion and so forth the foundation and contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), one is able to attain Arahantship. For such a person...
"Compassion has the state of an Arahant as its ultimate limit; the same should be said for sympathetic joy and equanimity"—this is what is being referred to by way of analogy.
Furthermore, the purpose for beginning the teaching with the phrase "by this method" is exactly as indicated below.

Regarding "having beauty as their ultimate," etc.: for loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, having beauty as their ultimate means having the base of infinite space as their ultimate.
The limit of the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana-paramatā*) and the limit of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-paramatā*).
"Of each respective one" means because they serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the three lower formless jhānas and for the beautiful liberations (*subha-vimokkha*), respectively.

"Familiarity with the unrepulsive" means the frequent application of attention (*manasikāra-bahulīkāra*) toward a desirable object. "With ease" means simply with comfort. "Therein" refers to the desirable color-kasinas (*vaṇṇa-kasiṇa*) due to their purity.
"Mind" refers to the mind consisting of development (bhāvanāmaya-citta), which leaps forward by way of absorption (appanā). "Beyond that":
beyond that beautiful liberation (subhavimokkha), there is nothing further called a decisive support (upanissaya) for the liberations;

rather, it should be understood as a state accompanied by loving-kindness (mettā). "For one who contemplates the suffering of beings" means the suffering arising among beings caused by physical factors brought about by such things as sticks.

For one who investigates with wisdom: it is said that "the mind plunges into that with ease" because, for one who dwells in compassion, the suffering arising among beings—which has the sign of form as its object—especially leaps forth by means of wisdom;
it is not, however, because of seeing advantages in the formless realm in every respect.

"Regarding one who regards consciousness (*viññāṇa*)": this is stated on the grounds that by means of grasping the joy (*pāmojja*), the grasping of the consciousness that is its support becomes possible. "Accustomed to the grasping of consciousness": it is accustomed to the grasping of consciousness in the manner already described.

"Of one abiding in equanimity (*upekkhā-vihārin*)": of one who dwells in the divine abode of equanimity (*upekkhā-brahmavihāra*). "Due to the absence of mental application (*ābhoga*)": due to the absence of applying the mind toward pleasure and so forth. "...pleasure... can arise":
because there is the possibility of being turned away from grasping at ultimate objects such as pleasure and pain.

The "suffering of grasping at what does not exist" refers to the fact that even the grasping at the mere absence of this or that thing—which is habituated to grasping at the designation of a being (*sattapaññatti*) that does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*)—is suffering, even though it may be wholesome. The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Mettāsahagata-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta 236.
“Even before” (*paṭhamaññeva*) means earlier still. The fact that there was no inspiration for mantras not previously recited is established even more so than “first”;
the intention is that there is nothing at all further to be said in that regard. *Pariyuṭṭhāna* means...

"Overpowering is grasping," he said; thus, "one who is obsessed by sensual lust" means "one who is seized by sensual lust. It is called "suppression" (vikkhambhana) because it suppresses or removes [the defilement];
it is called "escape" (nissaraṇa) because one escapes from it by means of its opposite. Thus, it is "suppression-escape" (vikkhambhananissaraṇa).
Therefore he said, "In that regard," and so forth. This applies to the remaining two phrases as well.
The same method applies here. One’s own welfare (*attattha*) is that which must be reached by oneself through effort; likewise, the welfare of others (*parattha*) is to be understood in the same way.

In such passages as “Contemplating [things] as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence,” because ill-will (*byāpāda*) and the other hindrances have not yet arisen, escape by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-nissaraṇa*) is not included in the section on non-ill-will.
Although it is not included there, nevertheless, by means of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*), that [hindrance] is to be dispelled.

It can be understood that the escape from those factors is indeed obtainable. The perception of light—whether it has reached access concentration (upacāra) or absorption (appanā)—is any form of serenity (samatha), such as the jhānas based on the kasiṇas. The discernment of phenomena (dhammavavatthāna) should be taken as including both access and absorption levels.
"Boiling" means hot. "Becoming warm water" means that very state of boiling has reached the condition of being warm water, that is, extreme heat.
Therefore he said, "heat has arisen. "By way of the sesame seed, etc. means by way of the sesame seed, the husk, the filament, and so forth.

"With moss... [and] "...with *paṇaka*" refers to the slimy substance of water. "Lacking confidence" is due to agitation. "Sitting down" is due to the arising of mud. "In a place without light" means in a place devoid of illumination.
The commentary on the *Saṅgāravasutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Abhayasutta* 237.
"In one sense, the Blessed One [said] 'hindrances'": in one sense indeed the Blessed One stated that these states are hindrances because they hinder the arising of the wholesome in the mind.
"Bodily fatigue" means bodily exhaustion; however, because it serves as a condition for the arising of the topic, it is called "distress."
[The word] *vutto* [is used]. Mental fatigue (*cittakilamatha*) should be understood as that which arises with it as its condition. Therefore he said: “It is said of him,” and so forth.

The phrase “mental distress (*cittadaratha*) was also stilled” is to be connected by supplying the words [from the previous context]. “By the path alone” means by the Noble Path (ariyamagga) as it had been attained.
“Of him” refers to Prince Abhaya. “This” refers to this pair of physical and mental distresses.
The commentary on the Abhayasutta is finished.
The commentary on the Sākacchavagga is finished.
7. The Ānāpānavagga.
1. Commentary on the Aṭṭhika-mahapphala-sutta, etc. 238.
"Perception arisen" refers to access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) by way of its characteristic of perception. Therefore he says, "But this," and so forth.
"Even the skin and hide appear": this is stated by taking both the animate and the inanimate body as a commonality of the body.
Regarding the phrase "when there is a residue of clinging" (*sati vā upādisese*): here, that which clings to and grasps its own object is called *upādi*, which is to say, clinging (*upādāna*).
The meaning is: "when a portion of this [clinging] has not been abandoned.
The commentary on the Ānāpānavagga is finished.
8. Nirodhavagga 1–10.
Commentary on the *Asubha-sutta* and others (248–257).
"Discontent" (*anabhirati*) means lack of delight, lack of longing. It is the perception occurring with respect to Nibbāna, which is the state of absolute cessation.
The perception of cessation (*nirodhasaññā*). Among these, that which is accompanied by the path is supramundane (*lokuttara*);

however, that which proceeds with an inclination toward Nibbāna and is accompanied by the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*) is mundane (*lokiya*). Thus it is said: "The perception of cessation is mixed.

The reading "of those nine" and so forth is a careless reading; one should adopt the reading: "There is absorption (*appanā*) in eleven [factors], and nine have access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*). Twenty.
"Subjects of meditation" (*kammaṭṭhānāni*): this is the method as it has come down here [in this work], not the method as it appears in the *Visuddhimagga* and other such texts.

And herein, having reached either absorption (*appanā*) or access (*upacāra*) concentration as appropriate among the objects of meditation and so forth, the factors of enlightenment consisting of insight and the path—which constitute the preliminary stage for one who has attained Arahantship—are explained.
The commentary on the Chapter on Cessation (*Nirodhavagga*) is finished.
The commentary on the Saṃyutta on the Factors of Enlightenment is finished.
3. The Saṃyutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness.
1. The Ambapālī Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Ambapālīsutta 367.
"Ekāyanvāya" is stated by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*): the vowel *o* is changed to *va*, and the vowel *a* is lengthened.
This, it is said, is a term from the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*; therein, the word *ayana* is a synonym for "path. It is not only this [term] that is so used.
Then, extracting the phrase "other synonyms for the path" (*magga-pariyāya*), he says "of the path," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection—"If the word *āyana* is a synonym for the path, why is 'path' mentioned again?"—he says "therefore," and so forth.
In that context, "one path" means there is only one path; for there is no other path leading to Nibbāna. [Objection: Is it not the case that the foundation of mindfulness...
Is it intended here that "the path" alone is meant, while there are many other path-factors besides it? True, they exist;

however, they are included by the mention of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) because they are inseparable from them. For while knowledge, energy, and so forth are mentioned in the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), their inclusion under mindfulness alone in the summary (*uddesa*) should be understood as being according to the inclinations of those to be trained, and for the purpose of showing that mindfulness itself possesses the nature of the path.
By the phrase "not being a forked path," he shows that this [path] lacks both a state of duality and a state of not leading to Nibbāna.
"In the sense of going to Nibbāna" means: it is "going to Nibbāna" (*nibbānagamana*) because one goes to Nibbāna by means of it;

that itself is the meaning in terms of unerring cultivation, and thus "in the sense of going to Nibbāna" means in the sense of being the means for the attainment of Nibbāna. "In the sense of being to be sought" means in the sense of its being something to be searched for.
"By lust and so forth" means by the stains of lust and so forth, which are described as: "Lust is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain.
Furthermore, since this purification of those with defiled minds, when accomplished, leads to the non-arising of sorrow and the rest, it is therefore said:
"for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation," and so on. In that context, "sorrowing" refers to [the grief] caused by the loss of relatives and other such misfortunes.
Sorrow (*soka*) is the burning of the mind, an inward brooding.

Lamentation (*parideva*) is the outburst of speech through the mode of wailing—such as “Where is my only son?”—produced by an excess of sorrow on account of the loss of relatives and so forth. Its non-arising in the future is what is meant here by “surmounting”;
thus he says, “for the sake of abandoning. Regarding the phrase “of pain and grief,” this refers to mental suffering (*cetasika-dukkhatā*).

Since it is already established that mental distress (*domanassa*) is included by the very term "suffering" (*dukkha*), and since there is no exclusion by means of the word [itself], a specific term is considered superior to a general indication;
thus, it is stated simply as "mental distresses" (*domanassāna*). The phrase "of mental distress" (*cetasika-domanassassa*) should be understood as a statement of its actual nature.
That by which one goes forth—that is, by which the Four Truths are penetrated exactly as they are—is called the "method" (*ñāya*), namely, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
Anticipating the objection, "Is this too not a path? Why then is it that only a path serves for the attainment of the path?", he says, "For this...
and so forth. Craving (*taṇhā*) is called *vāna* in the sense of binding or weaving together (*saṃsibbana*) the results of karma and the defilements.
Because it is devoid of that craving-attachment (*taṇhāvāna*), there is an absence of it; such is the meaning. "By making oneself an eyewitness" means for the sake of personal direct experience.
"Speaking in praise" means words of commendation. "Purity" means purification, the abandoning of defilements (*kilesa*). Regarding "should be mastered":

here, "mastery" (*uggaha*) refers to making [the text] fully committed to speech; it should be understood that "cultivation" (*paricaya*)—which consists in making [the text] familiar—is included by the mention of that very mastery, since it is rooted in inquiry (*paripucchā*).

"Not below that" is said with reference to the undesirable objects of perversion (vipallāsa-vatthu) among the preceding mentions, because the body and so forth intended here lack the intrinsic nature of feeling and the rest, and because the dhammas of the three planes—
body, feeling, mind, and liberation— are already grasped separately as distinct bases for perversion. However, regarding the fifth base for perversion...
He said, "Not above" by way of non-existence. For here, the classification of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is by way of the classification of the objects.

"Three foundations of mindfulness" is a demonstration of the extraction of the meanings of the term *satipaṭṭhāna*, not a demonstration of the meaning of the term *satipaṭṭhāna* as it is used here in the text.
In the phrase "in the beginning, etc.," the word "etc. includes [the passage]: "From the arising of contact..."

It includes those sections of the Sutta-piṭaka that elucidate the objects of mindfulness (satigocara) as stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta: “The origin of feelings, the origin of mind-and-body from the origin of name-and-form, and the origin of mental phenomena from the origin of attention.
Thus, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi as well, the word “etcetera” (ādi) should be understood as intended to show the remaining passages of the Canon.
“Foundation of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhāna*) means a place where mindfulness is established.
“Noble” (*ariya*) refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One because of his being far removed (*ārakatta*) and so forth. “In this” means in this *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga-sutta*. For therein it is said:
“There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One... [omitted] ...deserves; thus indeed has this been said. With reference to what was this said?”
It has been said: "In this case, monks, the Teacher, out of compassion and seeking their welfare, teaches the Dhamma to his disciples, motivated by compassion, saying:

'This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness. Yet his disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed in defiance of the Teacher’s instruction. In that regard,
“Monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased, nor does he experience displeasure;
he dwells uncorrupted, mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness, which a noble one cultivates… [as before] …it is worthy of him.
Furthermore, monks, the Teacher… [as before] …‘This is for your happiness. To him—”
Some disciples do not wish to listen... [as before] ...some disciples wish to listen... [as before] ...and they do not act contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
In this regard, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure;
nor is he pleased nor does he experience pleasure. And as for that displeasure...
Avoiding both of these, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
This, monks, is the second foundation of mindfulness... [as before] ...it is worthy of being attained. Furthermore, monks, ... "to happiness," his disciples listen attentively...
[as before] ...they conduct themselves accordingly. In that regard, monks, the Tathāgata is indeed pleased, and...
"He experiences mental gladness and dwells uncorrupted, mindful and clearly comprehending.
This, monks, is the third foundation of mindfulness.
Thus, there is non-corruption by way of aversion and attraction, through the constant establishment of mindfulness, and the transcendence of both.
It is called “satipaṭṭhāna. For it is only Buddhas who possess constant established mindfulness due to its being an exclusive quality (āveṇika-dhamma), not Paccekabuddhas and others.
The prefix *pa-* signifies commencement (*ārambha*), and since commencement implies activity (*pavatti*), he says: “the meaning is ‘that which should be set in motion.
*Satipaṭṭhāna* is that which is to be established (*paṭṭhāna*) by means of mindfulness (*sati*) acting as the instrument; thus, it is “satipaṭṭhāna. The word *ana-*...

For by the use of the frequentative suffix (*bahulavacana*), it also has the sense of an object (*kamma*); likewise, since it can also have the sense of an agent (*kattā*), it is stated: "It is *paṭṭhāna* because it establishes itself (*patiṭṭhāti*).
In the phrase "it stands near" (*upaṭṭhāti*), the prefix *upa-* indicates a leaping forward characterized by intensity; thus, [the meaning is] "it proceeds by leaping down and leaping forward."
Thus it was said. Again, while explaining the meaning of the word *bhāva* (state/essence) and the words *sati* (mindfulness) and *paṭṭhāna* (foundation), he says "Or else," and so forth.
By this, it is understood that in the previous alternative, the word *sati* and the word *paṭṭhāna* have the sense of the agent (*kattuattha*).

"In the sense of remembering" means in the sense of recollecting what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago. "This" refers to that which is stated as: "Mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness."
This has been stated; this is what is intended here in this section of the sutta.

If it is thus—that mindfulness itself (*sati*) is the foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), and mindfulness is a single dhamma—then, that being the case, why is there the plural form "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānāni*)?
He says: "Because of the multiplicity of mindfullnesses," and so forth. If those mindfullnesses are many, then why [is it called] the "Path"?
The construction is with the word "singular" (*ekavacana*). "In the sense of seeking" (*magganaṭṭhena*) means in the sense of leading out (*niyyānaṭṭhena*). For the dhamma of the path is leading-out;
by that very quality of being leading-out, it attains unity and goes exclusively toward Nibbāna, and it is sought after by those who desire that goal.
Thus he says, "For this has been said," and so forth. Therein, "and these four" refers to [the foundations of mindfulness] by way of contemplation of the body and so on.
And these four kinds of mindfulness, at a later stage— that is, at the moment of the Noble Path— accomplish their task.
Having previously operated individually by way of dispelling perceptions of beauty and so forth regarding objects such as the body,
they accomplish the task of abandoning at the moment of the Path by means of the total eradication of all four types of perversion simultaneously.
They go toward Nibbāna by way of making it their object; the plural designation is used for them with reference to their accomplishment of the four functions.
Nevertheless, because there is no difference in meaning, it is spoken of in the singular as "the Path. Therefore he said:
"Therefore all four are called 'one Path'."

The question arising from a desire to speak is distinguished from other types of questions because it is impossible for those others to occur here, and because it is stated as such due to the desire to teach by way of exposition and so forth.
In passages such as “this body and external name-and-form,” there is the pentad of aggregates;
in passages such as “he experiences pleasure with the body,” there are the three immaterial aggregates beginning with feeling; and in that which... [in that]...
In such passages as, "At that time there is tranquility and subsiding of the body," the three mental aggregates beginning with feeling are called "the body.
To distinguish this [from the physical], he says, "of the body" means "of the material body.

Regarding the term "contemplating the body," showing here its sense of habitual practice (*sīla*), he says, "one whose habit is the contemplation of the body. "He contemplates as impermanent" refers to the body arising from the fourfold origination.
“He contemplates ‘it is impermanent’ (*anicca*); thus contemplating, it is said that he contemplates even the aspect of impermanence.
And for one who has become such, there is no longer any distinction from the grasping at permanence; therefore it is said, ‘not as permanent.
For in this way, he is said to ‘abandon the perception of permanence. And here, in the phrase ‘he contemplates only as impermanent,’ the particle *eva* (only) is indicated by elision.”
In order to show that the meaning has been turned back by him, it is said: "not as permanent.

And here, one should not suspect a turning away from the contemplation of suffering and so forth, because the particle *eva* serves only to exclude its opposite, and because those [contemplations] will be introduced later in the teaching.

The same method applies to such phrases as "he contemplates as suffering" and so on. However, this is the distinction: because the impermanent is suffering, he contemplates that very body as suffering.
"Because suffering is non-self, he contemplates it as non-self.
Furthermore, since that which is impermanent, suffering, and non-self is not to be delighted in, and that which is not to be delighted in is not to be clung to with passion, therefore it is said:
"He contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent; he contemplates as suffering..."
“He does not contemplate [the body] as pleasant, but as non-self; he does not contemplate it as self. He becomes disenchanted, not delighted;
he becomes dispassionate, not impassioned. Thus, by being without passion, he causes passion to cease; the meaning is that he does not cause it to arise, nor does he create its origination.
Practicing in this way, he relinquishes and does not grasp. For this contemplation of impermanence and so forth functions by way of specific factor substitution (*tadaṅgavasena*).
Because it involves the relinquishing of defilements along with the bodily aggregates and their underlying formations,
and because it leaps forward into Nibbāna— which is the opposite of those formations— by seeing the fault in the conditioned and inclining toward that state,
it is called both "the relinquishment of abandonment" and "the relinquishment of leaping forward. Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with this [insight] abandons the defilements in the manner described.
He leaps into Nibbāna; being thus, through the act of relinquishing, he does not take up defilements, nor does he take up conditioned objects by way of seeing them as unlovely.
Therefore it is said: "He relinquishes; he does not take up. Now, in order to show which phenomena are abandoned by the contemplations based on the [three] supports, it is said:
"Contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence," and so forth.

It has been said. Therein, "perception of permanence" refers to the distorted perception (viparīta-saññā) that occurs as "formations are permanent. The inclusion of the term "perception" (*saññā*) is because the abandoning of the perversions of view and mind occurs precisely through the abandoning of the perversion of perception;
alternatively, it should be understood that those [other perversions] are also included under the heading of perception.
"Delight" (*nandi*) means craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*). The rest is exactly as explained in the method already stated.
By the word "dwells" (*viharati*), the dwelling in the postures of one who possesses the practice of contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) is expressed;

thus he says "he conducts himself" (*iriyati*), which means he carries out the postures (*iriyāpatha*). Because they pervade [the mind] by way of being made the object (*ārammaṇa*), it is said "in the three realms of existence" (*tisu bhavesu*);
however, by way of their arising, the defilements (*kilesa*) belong only to the limited plane (*parittabhūmaka*). Even though there is the abandoning of the defilements...

"Exertion" (*ātāpana*) exists even in right view and the other [factors of the path]; however, because the word *ātāpa*—just like the word *ātappa*—is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) specifically for energy (*vīriya*), it is said:

"This is a name for energy. Alternatively, because energy—which functions by way of the uplifting of associated states for the sake of abandoning opposing factors—is preeminently an exertion toward those [states], it is energy itself that is so [designated].
It is said [of this], not of other phenomena.
The vowel *ī* in the word *ātāpī* indicates praise or excellence; thus, by the inclusion of the term *ātāpī*, he shows possession of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).

Being "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) means understanding thoroughly, all-around, and correctly; it refers to the state of observing other phenomena through their distinct definition, without confusion.
“Rightly” means without error; the meaning is that one understands for oneself by way of comprehensive knowledge in all its aspects, through the occurrence of successive stages of excellence.
If one contemplates with wisdom, how is it called “the establishment of mindfulness”? To this he says, “For it is not,” and so forth.
Therefore, it is only when wisdom has received assistance from mindfulness that the practitioner of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhānika) [proceeds] here with respect to the body as described.
The bhikkhu is a contemplator; therefore, he is called "one who contemplates the body. "Internal contraction" means internal shrinking, the sense being indolence.
Regarding "the grasping of the means": here, the means consists of the purification of virtue and so forth, as well as counting and so forth, and skill in learning and so forth;
by way of its opposite, the non-means is to be understood. And because one whose mindfulness is established does not [neglect] the aforementioned means...
He relinquishes [them], and he does not grasp at what is not a means; therefore it is said: "He is one who is muddled in mindfulness... incapable. By this [it is meant]:
by way of his incapacity for discerning and avoiding the means and non-means, and for relinquishing and not relinquishing. For this yogi.
Since mindfulness alone is here called the *satipaṭṭhāna*, therefore its associated states, such as energy and the rest, constitute its factors (*aṅga*).
He said: "Having shown its factor of association. Here, the word *aṅga* (factor) should be understood as a synonym for cause (*kāraṇa*).

By the inclusion of mindfulness (*sati*) alone, the inclusion of right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) should also be understood here, because it is comprised within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).
Or rather, this teaching is headed by mindfulness; for the abandoning of defilements and the attainment of Nibbāna do not occur through mindfulness alone.

Nor does existence proceed alone; therefore, in this teaching on jhāna, the word *aṅga* should be understood as having the sense of a "constituent part," just as in the expression "with applied thought" (*savitakka*) and so forth, which shows a factor of association.
The term "factor of abandoning" (*pahānaṅga*) is used to show the factor to be abandoned, as in the passage beginning "quite secluded from sensual pleasures.
This is because the path of the prior stage (*pubbabhāgamagga*) is intended here.

It is not the supramundane path; therefore, showing only the preliminary stage of discipline (*vinaya*), he said: "either by suppression as a factor (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by suppression [of the defilements] (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).

"Of him" (*assa*) means of the practitioner (*yogī*). "Of those states" (*tesaṃ dhammānaṃ*) refers to states such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth. For since those [states] are not intended there [in the context of the path], he said:
"this was stated by way of a summary of meanings (*atthuddhāranaya*). "But as for 'that which'" (*yaṃ pana*) refers to the *Vibhaṅga*; the intention is that it refers to the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*.
"In this" means in this word "in the world. And these contemplations are indeed mundane, because they are termed "comprehension" (*sammasana*).
"As suffering" means as having the nature of suffering due to the suffering of change and the suffering of formations; the meaning is that they are to be contemplated as suffering.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "Whoever sees pleasure as suffering" refers to whichever bhikkhu [sees] a pleasant feeling as suffering.
He saw with the eye of wisdom that it is suffering due to the suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*). He saw suffering as a dart;
he saw painful feeling as a dart because it produces oppression, because it pierces within, and because it is difficult to extract.
"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekkhāvedanā*). It is "peaceful" because, unlike pleasure and pain, it is not coarse and depends upon conditions.

And it is "peaceful" because its intrinsic nature is tranquilized. He who saw that it is "impermanent" because it does not exist after having been, because it possesses arising and passing away, because it is temporary, and because it is the opposite of the permanent—he indeed is a bhikkhu with right vision;
the meaning is that this bhikkhu has, in every respect, or clearly, seen feeling rightly.

"Also as suffering": it is suffering by way of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*). I say that all that which is felt is included within and contained in suffering, because it must be described as the suffering of conditioned formations.

"And also by way of pleasure and pain": this is said because of the pleasantness of the knowledge of the stability and change of pleasure and so forth, and the painfulness of the ignorance regarding the change and stability [of those same things]; thus, all three [types of feeling] are [suffering].
The meaning is that they are to be contemplated as pleasant and as painful; these seven contemplations have already been explained above.

Regarding the "diversity of objects," etc.: this refers to the diversity of objects such as visible forms, which is further divided into categories such as blue and so forth; the diversity of predominance, such as desire and so forth, which is divided into categories such as inferior and so forth;

and the diversity of co-nascent factors such as knowledge and jhāna, which is divided into categories such as with effort and without effort, or with applied thought and sustained thought, and so forth.
The construction is as follows: it should be contemplated by way of the diversity of planes such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth;

the diversity of types of karma such as superior, middling, and so forth; the diversity of karma such as wholesome (kusala) and so forth; the diversity of destinations such as those leading to the deva-realm and so forth; the diversity of dark and bright results (vipāka);

the diversity of types of fruition such as those to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) and so forth; the diversity of functional (kiriyā) states such as those belonging to the limited plane (parittabhūmaka) and so forth; and the diversity of types such as those with three roots (tihetuka) and so forth.

By the word "etc. (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of various types—such as those with a physical basis (savatthuka) and those without a physical basis (avatthuka)—as well as the threefold classification beginning with the "person" (puggala), which is common to all three [types of persons].
Regarding the phrase "of those with lust, etc.," this refers to the classifications such as "with lust" (sarāga) and "free from lust" (vītarāga) as they appear in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

The construction should be understood as being "by way of both specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa)," namely, by way of their respective specific characteristics such as "touching" (phusana) and so forth, and by way of general characteristics such as impermanence (aniccatā) and so forth.
"Of the phenomenon of emptiness" means of that which has the intrinsic nature of emptiness, defined as selflessness (*anattatā*).

By the phrase "of specific and general characteristics," the non-existence of that self—which is imagined by outsiders as a master, a dweller, an agent, an experiencer, and a controller—within the conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*) is demonstrated, just as there is no permanence or pleasure among them. There is none of these [qualities] in them.
“Self” is non-self; however, because not even a single phenomenon among conditioned formations is a self, they are therefore called “non-self.
This is their state of emptiness (*suññatadhamma*). To clarify that state of emptiness, the teaching on the exposition of emptiness was set forth in the Abhidhamma, beginning with the words:
“At that time, indeed, phenomena exist,” and so forth. The rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the Ambapālīsutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Satisutta: 368.

One who remembers is "mindful" (*sato*). However, this does not mean one who is mindful by means of just any mindfulness; rather, showing that it is by such [specific] mindfulness, [the text says:]...
He said, “by means of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body, etc. By “wisdom of the fourfold clear comprehension” is meant the wisdom of the fourfold clear comprehension.
He said, “going forward is called *abhikkanta*,” for “*abhikkanta* is said to be going. Likewise, returning is called *paṭikkanta*;
he said, “*paṭikkanta* is turning back. And turning back is merely the act of returning; having turned back...
But going is simply going. "Bending the body forward" means inclining the body by way of approaching it.

By saying "even in standing," etc., he shows that "approaching" (*abhikkama*) is the forward movement of the body toward an object through the process of going and so forth, while "receding" (*paṭikkama*) is the drawing back of the body from behind.
"Of the seat" refers to a seat such as a stool and the like. "Facing the front part" means facing the front portion, such as the footstool and so forth.
"Crawling about" (*saṃsaranto*) means crawling forward. "Crawling back again" (*paccāsaṃsaranto*) means crawling backward.
By the phrase "this is the same method," he demonstrates the very crawling forward and crawling backward of the body.

"Full awareness" (*sampajānaṃ*) is correct understanding. One who is habituated to performing the duties that must be done by oneself through that [awareness] is "one who acts with full awareness" (*sampajānakārī*).

He said: "One who performs all duties with clear comprehension. For clear comprehension itself is indeed *sampajañña*. Or, "one who acts with clear comprehension" means one whose habit is to act with clear comprehension.
It means that he indeed practices clear comprehension; thus, he generates non-delusion regarding such things as "going forth" (*abhikkanta*) and so on.
Alternatively, "one who acts with clear comprehension" (*sampajānakārī*) means one for whom there exists the act of one possessing clear comprehension.

It is "purposeful" (*sātthaka*) because it proceeds together with a meaning that is reckoned as an increase in accordance with the Dhamma. Full awareness of what is purposeful is "full awareness of the purposeful" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
Full awareness of what is suitable—that which brings benefit and is conducive to one's welfare—is "full awareness of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).
This applies to walking and so forth within the sphere of the alms-round, as well as to other activities that are not abandoned.
Clear comprehension regarding the range, which is the sphere known as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), is "clear comprehension of the range.
Clear comprehension as non-delusion regarding going forward and so forth is "clear comprehension of non-delusion. "Having taken hold" means having weighed, having investigated;
the meaning is "having reflected. By the mention of "seeing the Saṅgha," going for the purpose of the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and so on, is included. "Seeing the foul," etc. [is also included].
By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and so forth is to be understood.
In order to explain the meaning stated in brief, it was said: "Even upon seeing a cetiya," and so on. "He attains arahantship" is a description of the highest attainment;

for even the arising of serenity and insight is indeed the growth of a bhikkhu. "At the southern gate" means at the southern gate of the cetiya courtyard; likewise with "at the western gate," and so forth.
"In the text of the Abhayavāpi" means on the eastern bank of the Abhayavāpi pond.
Because he had recited the *Buddhavaṃsa*, *Ariyavaṃsa*, *Cetiyavaṃsa*, *Dīpavaṃsa*, and other chronicles (*vaṃsa*), the Elder was known as the Great Reciter of the *Ariyavaṃsa*.

"At the place where the monument was visible" means at the location where the stupa could be seen. "In the lifting of a single word" refers to the shifting and establishing of the placement of a word.
Without making [the distinction] in one and the same situation. "Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri.
"But in that case," however, even regarding a journey undertaken with a purpose as determined by the clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*):
since "purpose" means growth in the Dhamma, someone might suspect that the journey intended as "having a purpose" must necessarily be beneficial (*sappāya*). Thus it might be thought.
To prevent that [unwise attention], the passage beginning with “First, the visiting of shrines” is commenced.
“Like paintings and figures” means like images made by painting, or like mechanical figures similar to images produced by the application of machinery.
“Non-observation” refers to unwise looking at the object and so forth, by way of the equanimity of ignorance associated with the household life. That which...
It was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*): “Upon seeing a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling,” and so forth.
There is a threat to life due to being trampled by elephants and the like. There is an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) due to seeing unsuitable forms and so forth.
From the day of their going forth, it has been the custom for monks to speak in accordance [with the rules], whereas speaking otherwise—
He said, “There was another [woman] named Aparā,” meaning that two such stories had never been told before.
By the word “thus” (evaṃ), he refers back to the entire manner already stated beginning with “But if...,” and not to what is being said here, namely, “the unattractiveness of a woman to a man.

Because it is the basis for the occurrence of the practice of yoga, the object of meditation is called a *kammaṭṭhāna* (meditation subject); thus he said, “reckoned as a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-saṅkhātaṃ*).”
"Range. "Having mastered" means having mastered by way of perfecting skill in mastery so that the learning-sign arises.
"Carries it along" means he sets the meditation subject in motion; the meaning is that he applies himself to it until his return from the alms round.

"Does not bring it back" means he does not withdraw the meditation subject from the time of consuming food until the time of approaching the daytime resting place. He conducts himself having taken it up.
Having correctly undertaken them, it proceeds by way of fulfilling those duties. "Body-care" refers to the maintenance of the body, such as washing the face and so forth.
"Two or three cross-legged postures" means two or three sessions of sitting, or two or three warm seats. Therefore he said: "causing warmth to arise.
"By way of the meditation subject alone" means by way of the meditation subject itself, not abandoning the meditation subject. By that [he implies]: "Even when..."
By the words "insentient," etc., he shows that one should not abandon the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that is to be practiced, or the meditation subject as it is being cultivated.

"In that very way" means exactly three times. Because the bodily relic-shrine (sarīracetiya) is more venerable than the shrine of use (paribhogacetiya), the instruction to "having paid homage to the shrine" indicates that paying homage to the shrine is the first duty to be performed. For thus it is said in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
It was said: “The branches of the Bodhi tree that obstruct the cetiya should be removed.
Because the prostration to the Bodhi tree occurs through the very recollection of the Buddha’s qualities, he said: “Having shown full reverence as if in the actual presence of the Blessed Buddha.
“Near the village” means in the vicinity of the village.
“For the purpose of gathering people” means for the purpose of gathering people through the support of the Dhamma, thinking, “If I do not speak, who else will speak to them?

Therefore—because the commentators say that “a discourse on the Dhamma must indeed be spoken,” and because there is no discourse on the Dhamma that is divorced from a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)—therefore, “precisely by way of the meditation subject. By himself...
Without abandoning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) while it is being set aside, he should deliver a discourse on the Dhamma that is conducive to it.

Regarding the phrase "having offered an expression of appreciation" (anumodanaṃ katvā), here too the phrase "by means of the meditation subject as the primary focus" (kammaṭṭhānasīseneva) must be supplied and connected.

"By the mere extent of what has occurred" (sampattaparicchedeneva) means without making distinctions such as whether one is familiar or unfamiliar with the person; it means simply by the limit of what has happened, or merely by the fact of their meeting.
"Bhayā" means fear from foreign armies and the like.
"Kammaja-tejo" refers to the digestive heat (*gahaṇī*). It does not enter the path of the meditation subject because the body is exhausted by hunger and fatigue, resulting in a lack of concentration.
"In the remaining places" means in those places other than where the rice gruel was taken. "Successively, one after another" refers to the continuous arising of the meditation subject.

This is the vision of non-interruption; that is to say, just as there is no interruption in a succession of arrows proceeding one after another, so too there is none in this establishment of the meditation subject—this is what is meant.
One who has laid down the burden [of negligence] in the application of development, having broken all the observances by failing to fulfill the practice of the duties.
“He is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; he is not free from lust for the body; he is not free from lust for forms.

Having eaten as much as he desires until his belly is full, he dwells devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness. He leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas.
Thus it is said that one whose mind is bound by the fivefold mental bond has “practiced” (caritvā); that is, having engaged [in such conduct].
“By way of the practice of going and returning”: that which possesses the going and returning—the act of going for alms and returning—with meditation (*bhāvanā*) is called *gatapaccāgatika*;

it is that very practice, and it is by way of that. Those who desire their own welfare and happiness are called *attakāmā*, meaning those possessed of the desire for the Dhamma. For “Dhamma” means welfare, and happiness is that which has it as its cause.
Alternatively, because it is the property of the wise and because it is concealed within the selfhood (*attabhāva*), it is called the "self" (*atta*) among phenomena.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Monks, dwell with yourselves as an island, with yourselves as a refuge," and so forth.
Those who desire that [self] are "desirous of self" (*attakāmā*). An *usabha* is twenty *yaṭṭhis*. "By that perception" means by that perception of the stone: "this much..."
The intention is that they know [the situation] has reached its proper stage. This same method applies to the passage beginning with "this monk," which was stated regarding standing;
that same method applies to sitting as well. It causes those coming from behind to cultivate proper attention even out of fear of having their meal interrupted.
"Crushing" means crushing rice heads in a place where grain is being processed. "I shall honor the Great Exertion"—for us...
"I shall worship, according to my ability, that very difficult practice performed for six years by the Lord of the World for the sake of others.

For the worship of the Teacher is the worship of his practice, not the worship of material offerings. "Only standing and walking" is said with reference to the specific times for postures, not as a prohibition against sitting, which must certainly be done at times such as eating.
Having descended onto the street, one should first observe the streets without looking here and there; thus he said, "having observed the streets.
With reference to this, it is said: "with a pleasing advance," and so forth. To demonstrate that, the passage beginning with "and therein" was stated.
Regarding the phrases "having established the perception of repulsiveness in food," and so on, whatever is to be said—

That has already been explained above. "Endowed with eight factors" means having made it endowed with the eight factors stated in the passage beginning, "only for the maintenance of this body," and so forth. The phrase "neither for amusement," etc., is a demonstration of prohibitions.
The connection is: "He realizes private enlightenment (paccekabodhi), provided he is possessed of the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya). And this is just as...
In the three places below, it should be connected by applying [the same principle] to the subsequent places as follows:

therein, for *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment), the perfection of the proximate cause (*upanissaya*) consists of two incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) and one hundred thousand aeons spent accumulating the requisite equipment of merit and knowledge;
for the *sāvakabodhi* (disciple-enlightenment) of the chief disciples (*aggasāvaka*), it is one incalculable aeon and one hundred thousand aeons; and for the great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*).
The accumulation of the requisite equipment for that [path] took exactly one hundred thousand eons;

as for the others, it was the wholesome state conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) produced in past births by way of reliance upon the process of turning away from saṃsāra (*vivaṭṭa*). As for the name "Bāhiya Dārucīriya":

he was called "Bāhiya" because he was born and raised in the territory of Bāhiya, and he received the designation "Dārucīriya" because of his wearing of bark garments (*dārucīra*). Indeed, that venerable one said: "Therefore, then..."
"Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: 'In the seen there will be merely the seen,'" and so forth.
By means of this very brief exhortation, which was given on a single day, he attained distinction more quickly than others. Therefore it is said:
"Or he is one of quick direct knowledge, just like the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya. Regarding the phrases "one of great wisdom" and so forth, they should be explained as appropriate to each case.
"Non-delusion regarding that. "Thus" (*evaṃ*) indicates the manner now about to be described.

By the phrase "the self advances," he shows the delusion of an ordinary blind person (*andhaputhujjana*) due to the grasping of a view; by the phrase "I am advancing," he shows it through the grasping of conceit (*māna*).
Since both of these do not exist without craving, [he shows it] also through the grasping of craving (*taṇhā*).

Confusion has indeed been shown; having stated, "one who is thus not confused," he spoke the passage beginning with "when the thought 'I am stepping forward' arises" in order to show that non-confusion which occurs through the resolution of the compact mass.
In this context, since the fire element accompanied by the air element is the condition for lifting up, it possesses the nature of lifting up.
"In lifting up the fire element" refers to the wind element’s state of being concomitant with that [fire element]. Therefore, he said, "In lifting up one foot...
they are powerful," demonstrating that here, by virtue of their functional capacity, these two elements are predominant while the others are subordinate.
Furthermore, because the wind element is concomitant with the fire element, [it is responsible for] the drawing back and the stretching forward.

This is the condition. For since the air element (vāyodhātu) possesses an especially predominant function in the acts of drawing forward and drawing back within the horizontal movement, the fire element (tejodhātu) exists as its follower;

therefore, he said, "likewise in the acts of drawing forward and drawing back," showing that here these two possess intensity due to their functional capacity, while the others are weak. This is so even though there exists a distinction between the quality of following and that which is followed.
The word “thus” (*tathā*) is used with reference to the mere state of the fire element and the air element.
In this context, “lifting up” (*uddharaṇa*) is the raising of the foot from the place it has stepped upon;

“shifting forward” (*atiharaṇa*) is carrying it forward beyond the place where it was standing. This is for the purpose of avoiding trees, stumps, and so forth, and for the purpose of avoiding contact with the foot already planted on the ground.

Or, "carrying across" (*vītiharaṇa*) is the shifting [of the foot] sideways. As long as the foot has not yet been set down, it is "bringing forward" (*āharaṇa*) and "carrying beyond" (*atiharaṇa*); after that, it is "carrying" (*haraṇa*) and "shifting across" (*vītiharaṇa*).
This is the distinction between them. Because the water element (*āpodhātu*), which follows upon the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), is the condition for the releasing [of the foot].
For since the water element has the nature of being heavy, its state of following upon the earth element occurs during the releasing.
Therefore, showing that between those two [elements] there is a preponderance of capacity in one and a deficiency in the others, he said:
"In the act of relinquishing... they are powerful. For the earth element, which follows upon the water element, is the condition for depositing;
because its function is especially predominant not only in providing a foundation but also in establishing [the body], it [belongs] to the water element.

The state of being accompanied by [the water element]; likewise, because the compression effected by the action of striking is accomplished by means of the earth element, there too the earth element is accompanied by the water element. Therefore it is said:
"Likewise in the cases of placing down and compressing. Therein means: in that forward movement, or in those six parts mentioned, beginning with lifting up. In the case of lifting up...
At the moment of extraction. "Material and immaterial phenomena" refers to material phenomena occurring in the mode of being extracted and the immaterial phenomena that originate them.
They do not reach across [to another place] because they exist for only a single moment.
"Right there, right there" means wherever they have arisen, right there; for there is no movement of phenomena from one location to another. Section.
It should be understood that this is stated with reference to the sections such as the "leaping forth" (*pabbanta*) and the "drawing up," by way of a homogeneous continuity (*sabhāga-santati*).
For the moment of occurrence even for material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) is exceedingly swift;

it is swifter than the meeting of the sharp edges of hooves on the heads and feet of the sons of gods who delight in racing, as they run toward one another in alternating upper and lower positions. Just as...

Just as the breaking of sesame seeds being crushed is indicated by their *taṭataṭāyana* (crackling sound), so too, for the purpose of showing that conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*) break up through their arising, it is said "crackling" (*taṭataṭāyantā*). For those things that have arisen necessarily break up.
The phrase "together with form" (*saddhiṃ rūpena*) refers to the material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) that cease together with the cessation of each respective state of consciousness.
This has been stated regarding that which arises at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) of the seventeenth consciousness from that point.
Otherwise, if material and immaterial phenomena were simultaneous, there would be a contradiction with such statements as, "Material form is heavy in its transformation and slow in its cessation.
Likewise: "Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other phenomenon that changes so rapidly."

And by such scriptural passages as, "This mind... and so forth. For consciousness and mental factors, having the nature of possessing an object (*sārammaṇa*), arise only while manifesting the object that serves as their objective condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) according to their respective capacities;
thus, their cessation occurs immediately after the accomplishment of that manifestation of their own nature.
Material phenomena (*rūpa-dhammā*), however, are without objects and must be manifested [by consciousness]. Thus, for them, there is the accomplishment of the state of being manifested.
"It occurs with sixteen types of consciousness"— by this, their momentary existence (*taṅkhaṇāyukatā*) is intended.
Because the three aggregates have as their condition merely the contact with an object, and because consciousness has a rapid turnover due to that mere contact with an object,

while material phenomena have a slow turnover due to their dependence on the gross primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the Tathāgata alone possesses the knowledge of the various elements (*nānādhātu*) as they really are.

Furthermore, since only material phenomena (rūpadhamma) are stated to be the prenascence condition (purejātapaccaya), and the postnascence condition (pacchājātapaccaya) applies to those same [material phenomena], it is not logical for material and immaterial phenomena to be simultaneous;
therefore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method already explained.
"One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases": that consciousness which arose previously is "another."
Furthermore, as that [consciousness] ceases, it does so only by acting as the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and other such conditions for another;

thus, another consciousness arises having obtained those very conditions. If one were to ask, "In that case, would there not be an interval between them? he says, "It is an uninterrupted succession" (*avīcimanupabandho*).
Just as no interval (*vīci*) is found, such that those who perceive without distinction think, "This is that very same thing," so too is the continuous succession (*anu-anu-pabandho*).
The mental continuum and the physical continuum proceed like the flow of water in a river.
"Looking forward" (*ālokita*) means looking directly ahead; thus it is called "gazing from the front.

Since looking toward whichever direction one is facing while walking, standing, or sitting is "looking forward," therefore, looking toward the intermediate directions that follow from that is [called] "looking aside" (*vilokita*).
He said, "Vilokita means looking toward the intermediate directions.

He stated, "By this term 'mukha' (opening/aspect), all of those [other types of looking] are indeed included," because it is possible for *olokita* (looking down) to occur when performing tasks such as sweeping or plastering;
for *ullokita* (looking up) when taking down rafters and so forth; and for *apalokita* (looking back) by way of avoiding dangers approaching from behind.

"Body-witness" (kāyasakkhin) means one who has realized [the truth] with the body; the meaning is "one who acts through direct perception. This venerable one, at the very time of insight (vipassanā), became filled with effort, thinking:
"I shall thoroughly restrain that very same [fault] by relying on which I fell into such adverse states as lack of delight in the Teaching due to not guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
Thus he possessed powerful moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa), and because he had performed his duties therein.
Having reached the highest perfection in the restraint of the sense faculties, for that very reason the Teacher placed him in the foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples in guarding the doors of the sense faculties, namely Nanda.

The connection [of the text] is to be understood by bringing forward the words "looking ahead and looking aside" (*ālokitavilokita*) as being characterized by purposefulness (*sātthakatā*) and appropriateness (*sappāyatā*). Therefore...
He reiterates the very point already stated—that the state of clear comprehension of the range of movement consists precisely in not abandoning the meditation subject—as a supporting reason.
The intention is that looking forward and looking aside should be done solely by way of one’s own meditation subject;

those whose meditation subjects are the aggregates and so forth need not seek any other method. This is because even designations such as "looking forward" are merely specific modes of occurrence within mere phenomena (dhamma-matta).

Therefore, in order to show that the thorough understanding of it as it truly is constitutes "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*), the words beginning with "within" (*abbhantare*) were spoken.

"By way of the expansion of the wind-element produced by mental activity" (*cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasena*) means by way of the occurrence of the wind-element originated by functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*) in the mode of movement.
"Sinks down" (*adho sīdati*) means it descends slightly. "Leaps up" (*uddhaṃ laṅgheti*) means leaping upward.
It goes upward as if [rising].
"Accomplishing its own function" means producing the primary function of its constituent parts; the meaning is that it becomes the body of the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
That this does not occur in the first impulsion (*javana*), nor even in the seventh impulsion, refers to the cognitive process (*vīthi*) of the five-door consciousnesses.
The expression “woman, man” is stated with reference to the absence of lust and so forth [in the five sense doors].
For therein, through improper adverting and apprehending, there arises mere greed for a desirable object such as a woman’s form, and mere aversion for an undesirable one;
however, in the mind door, there occurs lust and so forth regarding “woman, man,” and following that, there is the impulsion of the five sense doors.

The root, or rather, all [factors] beginning with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as previously described. Thus, the full understanding of the root (*mūlapariññā*) is stated by way of the thorough comprehension of the states that serve as the root for the javana of the mind-door;
however, the adventitious and temporary nature is stated specifically of the javana of the five doors, by way of its being unprecedented and its being momentary.
"Having fallen after breaking up in an upper-lower sequence" refers to the lower one...
And he states that the subsequent [moments] of the final [consciousness] reach dissolution.

"That" refers to the impulsion (javana). The connection is: "it is not appropriate for that impulsion. "A newcomer" means one who has arrived. "Tāvataka" means those whose duration is limited by arising and passing away.
This is the clear comprehension of non-delusion. "In a gathering" means in a collection. "Therein" refers to the looking and looking-about by way of the five aggregates.
When that [body] is being perceived, who is it—distinct from it—that looks forward or looks around?

The term "decisive support condition" (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is stated here figuratively according to the method of the Suttas. "Conascent condition" (*sahajāta-paccaya*) is merely an illustration, since other conditions such as the mutual, associated, presence, and non-disappearance conditions are also applicable here.

"At the time" means when bending at the appropriate time for bending, and likewise when stretching at the appropriate time for stretching. They say, "The *maṇisappa* is a particular species of snake. "Lolling" (*laḷana*) means shaking, or performing a playful movement.
One who is accustomed to heat has a body full of feverish distress. That which arises through wrong livelihood is unwholesome because it brings harm by way of defiling one’s virtue.
By the statement, “Even a robe is insentient,” etc., [the author] shows that the body, like the robe, is insentient;
thus, by demonstrating the body’s emptiness of a self, he further elucidates the meaning already stated in the passage beginning with “within,” etc., regarding contentment with whatever is available.
It shows the reason. Therefore, he says "tasmā" (therefore), and so forth.
"Struck by four or five knots" means one whose four or five knots have been struck out, or whose beauty has been destroyed by four or five knots.
"The eightfold meaning" refers to the eightfold distinction of purpose according to the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsiva. "Of this... [text fragment]
It should be understood as stated in the manner beginning with, "for the maintenance of the body.

However, in this alternative view, it should be understood that the passage beginning with "not for sport" was spoken by way of showing the aspect of prohibition, considering that it has come down in the Pāḷi.
Just as water, which sustains the earth, is sustained by the wind, so too is the consumed nutriment sustained by the air element alone.
Regarding its "abiding in the seat," it is said: "It remains by means of the air element alone. "Carries forward" (atiharati) means it carries [the food] as far as the mouth.
"Carries across" (vītiharati) means it carries it while mixing it within the stomach. Alternatively, "carries forward" means it carries it while passing through the gateway of the mouth;
"carries across" means it carries it while looking toward what has entered the stomach. "Turns over" (parivatteti) means it moves it back and forth.
And here, it is the air element together with the earth element that performs the supporting, transforming, pulverizing, and drying of nutriment, not the air element alone;

thus, these functions are stated as belonging to the earth element by way of its functional role. It is said that the earth element is "common" (sādhāraṇa) because it performs those functions of supporting and so forth. Furthermore, it "protects its moistness," just as the air element and the others do.
There is no drying up by other factors; thus it preserves its moist state. "The fire element" refers to the fire element known as the digestive heat (*gahaṇī*).
For that ripens the food once it has entered within. "It becomes a direct path" means it serves as the route for the entry and so forth of the food.
"It bends" means by way of seeking [food], and by way of experiencing the swallowing, the digestion, the non-digestion, and so on.

And it "turns toward" (āvajjeti); the meaning is that it cognizes. For the very application (payoga) that serves as the condition for the cognition of this or that object is called "right application" (sammāpayoga).
For by whatever application the seeking and so forth are accomplished, that [application] also brings about the cognition of that object, because the two are inseparable.
Alternatively, having relied upon right application—that is, right practice—one "bends toward" (ābhujati).
It attends. For it is said that every function of consciousness is preceded by mental application (*ābhoga*).

"By way of going" means by way of going toward the village of the alms-round for the purpose of seeking alms. "By way of seeking" means by wandering about in the village of the alms-round for the sake of alms.
"By way of enjoyment" means by the consuming of food. "By way of the seat" means by way of the seat of bile and so forth.

It is called *āsaya* because, although occurring together as one, it lies (*sayati*), remains, and proceeds there, established by the power of karma and abiding without mutual confusion by way of its own boundaries.
It refers to the bile and other secretions that reside above the stomach (*āmāsayo*). For this prefix *ā-* has the sense of a boundary.
It is called *koṭṭhāsa* because food, according to what has been eaten, remains stored (*nicito*) therein.
"Storehouse" (*nidhāna*): from that which is stored. "Unripened" (*aparipakka*): because it has not been digested by the kamma-born heat known as the *gahaṇī*.
"Ripened" (*paripakka*): because of the state of digestion of the food as it was eaten. "Fruit" (*phala*): because of its production.
"Exudation" (*nissanda*): because of trickling out here and there. "Smearing" (*sammakkhana*): because of smearing all over. This is the meaning here.
This is the summary; the detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Sweat breaks out from the body" means that sweat is released from the body due to the fever (*pariḷāha*) produced by the suppression of natural urges.
"And other diseases" refers to ailments such as earache, fistula-in-ano, and so forth. "In an improper place" means in a location that is unsuitable for being occupied by humans or non-humans.
In fields, shrines, and so forth. For when humans or non-humans are provoked to anger, they may bring about the end of one’s life.
Because it has been abandoned, it belongs neither to that bhikkhu himself—since he has not relinquished it to anyone—nor to another, because it is loathsome.
"From a water-vessel" means from a bamboo tube or other such water container. "That" refers to the discarded water.
And here, one posture (iriyāpatha) occurs in two places; that was previously included by the mention of "going forward and returning.
Others say: "Since the movement of the body both forward and backward was already mentioned, what is taken here is simply 'going'.
Because in this discussion of clear comprehension (sampajañña), non-deluded clear comprehension alone is the primary focus, therefore, from time to time...

The state of acting with clear comprehension is understood here as the vision of the cessation of both material and immaterial phenomena, as they occur within each respective mode of conduct (*iriyāpatha*).
However, the reciters of the *Majjhima Nikāya* speak thus: "For one bhikkhu goes while thinking of something else, while reflecting on something else;
another goes without ever relinquishing his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); likewise, one stands [in such a manner]."
When sitting or lying down, he lies down thinking of something else, reflecting on something else; he lies down without having relinquished his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
However, this much alone does not make it clear, so they illustrate it by means of walking meditation (*caṅkama*).
A bhikkhu who, having descended to the walking path, stands at the eastern end of the path and examines: "The material and immaterial phenomena occurring at the eastern end of the walking path..."
Without reaching the western end of the walking path, they cease right there; even those occurring at the western end of the walking path cease right there without reaching the eastern end;
those occurring in the middle of the walking path cease right there without reaching either end;
and the material and immaterial phenomena occurring on the walking path cease right there without reaching a fixed location.
“Having ceased while standing, it proceeded to sitting and ceased right there; having proceeded to sitting, it proceeded to lying down and ceased right there.
As he examines [the mind] thus again and again, he causes the mind to sink into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
However, when rising, he rises only after taking up the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). This is the bhikkhu regarding the states of going and so forth.
"He is one who acts with clear comprehension.
In this way, too, the meditation subject remains unmanifest in the sutta;
and since a meditation subject that is unmanifest should not be practiced, that bhikkhu, as long as he is able, should walk, stand, sit, and lie down while thus encompassing it.

He reflects: "The body is insentient, the bed is insentient; the body does not know 'I am lying on the bed,' nor does the bed know 'The body is lying on me'; the insentient body lies on the insentient bed.
While grasping [the object] in this way, he causes his mind to descend into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); upon waking, he wakes having taken up the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). This is...

One is called "practicing with clear comprehension while asleep" because one understands that when there is sleep, it is called "awake" by way of discerning that the entire process occurring at the six sense doors is a process consisting of functional activity (*kiriyā*).
