This is because [the mind] consists of that [activity], because it produces the act of adverting (*āvajjana*), and because it arises from the act of adverting;

thus, the impulsion (*javana*)—or indeed all activity proceeding through the six doors—is called a process made of functional activity. Discerning this, one is said to be practicing with clear comprehension while awake.
Furthermore, by dividing the day and night into six parts and remaining awake during five of those parts, one is said to be "practicing full awareness while awake.

Likewise, when standing at the head of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*) and teaching the Dhamma, or when abandoning the thirty-two types of frivolous talk and engaging in appropriate talk based on the ten topics of discourse, one is said to be "practicing full awareness while speaking.
[One should also apply this] to the mental inclination toward any of the thirty-eight meditation objects...
Even while attending to the object and entering the second jhāna, one is said to be "practicing with clear comprehension" in silence.
For the second jhāna, specifically due to the abandoning of verbal formations, is called "silence.

In the passage beginning with "the lips," the word "and" (ca) should be understood as including the throat, head, navel, and so forth. "The appropriate application" refers to the means for its arising.
The "appropriate application" refers to the mode of mental activity by which all investigations and so forth are accomplished.
"In the occurrence of derived matter" means in the arising of the sound base accompanied by intimation and transformation. "In this way" means according to the manner described.

It is called "mixed" because it does not cause confusion even across the seven locations. This is also because right mindfulness of the path conforms to the contemplation of the body and the other foundations.
The preliminary stage corresponding to clear comprehension is entirely mundane because it pertains to the seven or eight bases.
The commentary on the *Sati-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Bhikkhu-sutta*.

369. Since that bhikkhu requested a concise teaching of the Dhamma, saying, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief," and because of his inclination toward what is concise, the Blessed One—desiring to teach the Dhamma in just such a concise manner—spoke the words beginning with "Therefore, in this case.
Thus it is said: "Because you request a teaching in brief, therefore..."

Only for one who possesses the view of being the owner of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*) and so forth do the various mundane and supramundane qualities succeed, not for one whose view is corrupted;
therefore it is said: "View means the view of being the owner of one's own actions and so forth.
4. Commentary on the *Sāla-sutta*.

370. “Dhamma” refers to the teaching (sāsana-brahmacariya), which in the sense of upholding—by preventing one from falling into the suffering of the states of misery for those who practice according to the instructions—is called “Dhamma.
That same teaching is called “Vinaya” in the sense of disciplining the defilements by means of the “discipline of its constituent parts” (tadaṅga-vinaya) and so forth.
Thus he said: “It is called ‘Dhamma’... [and] ‘Vinaya’. Because it arises alone, being unoverpowered by opposing states, it is called “ekodi.”

"Unified" (*ekodibhūtā*) means that concentration has become and arisen as one for these [monks]. Here, by the term "unified," the preliminary-stage concentration that brings about access-meditation (*upacāra-jjhāna*) is expressed.
By the term "composed" (*samāhitā*), both access and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) are expressed.

By the term "one-pointed in mind" (*ekaggacittā*), it should be understood that well-developed, mastery-attained absorption concentration is expressed. They have developed the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) through their years as newly ordained monks.

They belong to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), for they have been developed for the sake of knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*). Here, "knowledge of things as they truly are" is intended to mean the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
The foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) developed by those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) also belong to the preliminary stage;

for them, having already accomplished what was to be done, the development of the foundations of mindfulness is for dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*). However, the development of the foundations of mindfulness for those in training (*sekkha*)—
"Mixed" is said because those that proceed for the sake of full understanding are mundane (*lokiya*), while those that proceed by way of the act of fully understanding are supramundane (*lokuttara*).
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Heap of the Unwholesome (Akusalarāsi-sutta) 371.

In the fifth [discourse], "entirely" means unmixed with wholesome states; for that very reason, it refers to the whole bright side in the sense of being blameless. The rest is exactly as explained by the method already stated.
6. Commentary on the *Sakuṇagghisutta* 372.
Because of its powerful nature among the common species of birds and because it kills them, it is called a "hawk" (*sakuṇagghi*).
It is said that "this is a designation for a hawk," yet it should be understood as a specific kind of hawk. Because it has come for the sake of food, [it acts] through greed and violence.
"Attained" is what was stated; the meaning is that it was attained by means of a lustful sign and through a violent manner. "Ploughed with a plough" is *naṅgalakaṭṭha*;
because it is there that such [ploughing] is performed, it is called *naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇa*. Thus he said: "Now, 'kaṭṭha' refers to a field-plot.
A "clod-throwing place" (*leḍḍuṭṭhāna*) is where clods of earth stand; it is a place ploughed for the purpose of a target for clods.
*Vajjati* means "speaking"; *avadaṃ* means "speaking badly. This negative particle (*a-*) is used here in the sense of reproach, as in the expressions "childless" or "without a wife.
*Avadamānā* means "one who holds herself in high esteem while not speaking"; the meaning is that she speaks while disregarding the quail due to the intoxication of her own power.
For this very reason he said: "Go then, you quail; even having gone there, you shall not escape me."
As for what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Speaking highly of her own strength,” this is said there by taking the word *atta* as derived from *ātman*.
Alternatively, the reading is *vadamāno*, meaning “challenging” in the sense of provoking a dispute.
Therefore he said: “Come now, O hawk! “Having well-settled” means by making [the arrow] ready for a swift flight, like one whose string is released.
Having placed both sides correctly. "Ayanti" means a hawk. "Ñatvā" means having known through one's own knowledge by seeing things as they truly are.
"Phālīyittha" means it was shattered against a dry clod of earth with a sharp edge like a plowshare.
7. Commentary on the Monkey Sutta.
373. *Sañcāro* means moving about. *Lepaṃ* refers to a plastering substance similar to glue.
*Kājasikkā viya* means like a net that is to be hung on a bamboo pole; furthermore, there are five places: four ropes and the place for binding above.
*Oḍḍito* means suspended. *Thunanto* means snorting.
8. Commentary on the Sūdasutta 374.
One who "cooks" (*sūdeti*)—that is, prepares—the various bases for food by means of providing nourishment is called a *sūda*, a cook.

Because they must be "transcended" (*accetabbā*) or passed beyond by those who are young and desirous of pleasure, they are called "transgressions" (*accayā*); that is, the particular flavors in food. Therefore...
“By various juices” (*nānaccayehi*) means by various distinct types of flavors; thus it was said, “by various juices,” and so forth.

It is called *agga* because it is distinguished or analyzed from what is not mixed with it; since sourness itself is the *agga*, he said, “sour-agga” (*ambilagga*), meaning “by portions of sourness” (*ambilakoṭṭhāsehi*).
They are called *abhihāra* because they are to be brought forward for the purpose of giving; they are the objects to be given. Thus he said, “of the gifts that have been brought forward.”
"This meditation subject of mine is in conformity" means: "This meditation subject of mine, while proceeding in this way, remains only until the end of the stage of conformity.
Thus, when it proceeds again, it serves only for the purpose of exerting effort to produce the distinction.
In this way, the fool who is incompetent is unable to grasp the sign, but the wise man is able. "Of his own mind... [and so forth].

Of one’s own mind in development. The preliminary stages of insight (pubbabhāgavipassanā) are indeed called the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), because it is said: “One grasps the sign of one’s own mind.
9. Commentary on the Gilānasutta.
375. *Pādagāma* is a large village similar to a city. For this very reason it is said: "He dwells at Vesālī in the village of Veḷuva.
Those who possess the quality of friendship—characterized by preventing what is harmful, enjoining what is beneficial, and abandoning one in times of misfortune—are called *mittā*.
Those who are companions merely by sight are *sandiṭṭhā*. Those who possess exceptional devotion are *sambhattā*.
Showing this, he said: “One who has friends is called ‘one who possesses friends,’” and so forth. *Assa* means “of the Blessed One.
On the fifth, the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth—counting four times in each fortnight—there are eight times in a month.
Because of the intensity of the sensations, it was harsh, rough, and severe. *Ābādho* (affliction) refers to that which arises from karma due to the cause of previous deeds.
Affliction, defined as the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*), is called a "concordant disease" because it pertains to the body at all times.
This present affliction is not like that; rather, due to its extreme intensity, it is called a "discordant disease. Since the word *anta* (end) implies proximity, he says:
"the end of death, the vicinity of death. [The phrase] "feeling... and so forth... [is used] because one does not do so when the body and other factors have been developed to the highest degree.

“Being oppressed” means as if being oppressed. He said, “The authorization of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus for the exhortation itself,” meaning that it is stated: “without giving the exhortation and instruction.
What is called “preliminary energy” is the energy of insight (vipassanā) which serves as the preparation for the attainment of the fruit.
It is called “the formation of life” because, by not allowing the life-formation (jīvitasaṅkhāra) to fall away, it constructs the personal existence (attabhāva).
“Momentary attainment” (*khaṇika-samāpatti*) is an attainment characterized by a specific temporal limit, such as: “I shall emerge after this much time has passed.

“Having made it free from thicket and free from tangle” means having made the cultivation of insight—which proceeds by way of the sevenfold sets of materiality and immateriality—entirely free from barrenness (*khila*) and free from tangle due to its lack of confusion. “By way of great insight” (*mahā-vipassanā-vasena*)...

The attainment that has been entered upon after having practiced insight by way of the eighteen great insights and so forth—which have been individually and specifically detailed—thoroughly suppresses feeling due to the great strength of its prior object and the great power of the energy of insight as it proceeds in such a manner.
The illustration of this is given by the passage beginning with "Just as if... and so on.
He shows this. "Feeling" refers to painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*). "By way of fourteen modes" means he speaks by way of those two sets of seven.

"Having moistened" means having saturated [the body] with the moisture of the rapture (*pīti*) and serenity (*sineha*) of insight (*vipassanā*) produced by the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) entered into from time to time.
"Attainment" refers to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
“Recovered from illness” means recovered from the state of being ill.

He said, “having become heavy and stiff,” because the body’s attainment of heaviness and rigidity is called “sweetness. “In various ways” means according to the divisions such as the eastern direction and so forth.
“The states of the foundations of mindfulness” refers to the states of the foundations of mindfulness that were previously cultivated by oneself; they do not become manifest.
Because of the unserviceability of body and mind. "That" refers to the teachings; thus, the teachings of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) are not understood.

"Without internal or external" means that one does not distinguish between internal and external in terms of either the Dhamma or the person. By the words "only this much," etc., he explains the very meaning already stated.
"In my childhood" means during one's own childhood. "It is not so" [refers to the thought] "I [will lead] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus..."
The mode of occurrence of envy and avarice rooted in conceit and craving—such as "I shall avoid [this]" and so forth—does not exist in the Tathāgata;
it is even more non-existent because those [defilements] have been utterly eradicated. Thus he said, "Right on the seat of enlightenment," and so on.
By means of a repair combined with a patch. He conceives [of himself] as if by that aforementioned thing called a repair, combined with a patch.
"An old cart. "By the wrapping of the fruit of arahantship" means by the wrapping of the state of existence known as the attainment of the fruit of arahantship.
Because the attainment of the fruit is intended here, it is said: "of certain feelings," meaning "of worldly feelings. Regarding the phrase "with oneself as an island":
here, by the word *atta* (self), only the Dhamma is meant; this meaning has already been explained above.
The ninefold supramundane Dhamma is to be understood. For it is called an "island" because it cannot be overwhelmed by the four floods.
"At the summit of darkness" means at the pinnacle of the world with its devas, due to the absence of connection with darkness. "Of all" means of all those who desire training.
Those monks who dwell as "islands of Dhamma," having the four foundations of mindfulness as their domain, will be at the summit.

10. Commentary on the Bhikkhunupassaya Sutta 376. *Kammaṭṭhānakammikā* means those devoted to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). It is called a *visesa* because it distinguishes; that is to say, it is an excellence or pre-eminence. Since this distinction between what precedes and what follows must be grasped in each successive stage, he said "Therein... and so forth to demonstrate it.

"The fever of the defilements arises" refers to the lack of attention directed toward the body by way of the foul (*asubha*) and other such subjects. [This occurs] for one who does not apply attention...
By not entering upon the path, the fever of the defilements arises with the body as its object through [the perception of] beauty and so forth.

Due to the absence of the exertion of energy, there is either sluggishness of the mind toward that object, or the mind is distracted by various external objects outside the range of its proper domain.
Thus, by means of the phrase "in the fever of the defilements" and so forth, the threefold state of being a basis for the defilements in the application of meditation is shown.

This was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* by way of a collective inclusion (*samuccaya*). However, because those states—feverishness (*pariḷāha*), sluggishness (*līnatta*), and distraction (*vikkhepa*)—do not occur simultaneously, the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the *Pāḷi* in the passage beginning with "having the body as its object," etc., to signify indefiniteness.
"By one who is stained by defilements" means that one should not act while having a mind discolored by defilements. But how?
"It should be practiced," he said, "in some [particular] way.
"Neither thinks nor reflects" means that he does not set in motion the thought and reflection associated with the defilements. "Happy" means happy by means of the jhāna-happiness.
The connection is: "The development of this bhikkhu proceeds. For it is because of that original meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of this bhikkhu...
When an obstacle arises, having set it aside and gladdened the mind by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha and so forth, the cultivation of the primary meditation subject proceeds;
therefore, the connection is that it is called "cultivation by means of aspiration. "Having set aside" should be understood as "having prevented the mind from proceeding [toward the obstacle].
An application of the meaning is possible by way of all three—meditation subjects and so forth. Hence he said:
“*Tatthā*,” and so forth. “As if driving it” means as if driving a chariot. “As if inserting [wood] cut to the proper measure by means of an adze and the like.

By means of these two similes, he shows that the practice of insight (*vipassanā*) has been undertaken and is free from obstacles, [describing him as one who] easily allows no room for the defilements (*kilesa*), neither stumbling nor clinging in the interval.

“By means of a staff” (*byābhaṅgiyā*) means by means of a wooden stick. “Of the fever of the defilements, etc. refers to the fever of the defilements, sluggishness, and distraction. “Molasses, sugar-candy, etc.

refers to products of sugarcane such as molasses, sugar-candy, and pieces of sugar. Because of the statement beginning with “I dwell contemplating the body in the body,” it is said that “the preliminary stage of insight (*pubbabhāga-vipassanā*) has been explained.
The commentary on the Ambapālī-vagga is finished.
2. The Nālandā Chapter.
2. Commentary on the Nālandā Sutta. 378.
Since the first sutta in the second chapter is easy to understand because its method has been explained above, it is passed over and the word "in the second" is stated.
“More widely known” means distinguished as being superior to [others] regarding enlightenment (*sambodhi*). “Possessing more higher knowledge” means having wisdom that exceeds that of all beings;

hence he said, “possessing superior knowledge. He said, “regarding enlightenment,” meaning “in omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),” because one awakens correctly and without remainder by means of it.
Thus, the qualities of a Buddha are taken without limitation, meaning they are exhaustive.
It is grasped by means of the attainment of the supreme path alone, because all qualities have been accomplished by the Blessed One.

And showing that not only for Buddhas, but also for the chief disciples and paccekabuddhas, the accomplishment of their respective qualities occurs only through the attainment of the supreme path, he said:
"The two chief disciples," and so forth.

Another method: By the word "confident" (*pasanna*), the present state of confidence is indicated; by the phrase "one who has arisen faith" (*uppannasaddho*), the actual occurrence of faith is likewise made manifest.
Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'I believe thus'. One who knows all that is to be known face-to-face (*abhimukha*) is "possessed of direct knowledge" (*abhiñño*);
one who possesses superior or excessive direct knowledge is "one of superior direct knowledge" (*bhiyyobhiñño*). He [is so called] by way of the desire for words expressing excellence.

Because it was stated as "one who possesses even more higher knowledge" (*bhiyyobhiññataro*), he said: "One who is more widely known through higher knowledge" (*bhiyyataro abhiññāto*). However, in the second interpretation: "He knows directly" (*abhijānāti*) is *abhiññā*;
it is distinguished wisdom (*abhivisiṭṭhā paññā*). One who has more higher knowledge than that is *bhiyyobhiñño*; by means of a desire for an expression of excellence, he is *bhiyyobhiññataro*.
Since this excellence of his is produced by the abundance of higher knowledge, he said: "One who possesses more abundant higher knowledge" (*bhiyyatarābhiñño*).
"Or" (*vā*). It is "enlightenment" (*sambodhi*) because one awakens by means of it; that is, omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamaggañāṇa*).

For the knowledge of the supreme path has omniscience as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), and omniscience has the knowledge of the supreme path as its proximate cause; this is what is called enlightenment.
In this context, the first alternative is according to the predominance (*padhāna*) [of the factor], while the second alternative is according to the proximate cause (*padatthāna*). Why?
But here, only the knowledge of the path of Arahantship is intended.

Is it not the case that even the lower path-knowledges of the Blessed One occurred by way of destroying their respective opposites together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*)? For the abandonment of latent tendencies is indeed the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*).

True, this is so; however, that [lower knowledge] was incomplete because the destruction of the opposites was not fully accomplished. Therefore, he said: "In the knowledge of the path of Arahantship..."
“Or all”: “all” means everything that is to be realized by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Because of the power of its delicious taste, the excellence of the solid foods is indicated by the words “it becomes sweet.
Because of its distinguished nature, the excellence of the praise is indicated by the word “best. Because of its great magnitude, the excellence of the radiance is stated as “vast.”
It is "bull-like" (*āsabhī*) because it comes from a bull (*usabha*); here, however, it is "bull-like" because it is like a bull. Therefore he said: "resembling the speech of a bull.
To show by what quality it resembles that [bull], it is stated: "unwavering and unshakable. *Anussava* is oral tradition from any source whatsoever.
It makes known various meanings to teachers who have cultivated familiarity with the branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
*Paveṇī* is the succession of teachers. *Itikirā* is the mere imagining based on one's own intellect, thinking "thus, indeed," or "so, indeed.
*Piṭakasampadāna* is the grasping of that [teaching] as it truly is, through the transmission of the texts of the Piṭaka.
*Ākāraparivitakka* is the thorough reflection upon the manner of oneself regarding what has been heard. In that same way, one reflects: "This is exactly so."
"Acceptance through reflection on views" (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*) means the acceptance [of a view] after reflecting upon it.

"Reasoning" (*takka*) is the process of reasoning based solely on oral tradition, without [the support of] scripture or realization. "Adherence to a method" (*nayaggāha*) is the grasping [of a conclusion] by relying on the method of inference.
Since this censure of the Blessed One by the Elder was made while standing within the domain of the Buddha, and that [domain] is not the Elder's own domain, therefore...
It is said: “as if having penetrated [the truth] through directly realized knowledge. It is like a lion’s roar;
it is called a “lion’s roar” because of its similarity to one in terms of its excellence. Showing that this is to be understood in this way, he said “a lion’s roar,” and so forth.
“Making it resound” means making it like a thunderbolt.

"Anuyogadāpanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of having the interrogation cleared up. For one who roars a "lion's roar" capable of withstanding crushing [objections] clears up the interrogation in terms of its meaning;
and one who is being interrogated clears it up as well. "Dātuṃ" means to clear it up.
Some state the meaning as "dānatthaṃ" (for the purpose of giving), but that is not correct. For it is not the case that he who roars the lion's roar is himself the one who gives there.
"It gives instruction" (anuyogaṃ deti) is appropriate. "Rubbing" (nighaṃsanaṃ) means grinding. "Heating" (dhamamānaṃ) means warming.
And here, "heating" is spoken of by way of the process of heating [metal] in a crucible.
"All those" (sabbe te) refers to all those Perfectly Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddha) who have passed away and ceased in the past. By this he shows: those who existed...
Regarding the past time prior to your own initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*), you might— like Māra and others—
be able to know the worldly mental conduct of those Perfectly Enlightened Ones by delimiting the phenomena within the range of their disciples' knowledge.

However, as for those who have passed away even further back than that— those for whom the path has been cut off, whose proliferations (*papañca*) are severed, whose cycle of existence is exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering— [you cannot know them].
"How will you know those phenomena which are beyond the scope of the knowledge of your disciples, even for all those Perfectly Enlightened Ones?
By "that" is meant the knowledge of the path to Arahatship, which has omniscience—known as "perfect enlightenment"—as its proximate cause. "Of such virtue" means possessing such virtue.

"Wings of concentration": both concentration and the factors conducive to concentration are called "wings of concentration" by way of the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (retaining only one term from a group of similar things).
In this context, it should be understood that energy, mindfulness, and those factors conducive to them constitute the side of concentration (*samādhipakkha*).
Regarding the meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*), the term "abiding" (*vihāra*) is generally used; since the meditative attainments are dominated by concentration, it is said:
"Because the factors on the side of concentration are included, the abiding is included."

Just as concentration and wisdom, though already mentioned below, are mentioned again under the category of "liberation" by way of showing their specific function known as "being liberated" because they are liberated from their opposites—
expressed as "thus liberated"— so too the divine abiding is mentioned again by way of showing its specific excellence as "thus abiding.
Therefore, the meaning here is appropriately understood in terms of all the attainments and abidings.
It is to be seen. It is called "liberation" (*vimutti*) because it has been liberated; this same method applies to the others as well.

"In the state of subsidedness" means by way of the allaying and cessation [of defilements]. Because it has escaped from all defilements, because it is unmingled with them, and because it is liberated from them, the escape-liberation (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*) is Nibbāna.
As for the phrase "but of future Buddhas," the word *pana* indicates a distinction; by that, first, regarding those of the past, of the aggregates...
Because it has occurred previously, there may be a movement of knowledge within its own domain; however, regarding the future, which is entirely unarisen, how [can this be]?
This explains that point. Therefore he said, “The future as well,” and so forth. Why was it stated, “Having delimited them with one’s own mind, they are known”?
Is it not the case that the consciousness occurring during the past and future seven-day periods is indeed the object of the knowledge of others’ minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa)?

Is it not the case that [the object] does not extend beyond that? This was not stated by way of the function of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*); rather, it was stated by way of the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*).

Therefore, there is no fault here. One does not perform [the act] in a place where it is known [to be forbidden], because such a prohibition has already been established by the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) itself, and because of the destruction of the bridge (*setughāta*).
But how is it that the Elder [Mahāmoggallāna] stated only a prohibition when both possibilities existed?
"He did not answer by analyzing" means that he said, "It is said that the Elder... and so forth. It measures the further limit (*pāra*), thus it is a *pāramī*;
that itself is knowledge, thus it is *pāramiñāṇa*. The *sāvakapāramiñāṇa* is the knowledge of the *pāramīs* belonging to disciples.

This inquiry does not concern the knowledge of disciples when it has reached its highest possible limit; rather, it concerns the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), that is, the knowledge of omniscience itself.

Some, however, explain the meaning as "the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections" (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*) being "within the range of the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections," and likewise for the remaining terms.
"Capable of [knowing] virtue... and so forth means capable of knowing the causes comprised of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge of liberation.
For the virtues and other qualities of the Buddhas are the cause for the Buddhas' own Buddha-activities and for others' knowing that "these are Buddhas."

Because it does not remain in a state of doubt like inferential knowledge (*anumāṇañāṇa*), but rather bears and determines the knowable object according to its true nature as "this is this," it is called *dhamma*.
Thus he says, "of the knowledge of the Dhamma through direct perception" (*paccakkhato*).

He says, "having followed the application" (*anuyogam anugantvā*), because it follows after what is called an *anvaya* (concomitance). For, having followed an object established by direct perception, inferential knowledge...
The occurrence [of this knowledge] should be understood as "the inference of the unseen by means of the seen.

Since the knower of what is known is also, in fact, known, it is said: "The grasp of the method is known through inferential knowledge (*anumāṇañāṇa*). "Known" (*vidita*) means pierced, obtained, or attained.
"Immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) means unlimited because its scope is vast; thus he says "without end. "By that" refers to...

Because of its boundlessness; or, by means of that boundless knowledge. By this, the Elder shows that whatever object he desires to know through inference, in each and every case his inferential knowledge proceeds unimpeded and unobstructed. Therefore he said, "By this," and so forth.
In that context, "by this" means by this reason.

It is called *uddhāpa* because it causes the stability of the wall to reach higher and higher; thus, it refers to the base of the wall. By the word "etc.," the inclusion of the gate-barriers, moats, and so forth of the wall should be understood.
That which exists on the border is "borderland" (*paccantima*).
Having placed himself in the position of a wise gatekeeper, the Elder showed himself; thus, he raised the objection: "Why did he say 'with a single gate'?"
He says, "endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*)" to indicate that it is by virtue of which wisdom a person is called wise.
Skillfulness, proficiency, and dexterity regarding various duties to be performed is *veyyattiya*. It is called *medhā* because it measures, harms, or dispels ignorance;
one who possesses this is *medhāvī*. [The term] refers to its arising in various instances.
"Belonging to this" means *ṭhānuppattikā*, which is wisdom (*paññā*) arising from the occasion. "Anupariyāya" means that by which one goes around;
that itself is the path, thus it is the "path of circumambulation" (*anupariyāyapatha*), the way for walking along the perimeter of the wall.
"Pākārasandhi" is where the sections of the wall are joined; it is a section of the wall where it has bulged out. At its narrowest point, it is [the space between] two bricks.
He said, "the place where two bricks have been removed," because it is by such disappearance that this is expressed.
"The severed place" (*chinnaṭṭhāna*) means a portion that has been cut or broken, or simply a severed place; for that is called a "gap" (*vivara*). "Stained" (*kīḷiṭṭha*) means soiled.

"Afflicting" (*upatāpenti*) means they cause torment through the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*). "Oppressing" (*vibādhenti*) means they press down upon one. [This refers to] wisdom that has arisen.
He said, "Nothing can be done because of the hindrances," meaning they do not allow wisdom that has not yet arisen to arise.

"Therefore" means because they do not allow [wisdom] to arise by way of obstructing its conditions. "One whose mind is well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness" means one whose mind is properly established and settled through the fourfold cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness. By way of their true nature...
“Having developed” means having developed in such a way that the opposing factors are completely eradicated exactly as they are.
In the previous method, the foundations of mindfulness and the factors of enlightenment were intended as mixed; therefore, to state it otherwise, the passage beginning with “Furthermore, here...
was spoken. “Mixed” means mixed by way of serenity, insight, and the path. “With a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness...”

"Because they are mentioned first among the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), and because it is stated that one should 'develop the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) as they really are' after taking up insight (*vipassanā*),
and because these possess the status of being factors of enlightenment in the primary sense only when included within the Path (*magga*), and since they are indeed attained therein—
the question would be excellent if the factors of enlightenment, the Path, and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) were thus taken together," said the Elder Mahāsiva.

He said: "But it was not understood in this way by the ancients"—this is the intended meaning. "Iti" (thus) is a reference to the manner already described. "Thera" refers to the Elder Sāriputta. "Tattha" means among those border towns and so forth.
Nibbāna is like a city because it is to be approached by those seeking it, and because for those who have approached it, it is a place where one attains happiness free from danger.
Virtue is like a rampart for those who have approached it.
Because it provides protection on all sides; because it serves as the foundation for the rampart of virtue, like a circumambulatory path—as it is said:
“‘Circumambulatory path,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for moral shame (hirī)”; because it is the direct way for entering the city of Nibbāna, like a gate;
and because he is like a wise gatekeeper, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta).
This is because it characterizes those beings who have entered and are entering the city of Nibbāna. "Given" (*dinno*) means caused to be given;
the sense is "purified. The remainder is easily understood.
3. Commentary on the Cunda Sutta.
379. Because he had previously gone from Sāvatthī to the village of Veḷuva, it is said: “returning by the very path by which he had come. “Of seven” refers to these seven Arahants:
Upasena, Revata, Khadiravaniya, Cunda, and the novice Saṃanuddesa—these four;
and Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—these three. “Is there not indeed... [etc.]
Here too, the connection is made by supplying the word "looking back" (*olokento*) according to the method of the lion’s backward glance.
The connection is: "There will be those who say of me, 'He was unable to carry it away. The phrase "this is now the final look" is merely a statement of fact;
it does not indicate any lingering attachment there, just as when the Tathāgata, having departed from Vesālī, performed the "elephant-look" (*nāgāpalokita*).
The manifestation of various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhi*) by means of resolving upon specific qualities is called the transformation of supernormal power (*iddhivikubbana*).
This discourse on the Dhamma is said to be "like the lion’s play" because it is like the roar of a lion after he has played about by stretching his limbs and so forth.
In the phrase "It is time for me to depart," the word *iti* indicates completion; it refers to the sequence of speech as it was undertaken by that Elder.

It illuminates the state of having been completed. This same method applies to all other such places as well. Yugandhara and the others should be understood as the peripheral mountains (*paribhaṇḍapabbata*).
"As if at one and the same time" means "as if by a single stroke. Furthermore, this word *iva* ("as if") should be brought over and connected with the phrase "I am not able."

"I shall cause to proceed" means I shall cause my standing body to proceed. At the time of the aspiration, with reference to the mere fact of it being seen by knowledge in accordance with what was heard from the words of the Blessed One Anomadassi, it is said: "that first sight. Being unable to bear the essence of his virtues.
"This is the path" means this is the way leading to death for beings who are born. Furthermore, for those of such a nature...
"Formations called 'name'" means that formations are of such a nature; the meaning is that they end in death. "So much" means for so long a time.
"Having gathered together" means having brought together. "Having closed the mouth" means having covered the opening.
"Hundreds of flower-stalks" means hundreds of shrines consisting of buds and sprouts.

"On a previous day" means on a past day. Since the assembly of the Teacher’s disciples occurred on the very day the Dhamma-Senāpati attained Arahatship, it is said: "This bhikkhu has fulfilled the assembly of disciples.
"Five hundred births" is used in the locative sense, or as the accusative case expressing continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

“With a *kaḷopi* in hand” means with a vessel made of bamboo in hand; some also say it means with a vessel made of leather in hand. “In the midst of the city” means in the center of the town. “In the forest” means in the wilderness.
“Free from the manner of shrinking back” means free from the causes for retreating from the teaching of the Dhamma.

“Confident” means free from timidity. “The essence of the Dhamma” (*dhammoja*) means the flavor of the Dhamma; the meaning is the nutritive, vitalizing Dhamma of the teaching. “Enjoyment of the Dhamma” (*dhammabhoga*) means the utilization of the Dhamma.
“Enjoyment of the Dhamma” (*dhammasambhoga*) refers specifically to the teaching of the Dhamma as it proceeds by way of sharing with others.
Therefore, it is said: “By both [terms], the enjoyment of the Dhamma alone is expressed. [It is called] “dear” (*piya*) because it is to be cherished;
“agreeable” (*manāpa*) because it increases the mind. “By birth” (*jātiyā*) means by birth such as that of a kshatriya and so forth. “Difference” (*nānābhāva*).
Non-coexistence is separation. Change-of-state is alteration. "Body" refers to the body designated as the aggregate of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).
For when the material body breaks up, it indeed breaks up. "He would break up" means that great mass would break up.
"Gone to the southern direction" means proceeding toward the face of the southern direction. "Like a great trunk" means like a large, solid trunk.
Like a branch and a trunk. For the branches and trunk have a form that extends toward the directions, whereas the root-trunk has risen upward.
"Of the sixteen questions" means of the sixteen matters that proceed from one life to another. For a matter that is desired to be known is a question.
4–5. Commentary on the Ukkacelasutta, etc.

380–381. *Amāvasuposatha* means on the Uposatha day of the new moon; the meaning is "the Uposatha of the dark fortnight. *Purimanayeneva* means by the very method stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
6. Commentary on the *Uttiya-sutta* 382.
*Maccudheyyassa* means of the domain of death, that is, the sphere where death operates.
8. Commentary on the Brahma Sutta 384.
"At that time" refers to the period of the first full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*). There were no monks at all because the Wheel of Dhamma had not yet been set in motion;

for one becomes a monk only through connection with the characteristics of a monk. It is a "single path" (*ekamagga*) because it is a path that is singular, not one that has become a forked road. That—
The single path. The "end of birth" (*jātikkhayanta*) refers to Nibbāna, because the destruction of birth constitutes the end of the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
Since he has seen that, the meaning here should be understood as "one who sees the end of birth.
9. Commentary on the *Sedaka-sutta*.
385. "This is his doctrine" means this doctrine of that teacher which is now being stated.
"Without bending [the body] toward it" means without bending the body toward whichever direction the bamboo pole leans. For by leaning in that way, one would fall and be reduced to powder and dust.
"It" refers either to the body or to that bamboo pole. "As if pulling it" means pulling it from the point where it has been bent toward the opposite side.
"Having made it one-sided" means having made the aforementioned mindfulness well-established and inclined [towards the object].
He says, "having caused it to take hold of the support of the wind," because that act of making it so is done by causing it to grasp the support of the wind.
And that is done through the establishment of mindfulness for that purpose; thus he says, "having made mindfulness well-established. It is indeed motionless...
While sitting, the pupil protects the teacher; this much was said with reference to the teacher’s gain.
“The teacher, grasping the lineage well,” and so forth—all of this follows the same method explained below.
“He protects himself alone”: this was stated making his own protection the primary concern, not that of the pupil.
The fruit is restriction. Furthermore, when self-protection is accomplished here, the protection of the pupil is also necessarily accomplished.

The same method applies to the second alternative as well. "That is the principle there" means that whatever constitutes one's own protection is, in its essential meaning, also the protection of others;
this is the principle and the logical application here. "For further increase" means for the successive increase of that which has already increased.
By this, the mode of joy associated with what has been attained is shown; thus he said: "The meaning is 'with sympathetic joy together with its preliminary stage.

As for the words beginning with "by cultivation" and ending with "compassion" (since these demonstrate that for one who cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, the protection of both oneself and others is accomplished), [he says]: "Bhikkhus, thinking 'I shall protect myself'..."
"Mindfulness should be cultivated," and so forth, was said.
10. Commentary on the Janapadakalyāṇī Sutta: 386.
"A beauty in the land" means one who is excellent throughout the entire country by virtue of her physical perfection and her perfection in training.

And they were beautiful and excellent. Since the perfection of form consists in the complete fulfillment of the qualities of form through the total absence of any defects of form, both of these points are shown by the statement:
"free from the six bodily defects and endowed with the five kinds of excellence. Explaining those two types [of excellence], he said:
"She indeed," and so forth. "Endowed with the five kinds of excellence" means by way of the perfection of the fivefold qualities of the body.

She is endowed [with these qualities]. "Neither too tall nor too short" means she is of medium height; she is not of excessive height, nor is she too short, nor does she have the appearance of a dwarf.
"Neither too thin" means she is not excessively emaciated, with flesh and blood so depleted that her skeleton and network of veins are visible.
"Neither too stout" means she is not heavy-fleshed or pot-bellied. "Neither too dark nor too fair"—
She is not excessively black-colored like a burnt ember, nor does she have the color of polished bronze after being wiped with curd, buttermilk, and so forth.
She has "surpassed human appearance" because such perfection of form does not exist in the human world.
Just as she is possessed of the proper proportions, she is likewise pleasing to others due to her height and girth, being neither too tall nor otherwise. Thus...
It is said, "not having attained the divine beauty," referring even to the perfection of divine form for human beings.

Here, by the statement that [the body] is neither too tall nor too short, the perfection of height is expressed, because of its inspiring grace through its vertical dimension. By the statement regarding the absence of the defects of being emaciated or corpulent, the perfection of girth is expressed.
By both of these, the perfection of configuration is revealed; and by the statement that it is not too dark, the perfection of complexion is expressed.
Because of the absence of discoloration. "Piyaṅgusāmā" means she whose bodily luster resembles the color of a ripe piyaṅgu flower.
"The edge of the face" refers to the lower lip. This is the aforementioned excellence of bodily complexion. "Her" (assā) refers to Janapadakalyāṇī.

Her "excellence of skin" (chavikalyāṇatā) is due to the perfection of her skin. The same method applies to the remaining [parts]. The nails themselves, because they resemble leaves, are called "nail-leaves" (nakhapattāni).

"Movement" (*pasāvo*) means moving about by means of a limb of the body; thus he said, "the meaning is 'activity'. Movement occurs exactly according to what has been determined, not as a maintenance of its own inherent nature (*sabhāva*).
According to its manifestation (*vibhāva*), it dances the highest dance.

Or rather, because of their activity having reached the state of being sustained for more than twenty years, there is a dullness of activity; thus, due to the excellence of the manifestation of the sun (*vibhāvasu*), it indeed dances the highest dance.
And the meaning is that he sings a song. (The text up to this point is corrupt and difficult to correct; the correct reading should be sought.
"A bowl of oil filled to the brim" means an oil vessel whose mouth is filled with oil level with the rim.
"In the midst of a great assembly and in the midst of the most beautiful woman of the land" refers to the most beautiful woman of the land; of her...
And it [the oil] must be carried and led through the midst of a great multitude of people gathered to watch dancing, singing, and performances.
"It" refers to the oil. "Should carry" means he would incur [an offense]. Herein, this is the application of the simile: mindfulness directed to the body is like the oil-filled bowl;
the person carrying it is like the practitioner of insight (vipassaka); the crowds of people are like the various objects of perception; and the man with the sword is...

The arising of the mind is like the pouring of oil; the production of defilements is like the spilling of that oil; and the non-arising of the head of noble-path knowledge is like the falling of the *sīsa* fruit.
Because it is said, “Mindfulness directed to the body has not been developed by us... [it] should be practiced,” it is stated that “only preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) is being discussed.
The commentary on the Nālandavagga is finished.
3. The Chapter on the Stability of Virtue (Sīlaṭṭhitivagga) 1–2. Commentary on the Discourses on Virtue, etc. (Sīlasuttādīnaṃ vaṇṇanā) 387–388.
"Virtues" (sīlāni) is in the plural because virtue is of many kinds. For although it is of one kind in the sense of "steadiness" (sīlana), [it is manifold in its specific forms].
It is of many kinds by way of conduct (*cāritta*) and so forth. Therefore he said: "the fourfold purification of virtue" (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
"Investigation of a question" (*pañhagavesana*) is the examination of a matter desired to be known. Therefore he said: "the seeking of a question. 3–5.
Commentary on the *Parihānasutta* and others.

389–391. Decline occurs by way of the person (*puggala*), not by way of the phenomenon (*dhamma*). It declines only for one who does not cultivate [the path]. Therefore he said, “For whoever,” and so forth. 6.
Commentary on the *Padesasutta* (Discourse on the Partial): 392.

“Because it has been cultivated only partially” means because it has been cultivated only in part, due to the non-attainment of the fullness of cultivation (*bhāvanāpāripūri*). Therefore he said, “For there are four paths,” and so forth.
7. Commentary on the *Samatta-sutta* (Sutta 393):
"Because they have been mastered and developed" means because they have been thoroughly mastered and cultivated.
8–10. Commentary on the *Loka-sutta* and following suttas.

394–396. One who possesses great direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) because they have a vast range is "one of great direct knowledge" (*mahābhiñño*); the state of being such a person is to be explained in its entirety.
Having stated, "It was spoken by way of his constant dwelling," the passage beginning with "The Elder, it is said... was spoken in order to make that meaning clear. "Of him" means of the Elder.
"The course of adverting" (*āvajjanassa gatiṃ*) refers to the path of movement of a single act of adverting alone. "He follows after" (*anubandhati*).

This shows that by means of a single act of adverting the mind (*ekāvajjana*), one is capable of knowing whatever desired object exists within a thousand world-systems (*sahassalokadhātu*) consisting of a thousand world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*).
The commentary on the Chapter on Virtue and Stability is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Chapter on What Has Not Been Heard.

397–407. “Having comprehended whatever feeling” means having comprehended whatever feeling belonging to the three planes. “That very [feeling] for him” means that very feeling belonging to the three planes belongs to that bhikkhu.
This is stated by way of similarity; having been known in the prior stage through the comprehension of impermanence and so forth, they appear at the time of comprehension.
“In those that have been grasped” means in those that have been taken up after being delimited by way of full understanding (*parijānana*).

“They say that feeling, thought, and perception are stated as the contemplation [of the aggregates] by way of being the roots of the proliferation of craving, the proliferation of conceit, and the proliferation of views, respectively.
Others say: “Feeling, thought, and perception are [stated] by way of showing the roots of the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views.
The commentary to the *Ananussuta-vagga* is finished.
5. The Chapter on the Deathless (Amatavagga) 2. Commentary on the Discourse on Origination (Samudayasuttavaṇṇanā) 408.

“The foundations of mindfulness characterized by objects” means that the foundations of mindfulness are described here as being defined by their objects, not by the characteristic of mindfulness itself.
4. Commentary on the Satisutta 410.
Having made it simple and having treated each [factor] separately. And so it is said in the Pāḷi: “Or, monks, in regard to the body.
6. Commentary on the Pātimokkhasaṃvarasutta.
412. "Foremost virtue" (*jeṭṭhakasīla*) means preeminent virtue. For in the Canon, the mention of "virtue" (*sīla*) occurs specifically by way of the restraint of the Pātimokkha.

Therefore, he said: "But the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga," and so forth. In that context, the restriction "the restraint of the Pātimokkha alone is virtue" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ*) illuminates that the other three [bases of virtue] are, in part, included within the Pātimokkha. For instance, in the case of "not looking where one should not look":

An offense is prescribed for transgressing the six training rules for the sake of livelihood, as well as for the unreflective use of requisites for the sick. "Three" refers to the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth.

Regarding the statement that there is no place where they are called "virtue" (sīla), this means there is no place in any sutta where they are included under the designation of virtue; thus, it rejects their status as absolute virtue.
"Merely guarding the six doors" refers to its ease of practice, because it returns to its natural state through the mere resolve of the mind.
The same method applies to the other two as well. "The mere arising of conditions" shows the cause by means of the fruit;
for the arising of conditions has production as its cause. "This purpose" means this motive for the utilization of these conditions.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). By the phrase "not figuratively" (*nippariyāyena*), he shows that the three [virtues] beginning with restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) are called "figurative virtues" (*pariyāyasīla*) because they function as the preservation and purification of the virtue of exertion (*padhānasīla*).

Now, in order to clarify through a simile—both by way of contrast (*vyatireka*) and by way of agreement (*anvaya*)—the preeminence of the Pātimokkha virtue itself, he says "of whom," and so forth. Therein, "he" refers to the restraint of the Pātimokkha (*pātimokkhasaṃvara*).

The remaining [virtues], such as restraint of the sense faculties and so forth, are included. Furthermore, the meaning of the word *pātimokkha* has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā* and other works;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated therein.

"Endowed with proper conduct (*ācāra*) and resort (*gocara*)" means being endowed with conduct consisting of the non-transgression of bodily and mental [precepts], and with a resort consisting of [avoiding] prostitutes and the like.
“Endowed with resort” means one who is endowed with proper conduct and resort (*sampannācāra-gocara*). “In even trifling matters” means in very slight matters that lead to non-offenses;
others say it refers to mere *dukkaṭa* and *dubbhāsita* offenses. “In faults” means in things not to be done, which are censurable.
Since those are exclusively unwholesome states, he says: “in unwholesome qualities (*akusaladhamma*)”. “Seeing danger” means seeing [them] as fearful.
"Of a nature to see" means being of a nature to regard even a fault as small as an atom as if it were the size of Mount Sineru.
"Having properly undertaken" means having properly, respectfully, and completely undertaken [them].

Regarding the phrase "in the training rules," he says "in the training rules, this or that training rule," etc., showing that the locative case is used in the sense of singling out a part from a whole.
The intention is that the training rule (sikkhāpada) must be undertaken and practiced. "Training" (sikkhā) refers here to the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā).
He said, "in the divisions of training," because while the word *pada* previously had the sense of a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna), it should be understood here in the sense of a portion (bhāga).
Whatever virtue is to be practiced and fulfilled—whether it be the original formulation (mūlapaññatti), a subsequent formulation (anupaññatti), or other such categories—that is what is meant.
He says, "It is twofold according to its door," namely: "either bodily or verbal.

In this interpretation of the meaning, the locative case in "in the training rules" (*sikkhāpadesu*) denotes the locus, because no separate category is mentioned apart from the constituent parts of the training. Therefore he says, "all that [pertaining] to each.
Because of the statement, "Therefore, O bhikkhu, relying on virtue," non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view are also included.
Since it was stated that "virtue" (sīla) is what is meant [by the term], it is said in this sutta: "Only the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is spoken of.
7. Commentary on the Duccarita Sutta: 413.
Here too, it is said "the latter three as well," taking it to mean that mental good conduct is also called virtue.

It should be understood that the qualities of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view constitute virtue (*sīla*), because after mentioning the good conduct of body and speech, the good conduct of mind is also stated, followed by the words: "Then, O bhikkhu, relying on virtue and established in virtue.
The rest is exactly as previously explained. Regarding the sixth and seventh [chapters]: there is nothing new in the sixth and seventh sections (*vagga*). Therefore...
It is said: "The meaning should be understood in the same manner as explained above.
However, from among the series of chapters (*vagga-peyyāla*) in this *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta*, only a few chapters have been included;

nevertheless, because there is no distinction in their meaning, they have been abbreviated by showing merely the headings in some manuscripts, while in others they are extremely abbreviated. Having grouped these together into two [sections] by way of summary—
"The sixth and seventh" has been stated.
The commentary on the Amata Chapter is finished.
The commentary on the Saṃyutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna) is finished.
4. Connected Discourses on the Faculties (Indriya-saṃyutta) 1.
The Chapter on the Pure (Suddhika-vagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Pure (Suddhika-sutta-vaṇṇanā)

471. Regarding the four planes (*catubhūmaka*)... [they] are obtained for those three faculties because of their being either wholesome (*kusala*) or indeterminate (*abyākata*). The faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*)...
[they] are obtained everywhere because they are common to the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*). "By way of the four planes...
means that it is stated both by way of delimiting phenomena belonging to the four planes and by way of delimiting all-encompassing phenomena such as the wholesome and so forth.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins (Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā): 477.

“By way of the truth of suffering” means they do not understand it as being the truth of suffering. For that [the five aggregates] is comprised within the truth of suffering because it is to be fully understood (pariññeyya).
“By way of the truth of the origin” means they do not understand craving, ignorance, and so forth, as being the truth of the origin for the faculty of faith.
"Cessation" refers to Nibbāna, the sign of cessation through non-clinging of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
"The way" refers to the Noble Path, the practice leading to the cessation of the faculty of faith.

"In the others" means in the case of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and so forth. "In the bright side" refers to the blameless category proceeding in the manner beginning with "understanding the faculty of faith. By way of resolve (*adhimokkha*).
"Arising from adverting" means by way of the arising of adverting through the resolution of faith (*saddhādhimokkha*) occurring in the prior stage in the manner beginning with "there is giving.
Therefore, it is faith itself that first arises which is here called "adverting," not the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*).
This same method applies to the others as well. Thus, the adverting that first arises is the basis for the production of the sharp [impulsions] of exertion.
It should be understood that the initial arising of the faculties of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and so forth is described by way of the process of adverting (*āvajjana*).
For the first-arisen [faculties] are weak due to the absence of exertion; thus, they are the "origination" (*samudaya*) of the faculties of energy and so forth once these have attained strength.

Consequently, they are called their "origination" because they occupy the position of adverting for those [stronger faculties]. This refers to what previously occurred by way of resolving (*adhimuccana*) and so on.
The meaning is "the arising of adverting. Again, "by way of desire" means by way of the unwholesome desire consisting in the wish to act;

that is, by way of the desire that occurs in the mode of wishing to arouse faith and the other [faculties]. "The arising of adverting by way of attention" means by way of the appropriate attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) that produces it—that weak [adverting] which occurs by way of the faculty of faith and so forth.
Regarding the arising of adverting (*āvajjana*): "In this way also" means even by the manner described in the passage beginning with "by way of resolution" (*adhimokkha-vasena*).

"In the six suttas" refers to the six suttas starting from the second. Only the Four Noble Truths are taught therein; for, by the apprehension of gratification (*assāda*), the truth of the origin (*samudaya-sacca*) is grasped;

by the apprehension of danger (*ādīnava*), the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) is grasped; and by the apprehension of escape (*nissaraṇa*), the truths of cessation (*nirodha-sacca*) and the path (*magga-sacca*) are grasped.
In the first sutta, however, there is merely a presentation of the actual nature of the faculties.
8. Commentary on the Dabbasutta 478.
It is called *sotāpatti* because one enters [the stream] by means of it; it is the first path toward the future. "Stream" (*sota*) refers to the stream of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

It should be seen. "Is incurred" means it is undertaken from the beginning. Here, the factors of one who has entered the stream (*sotāpanna*)—which are the signs for the attainment of the first path—are called "the factors of stream-entry.
These, moreover, should be understood as faith and virtue dear to the noble ones (*ariyakanta-sīla*), existing in three locations.
"In its own domain" means in its own sphere. "For the purpose of showing preeminence" means for the purpose of showing its primary status.
The meaning is: to show the preeminence of the function of those [faculties] such as faith (*saddhā*) where their activity is particularly outstanding.
Now, in order to clarify that meaning by means of similes, the passage beginning with “Just as... is stated. “Having reached” means having attained the position of its own preeminent function.
“Foremost” means that which precedes and leads the task of believing. “The rest” refers to the faculties of energy (*vīriya*) and so forth.
“Connected with that” means following after it; they are the factors belonging to that [set] beginning with the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*). This same method applies to the others as well.
Regarding “in the jhānas and liberations,” this refers to the jhānas—designated here as liberations—because concentration is predominant in them.
By taking it thus, the statement “having attained the factors of stream-entry” is justified. For morality has faith as its proximate cause (*upaniṣad*).
"Having reached the Noble Truths" means having attained the four truths that are to be fully realized (*abhisametabba*).
9–10. Commentary on the First Vibhaṅga Sutta, etc., §§479–480.
"Cleverness (*nepakka*) is called wisdom (*paññā*)," thus he said: "This is what is meant by wisdom. It leads away from the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*).
One who "clears away" or "expels" [the defilements] is "discerning" (*nipaka*); this refers to a person possessing firm and intense mindfulness.

Its abstract state is "discernment" (*nepakkatā*), and it is entirely appropriate that this discernment also applies to mindfulness. For in this way, the expression "by means of mindfulness and discernment" (*satinepakkena*) is justified;
and by being stated thus—as "mindfulness and discernment"—an explicit description of mindfulness is indeed established. [This is found in] such-and-such a sutta.

2. Mudutaravagga 1.
Paṭilābhasuttavaṇṇanā 481.
"With reference to the right efforts" means with reference to the right efforts by way of their cultivation. Therefore he said, "cultivating."

Just as in the exposition of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), the teaching comes down as, "One acquires energy by undertaking the four right endeavors (*sammappadhāna*)," so too in the exposition of the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*), it says, "One acquires mindfulness by undertaking the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

Therefore, it is said: "The same method applies to the faculty of mindfulness as well. However, in the expositions of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and the others, he does not teach in that way.
2. Commentary on the First Short Discourse (Paṭhamasaṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā) 482.
It is stated that "the state of the faculties being sharp, etc., should be understood by way of insight, or by way of the path, or by way of the fruit" (*tatoti...
pe... veditabbaṃ*). But is it not the case that only the state of being pliant (*mudubhāva*) is mentioned here in the text? This is true.
It is said that if there is no state of sharpness, then there is no state of being sharp and so forth.

For this [quality] receives the designation "this is soft" or "from this, that is sharp" because the states of sharpness and softness are established through mutual dependence, like "this shore" and "the further shore.
Now, in order to show in detail the meaning briefly stated by the words "from that" and so forth, [the text says] "fully completed," etc.
It has been stated. In that context, "perfected" (*samattāni*) means "accomplished. The other term is a synonym for that very same word.
Alternatively, "perfected" (*samattāni*) means "mastered"; such is the meaning of "perfected. Why was it said, "The faculties of the path of the Dhamma-follower are even more subtle than those"?

For by the word "than those" (*tato*), the very faculties of insight belonging to the stream-entry path are intended; thus, the first path mentioned as being "even more subtle than those" [is the path of the Dhamma-follower].
"Does it deviate [from the rule] that one must be either a follower of the Dhamma (dhammānusārī) or a follower by faith (saddhānusārī)?
This is not a fault, because the distinction in insight (vipassanā) is intended with reference to the first path attained by means of a portion of the stream-entry path itself.

For in the case of one who, having become a stream-enterer, reaches the once-returning path (sakadāgāmimagga) without disturbing his posture while remaining just as he was sitting, his insight-faculties..."
It was stated with intentional ambiguity and without distinction: "The insight-faculties of the stream-entry path are even more subtle than those.

However, for one who, having become a stream-enterer, later becomes a once-returner, the insight-faculties that arose for the sake of the stream-entry path are indeed what are called his insight-faculties.
If he belongs to the lineage of a follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārīgotra), then [his faculties] arise from the aforementioned insight-faculties.
"More supple" means "more supple than those [faculties] of the follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārī) path," as it has been stated.

The connection is made by supplying the words "the faculties of insight. He himself will later explain the reason why the faculties of insight of the follower by faith (saddhānusārī) are more supple than those of the follower by Dhamma.
One is a "follower by Dhamma" because one follows the stream of the path through the Dhamma, that is, through wisdom.

The noble one who has wisdom as his preeminent quality is the *saddhānusārī* (follower by faith), for he follows the stream of the path by means of faith; this is the noble one who has faith as his preeminent quality.
Having thus shown [the faculties] by way of insight (*vipassanā*), the passage beginning with "likewise" (*tathā*) is commenced to show them by way of the path (*magga*).

The faculties included in the path of Arahantship are the faculties of the path of Arahantship, both in terms of their association and their intrinsic nature. This same method applies here to the faculties of the fruit of Arahantship as well.

Now, in order to show [the distinction] by way of the fruit, it was said: "fully undertaken and fulfilled," and so forth. A differentiation has arisen by way of the person standing on the path of stream-entry;
therefore, the intention is that both of those [the path-attainer and the one established in the fruit] are not included here in the third stage.

To explain how the differentiation between the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) and the faith-follower (saddhānusārī) arises, he said: "by way of arrival and by way of the path. Demonstrating both of these, he said: "The person who is a faith-follower," and so forth.
"Causing to recite" means one who is receiving the recitation.
The path is sharp because of the sharp and intense state of the supporting faculties (*upanissaya-indriya*). Therefore he said: "It carries forth heroic knowledge.
"Without effort" means by its own inherent power; "without exertion" is a synonym for that same term. For the person who follows the Dhamma...
Upon arrival, one who suppresses the defilements is able to suppress them without pain, without difficulty, and without fatigue;
however, a person who follows by faith (saddhānusārī) is able to suppress them only after experiencing pain, difficulty, and fatigue.
Therefore, at the stage of the preliminary path, the knowledge that cuts off the defilements for one who follows by Dhamma (dhammānusārī) is unimpeded.

It flows with sharpness; just as when one cuts a plantain tree with a sharp sword, the cut surface becomes smooth, the sword glides swiftly, no sound is heard, and there is no need for strenuous effort—such is the preliminary development of the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī).
However, for the faith-follower (saddhānusārī), at the moment of the preliminary stage, it is the knowledge that severs the defilements.

Being dull, not sharp, and lacking courage, it proceeds slowly; just as when one cuts a plantain tree with a sword that is not very sharp, the cut surface is not smooth, the sword does not move quickly, a sound is heard, and a great deal of strenuous effort must be exerted—such is the preliminary stage of development for one who follows by faith (*saddhānusārī*).
Even so, regarding the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*), [the path is slow].

There is no diversity. Therefore he said, “But in the destruction of the defilements,” and so forth. Furthermore, the remaining defilements are destroyed because they are associated with the destruction of the fetters.
3. Commentary on the Second Brief Discourse (Dutiyasaṃkhittasutta).
483. “From that” means from the fruit; because of the difference in the fruits, there is a difference in conduct. There is a difference in the faculties (*indriya*) such as faith and the rest.
By way of the diversity of the faculties. "Diversity of fruits" refers to the diversity of the fruit of arhatship and so forth.
"Diversity of persons" refers to the diversity of persons such as non-returners and others. 4. Commentary on the Third Abbreviated Discourse.

484. By fulfilling completely through the aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth, as well as the faculties of faith (*saddhindriya*) and so forth, one who is making the path to Arahatship complete attains and produces the fruit of Arahatship by way of its accomplishment.

"Three partial paths" refers to the three lower paths which constitute mere portions due to the non-fulfillment of the aggregates of virtue and so forth. "Partial" refers to the three lower fruits. "In the four" refers to...
In this chapter, regarding the first four suttas: although it is stated here that in the third [sutta] the ablative case (*nissakka*) is used in the sense of a fruit (*phala*),
and in the fourth it is said, "One who fulfills [them] fully attains the full [fruit], one who practices partially attains the partial [fruit]," nevertheless,
because of the statement that "in all four suttas the faculties are described as mixed," they are also [to be understood] by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
It should be understood that the application [of the grammatical case] is indeed obtained.
5–7. Commentary on the First Detailed Discourse, etc. (Suttas 485–487).
In this sutta, the ablative case (*nissakka*) should be understood by way of insight (*vipassanā*), not by way of the path and fruit (*maggaphala*).

Because it is precisely the faculties of insight (*vipassanindriya*) in their entirety that are intended here. Now, in order to make this meaning clear, the passage beginning with “They are complete” is stated.

One who attains final nibbāna in the interval—namely, among the five Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) such as the Aviha—heya because he attains final nibbāna by means of the complete extinction of defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*) in the interim, without exceeding the midpoint of his lifespan there, and without exertion or effort (*asaṅkhāra*).

One who attains final nibbāna without exertion is called "one who attains nibbāna without exertion" (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*) because of passing away with ease; by contrast, one who attains it with exertion is "one who attains nibbāna with exertion" (*sa-saṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*).
One is "an upstreamer" (*uddhaṃsota*) because his stream of craving or his stream of the cycle of existence flows upwards due to his state of being carried upward;
or he is an upstreamer because his stream of the Path must be attained after going upward. He is "one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm" (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*) because he goes to the state of Akaniṭṭha.
In this way, the meaning of the word should be understood here.
Regarding the phrase "in this place," it refers to the place described as "the ablative by way of insight" (*vipassanāvasena nissakka*).

"Standing only in the path of Arahantship" means standing only in the path of Arahantship within this very existence, and not by standing in insight (*vipassanā*). There are five types of the ablative (*nissakka*).

“Those which are to be excluded” means that one should explain them by setting aside the five types of non-returners, beginning with “one who attains Nibbāna in the interval is [inferior] to those even milder than he.
Now, explaining this meaning, he says: “Of the path to arahantship,” and so forth.
Therein, because he attains final Nibbāna immediately after being reborn among the Aviha deities and so on, he is the first type of one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyī*).

In this context, one who attains *parinibbāna* before reaching the midpoint of the lifespan is to be understood as the second type of "one who attains *parinibbāna* in the interval" (*antarā-parinibbāyī*);

one who attains *parinibbāna* after reaching the midpoint of the lifespan is to be understood as the third type of "one who attains *parinibbāna* in the interval. Why was it said, "There are five departures" (*pañca nissakkāni*)?

Is it not the case that one should speak of "one who attains *parinibbāna* without exertion" (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*) and "one who attains *parinibbāna* with exertion" (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*)? [The author] shows that it should not be so stated.
He said: "There are these same five types of persons, including both those who attain parinibbāna without exertion and those who attain parinibbāna with exertion.
Regarding the three ablative cases: the three ablative expressions are "one becomes a stream-enterer by means of faculties weaker than those" and so forth.
Here, the once-returner is not included; he must be brought out by way of the path of non-returning, through the insight-faculties of the path of non-returning.
With [the faculties] that are softer, one becomes a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*). Regarding the phrase "softer still" (*mudutarānīti*):

this is stated by taking three [factors], namely, that the insight-faculties of the once-returner path are softer than the insight-faculties of the stream-enterer designated as "one-seeded" (*ekabījī*).

Since the pair beginning with the "Dhamma-follower" (*dhammānusārī*) is included within the pair beginning with the "family-to-family" (*kolaṃkola*), the passage beginning with "of the once-returner path" explains the meaning of what has already been stated.
The commentary. The remainder is exactly according to the method explained below. The sixth and seventh [sections] are according to the same method;

thus, the sixth and seventh suttas are according to the method explained in the second and third. However, there is this distinction: in those [previous sections], the mixed faculties were discussed, whereas here, the faculties of preliminary insight (*pubbabhāga-vipassanā-indriya*) are discussed.
8. Commentary on the Paṭipannasutta 488.
The word *taṃ* (that) is used in the sense of a genitive (*nissakka*) referring to the paths and fruits. This is precisely what is stated in the Pāḷi:

“He is one who has entered upon the way for the realization of the fruit of arahantship,” and so forth. “By eight” means by the four fruits and the four paths—thus, by eight. It is external (*bahibhūto*).
It is not an internal state. Only supramundane faculties are spoken of here, because they are included within the arising of consciousness associated with the paths and fruits.
9–10. Commentary on the *Sampanna-sutta*, etc. (489–490).

Regarding the phrase "endowed with faculties" (*indriyasampanno*), the word "endowed" (*sampanna*) has the sense of "fulfillment"; thus it says, "one whose faculties are fulfilled" (*paripuṇṇindriyo*). The faculties are spoken of as mixed, because they are taught in their general commonality.
The commentary on the Mudutaravagga is finished.
