2. Commentary on the Jīvitindriya Sutta.
492. *Itthibhāve* means in the state of femininity. It exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) because it serves as the common cause for the characteristics of beings attached to that state.
The faculty of a woman is the *itthindriya*. This same method applies to the male faculty (*purisindriya*).

*Jīvite* means in the living, sustaining, and maintaining of co-nascent phenomena. *Vaṭṭindriyāni* means the faculties that have become causes for the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). For among these appropriated faculties—
When there is existence, the round of rebirth proceeds and is made known.
3. Commentary on the Aññindriya Sutta: 493.
"A state (dhamma) never known before" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; likewise, "those very states already known" refers to those same truths.
This is the meaning here: it is called *aññā* (full knowledge) because one knows (*ājānāti*). The meaning is that one knows without overstepping what has already been known by the first path.
This is the name for the six types of noble persons, beginning with the stream-enterer. *Aññindriyāni* means the faculties of full knowledge. *Aññātāvīsūti* means among those who have fully known.
Because the function of knowledge regarding the states of the highest fruit is preeminent, therefore that same function [is present] in the remaining states as well.
Having added [the phrase], it is said: "among those who have realized the states of the fruit of arahantship. Therein, "in this or that" refers to those various paths and fruits.
"In this or that manner" refers to the manner of knowing what was previously unknown, and so forth.
4. Commentary on the Ekabījī Sutta (The One-Seed Sutta)

494. "Departing from insight" (*vipassanāto nissakkanti*) means departing by means of the faculties of insight (*vipassanindriyehi*). Now, expanding upon that very point which was stated in brief, he says, "fully completed," and so forth.
In this context, three departures should be brought out as five departures through the analysis of the "single-seeder" (*ekabījī*) and others.
Therefore, he says, "of the once-return path," and so forth. [This refers to] the stream-entry path.

The "insight-faculties" (vipassanindriyāni) referred to here are the insight-faculties of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) who is proceeding toward the attainment of the once-return path (sakadāgāmimagga) within that same existence.
Since all five of these belong to the very category of the stream-entry path, it is said that they "should be brought forth while standing upon the once-return path."
Regarding the term "Ekabījī" (One-Seeded): here, what is called "khandhabīja" (the seed of the aggregates) is being discussed.

For that stream-enterer who has one seed of the aggregates—that is, one more taking up of a personal existence—he is called an Ekabījī. Therefore it was said: "Having become a stream-enterer," and so forth.
Furthermore, while "human existence" is mentioned here merely as a pedagogical device, it is certainly appropriate to say that he produces a divine existence as well.
The Blessed One assigned these names. For it is when one has reached such a measure that the Blessed One gave them their respective names:
"one who has seven births at most," "one who goes from family to family," and "the single-seeder.
"Two or three existences" refers to two or three births among gods and humans alone. "Supreme" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Truths of full enlightenment.
That which has enlightenment as its destination, support, and goal is called *sambodhiparāyaṇa*. One who goes from family to family is called *kolaṅkola*.
For from the time one begins the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), there is no longer birth in a low family;
the meaning is that one is reborn only in families of great wealth. Indeed, even the word "family" (*kula*) alone refers specifically to a family of great wealth. Two...
“Two or three families” means two or three existences by way of gods and humans; this too is described as a mixed existence (*missakabhava*).
This is a name for one born through noble birth (*ariyāya jātiyā*), like a newborn boy;
that is to say, it is a designation such as “one who has seven births at most” and so forth. Showing this, he said: “By way of the name taken by the Blessed One,” and so on.

If, because of the necessity of past causes, the stream-enterer is considered "fixed," then since there would be no decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the three paths subsequent to the path of stream-entry, it would follow that there is no function for past causes;
thus, the path of stream-entry itself would have to serve as its own decisive support.
If even that [path] were to have a past cause as its decisive support, then prior to the arising of the path of stream-entry by way of such necessity—
Thus being determined, as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, that which is called his "prior cause" (pubbahetu) would become causeless;
consequently, its accomplishment would result in being without cause or condition. And why so?
Because if one is determined as a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), then by the very attainment of the first path, the functions of the three subsequent paths are accomplished in due order. Thus...

If there were a fixed rule such as "seven times at most" and so forth, then because suffering would continue beyond the seventh existence, the defilements that are the root of suffering would be exhausted by the first path alone; thus, the three subsequent paths would become redundant. Therefore he said:
"The decisive support for the first path has been established," and so on.
If the three higher paths were to determine one as "one who has at most seven more births" and so forth, then there would be no other stream-enterer (sotāpanna) besides them;
consequently, it would follow that the function of the path of stream-entry is unperformed and purposeless.

If, on the other hand, its function is the abandoning of personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and the rest—since by the abandoning of each of these, one is determined as "having at most seven more births" and so on—then [the function] must exist until...

"If they were only the higher paths," [it would follow that] because they do not proceed beyond the seven existences and because the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth cannot be abandoned without them, they must exist even without that [first path]; thus he says:

"It follows that the three higher paths have arisen even when the first path has not yet arisen. "Of the three paths" means of the three paths above. It is logical that "insight (*vipassanā*) determines" them.
Explaining the meaning already stated, he said, "If indeed," and so forth.
A stream-enterer (sotāpanna) has a disposition toward the round of existence (vaṭṭa). Therein, showing some who are well-known and famous, he said, "Anāthapiṇḍika," and so forth.

"Here, for one who is a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) mixed with the eight [attainments]" refers to one who, while established in this sensual realm (kāmabhava), exists as a human or a deva.
And by way of one who is born into various states of existence and is a dry-insight practitioner (*sukkha-vipassaka*), the name "one who has seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparamo*) is stated.
However, some say, "He is reborn only seven times in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*), and not beyond that"; this should be investigated. "I shall purify it" means:
"In Jambudīpa, together with any bhikkhu who is a master of the Three Piṭakas, [I shall verify] the Three Piṭakas themselves."
Thinking, "I shall purify [my understanding] by means of formal learning and interrogation," he went to Jambudīpa on the opposite shore. The construction is: "Whatever bhikkhu is capable.
Even for one who is intent upon a single aspect among the contemplations such as impermanence, when following the method of the Abhidhamma, one attains the path through the three liberations alone;
thus, due to the difference in their points of focus, these three types of persons have emerged from emptiness.
Likewise, there are six who have emerged from the three wishless [liberations], making twelve once-returners by way of the faith-follower and the wisdom-follower.
Similarly, there are five arahants— three who attain parinibbāna in the interval, one who attains parinibbāna upon landing,
and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm— and these become ten through the distinction between those who attain parinibbāna without exertion and those who attain parinibbāna with exertion.

495–500. 506. "Bodily" (*kāyika*) is stated as its definition by way of its basis; thus he says, "having the sensitive body as its physical basis.

9. Commentary on the Kaṭṭhopama Sutta (The Simile of the Fire-drill) 509.
"Of two fire-drills" (*dvinnaṃ araṇīnaṃ*) means of the lower and upper fire-drills.

To exclude the case where two things have merely come into contact but have not yet met together, the phrase "from their contact and meeting together" (*saṅghaṭṭana-samodhānā*) is stated. Again and again...

For the manifestation of heat occurs through friction. The physical basis and the object are like the lower fire-stick; even in the absence of effort, they serve as conditions for that kind of contact.
Contact is like the upper fire-stick, because it proceeds by means of the contact between the physical basis and the object.
The friction of contact is like the rubbing together of the two fire-sticks, proceeding in the manner of the friction of contact itself upon the physical basis and the object.

Feeling is like fire in the sense of burning and in its momentary destruction. Alternatively, the basis and the object are like the upper and lower kindling sticks, because their occurrence is possible through the exertion found in the striking, seizing, and so forth of the fuel;

510. *Rasa* means the breaking, the ceasing [of defilements]. Whatever is the *rasa* (taste/essence) of phenomena, according to the nature of those phenomena—that is, by that *rasa* according to the nature of the phenomena.

"In this analysis of the faculties" (*indriyavibhaṅge*) means in this analysis of the faculties known as the *Indriya-saṃyutta*. "Because it was not taught" (*adesitattā*).

"Touched by the harsh contact of the wrinkle" means touched by the roughness of the skin's folds. "That" refers to the sensation of thorns and the like. "Of this faculty of pain" (*dukkhindriya*).

"Of those various [faculties]" refers to the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) and the others. "Precisely by way of their respective causes" means by way of their specific, individual causes. For, in showing their specific causes, he said: "or of the bowl, robes, and so forth."
"Ekato va" means "all at once," without extracting the words again and again. The connection is made by supplying the phrase:
"They cease precisely at the moment of access (upacāra) to the second jhāna and so forth. "Of these" refers to the pain faculty, the mental grief faculty, and the rest.

"Complete cessation" (atisayanirodha) means thorough abandonment, a subsiding through their direct opposites. "Cessation itself" (nirodho yeva) means mere cessation. "In various adverting" (nānāvajjane).
The advertence by which the path of absorption (appanāvīthi) occurs may be either a single advertence or multiple advertences.
For in the path of absorption, access concentration involves a single advertence, whereas the other [preliminary stage] involves multiple advertences because it proceeds many times.

Fatigue arising from an uneven sitting posture is the affliction caused by an unbalanced seat. "By the suffusion of rapture" means because rapture has the function of suffusing. Of those things originated by rapture...
Or it is stated because of the pervading of the body by more sublime forms. Therefore he said: "The entire body becomes suffused with pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "even though there is a condition consisting of applied thought and sustained thought," the word *pi* (even/also) is used in the sense of "impossibility";

it should be brought over and connected with the words "of that which has been abandoned," as in "even though the faculty of grief has been abandoned. The connection is: "this faculty of grief arises."

From the statement, “As I was reflecting and examining for too long, my body grew weary and my mind became distressed,” it should be understood that weariness of body and mind has initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained examination (*vicāra*) as their conditions.

The phrase “the faculty of mental grief arises when there is initial application and sustained examination” should be supplied and connected [to the context]. “It may arise therein” means that its arising occurs in that state.
In the access to the second jhāna, there might be the arising of that mental distress (*domanassa*).
The phrase “there might be its arising therein” is a hypothetical statement intended to show that at the moment of access, mental distress has been thoroughly abandoned.

For it has been said: “But certainly not in the second jhāna, because the conditions for it have been abandoned. Even though the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) has been abandoned [in the second jhāna],...
It is said to be "near" because it is not made distant, like joy (*pīti*). He says, "having reached absorption," and so forth, to show this meaning:
that even though the factor of abandoning has been abandoned during the access stage of various adverting, it might arise again from time to time because it has not been struck down by its opposite.
[He says this] because such repetition is desirable, just as the two or three rounds of impulsion prior to the path-process consist of the same kind of contemplation.

They say: "Just as [in the case of the first jhāna], here too two or three rounds of impulsion (javana) proceeding prior to the section on absorption (appanāvāra) occur accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).
Regarding "without remainder" (aparisesa), it means "entirely," in the sense of being completely suppressed (suvikkhambhita) through suppression (vikkhambhana).

"For the sake of suchness" (tathattāya) means for the state of being thus, that is, for the possession of the first jhāna. Furthermore, that [possession] occurs either through its arising or, once arisen, through...
"It occurs either by entering [the attainment]" means "for the purpose of arising and for the purpose of entering," as it was stated. "In two" refers to the ninth and tenth Suttantas.

Now, in order to clarify that meaning by means of a simile, the passage beginning with “Just as indeed” was spoken.

"Of one another" means: one [person] [experiences] for another. One does not experience [the other's feeling] because the other is not within one's own sphere of experience. “He experiences the range of the object-domain. "Mindfulness of the Path" refers to mindfulness of the Noble Path. For when one is devoted to meditation, the impulsive mind (javana-mano), having exerted itself, [attains] mindfulness of the Path.

The five unwholesome states of consciousness—namely, those associated with wrong view and the mind accompanied by doubt—are abandoned through their total eradication (*samuccheda*). Regarding the "five hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*):

here, those leading to rebirth in the states of misery are abandoned by the first path itself, while the others are abandoned by meditative absorption (*jhāna*) through suppression (*vikkhambhana*). Thus, among the five...

1. Commentary on the *Apārasutta* 813.
"Concentration that proceeds by depending on desire" (*chandha-samādhi*) refers to the concentration obtained by making the desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) predominant.
"Exertive formations" (*padhāna-saṅkhārā*) is a designation for the energy of right effort (*sammappadhāna-viriya*) which accomplishes the four functions.

"By that" means by the volitional formations of desire, concentration, and exertion. "Bases of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) refers to these volitional formations associated with wholesome consciousness—such as access concentration and so forth—which are designated as "psychic powers" (*iddhi*) either in the sense of accomplishment (*ijjhana*) as a synonym for their production, or by the alternative method of explaining that through them faith and the other [faculties] succeed, become successful, grow, and reach excellence.
Thus, it refers to the volitional formations of desire, concentration, and exertion.
In the sense of being a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it is the "foot" (*pāda*); the meaning is that it is the basis for the remaining collection of consciousness and mental factors (*cittacetasika*).
And because that very aforementioned psychic power (*iddhi*) serves as the foot for each successive higher stage in relation to each preceding lower one, it is therefore said:

"The 'basis of psychic power' (*iddhipāda*) is the foot that has become psychic power. Regarding the "others," this refers to energy (*vīriya*), concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth; for therein, energy, consciousness, and investigation [are the bases].
Taking that as the dominant influence (*adhipati*), the concentration thus attained should be understood as "concentration through investigation" (*vīmaṃsāsamādhi*).
"Herein" (*idha*) means in this *Iddhipāda-saṃyutta*. This exposition of the meaning consists of a single chapter.

817. "A portion of the bases of psychic power" (*iddhipadesa*) means a single part of psychic power (*iddhi*). As to what that is, he says: "the three paths and the three fruits. 6. Commentary on the *Samatta Sutta* 818.

10. Commentary on the Cetiyasutta 822.
"At the shrine site of the yakkha Udena" means at the place honored by the great multitude, constructed with bricks under the designation of a devāyatana (shrine) for the yakkha named Udena.

"Cultivated" means brought to full growth by way of the completion of development (bhāvanā). "Repeatedly performed" means set in motion again and again by way of frequent practice through development.
