just as a harnessed noble steed, when directed by a skilled charioteer, is capable of proceeding according to one's wish, so too has it been brought to a state where it is capable of proceeding according to one's wish.

"In the sense of a foundation" means in the sense of a basis. "Made into a site" means that through the complete purification of all defilements, it has become the ground for the various supernormal powers (*iddhi*).
They are "made" because they serve as the basis for its occurrence, like a thoroughly cleansed site for dangers.

They are "established" because, through being well-cultivated, they are placed in a state of fitness for their respective foundations due to the removal of opposing factors. They are "heaped up on all sides" because they have been brought to the accumulation of development in every respect;
hence he said, "well-increased. They are "well-commenced" by means of the cultivation of supernormal power (*iddhi*).
"Properly cultivated until reaching the topknot.
"By way of non-restriction" means by the indefinite expression "of anyone whatsoever. "Having restricted" means having restricted it by specifying the form "of the Tathāgata.
"The measure of life" refers to the maximum measure of life. The reason for taking that [maximum] alone is explained in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.

This should be understood according to the method already stated. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, keeping in mind that the karma which grants rebirth to Great Bodhisattvas in their final existence is capable of producing an incalculable lifespan, remarked:
"Since the Pāḷi states that the life-force of Buddhas is capable of suppressing dangers, he [the Buddha] might remain for this very Fortunate Aeon."

"By the mention of 'being broken' and so forth, it is implied by the sense that just as there is no warding off of old age through the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*), likewise there is no warding off of death by it.
It should be understood that even though the Elder’s statement—"Where was the arrow shot?
Where did it fall?"—was uttered otherwise, it nonetheless supports the words of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). Therefore he said:
"But that was not pleasing to him... [and so on] ...it was restricted.
"With a mind obsessed" means with a mind overcome such that it is impossible to discern what is beneficial or harmful.
That overcoming was like a small amount of water being overwhelmed by a great flood of water.
It is said, “with his mind overwhelmed. “Another” means one other than the Elder, or anyone else, a mere worldling (*puthujjana*) distinct from the Noble Ones (*ariya*).

Here, the mention of the worldling is intended to show that just as one whose perversion (*vipallāsa*) has not been entirely abandoned and whose mind is obsessed by Māra is unable to discern what is beneficial or harmful, so too the Elder [was unable to discern] the manifestation of signs (*nimittobhāsa*) produced by the Blessed One.
“Completely does not perceive” is for the purpose of showing [this]. Therefore he said, “Māra indeed,” and so forth. The four perversions (*vipallāsa*) are:
the perversion of perception and the perversion of mind regarding the foul as “beautiful”; the perversion of perception and the perversion of mind regarding suffering as “pleasure.
These are the four perversions. By that [phrase], although the other eight perversions have been abandoned...
By virtue of the non-abandonment of the four perversions (vipallāsa) as previously described. "Assa" refers to the Elder.
"Maddati" means that by the mere act of contact, he acts as if crushing; otherwise, if beings were truly crushed by him, their death would surely follow.
The intended meaning is: "Will he be able [to crush them], or will he not be able? Why will he not be able? Is it not this very one?
"Has he entered the womb of the Chief Disciple, who possesses great psychic power and great majesty?
"He has indeed entered, but for the purpose of displaying his own majesty, not with the intention of causing harm.
It was said here, 'What will he be able to do? because the crushing of the heart is what is primarily intended. [Regarding] "the manifestation of signs":

In this context, the means (nimitta) is the production of a perception—by way of demonstrating his own capacity to remain for an eon through the power of his cultivation of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*)—under the guise of another matter, namely the request that he remain for an entire eon with the words, "May the Blessed One stay for an eon," followed by the statement, "Ānanda, whoever has cultivated the four bases of psychic power...
and so forth; and likewise, the employment of such a circuitous method.
Having set aside [all else], the radiance is that which directly reveals one’s own intention. "Knowing indeed" means knowing precisely that he was possessed by Māra.
He said, "By the attribution of fault for the purpose of thinning out the grief," because the grief of beings caused by one's own transgression becomes slight and not powerful.
But did the Elder later describe his conduct at the time when his mind was possessed by Māra?
Does he know? He does not know by way of his own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), but he knows through the power of the Buddhas.

Because he leads others toward what is harmful and kills them by destroying their virtues—or because, by obstructing dispassion (*virāga*), he is like one who kills those born here and there by means of the signs of birth—he is called "Māra" because he kills (*māreti*). Because he is exceedingly evil, he is the Evil One (*pāpimā*). He is endowed with dark qualities (*kaṇhadhamma*).

He is *Kaṇha* (the Black One). He is *Antaka* (the Ender) because he brings an end to qualities such as dispassion (*virāga*). He is *Namuci* because he does not release beings from their harmful course of conduct.
He is *Pamattabandhu* (the Kinsman of the Negligent) because he binds those who are heedless with his own snare of Māra, or because those who are heedless are his kinsmen.
He says "in the eighth week" with reference to the seven days following the seventh week, but not to the seven days of the sitting cross-legged (*pallaṅka*) and so forth.
This is because it receives the name "the eighth week" as if it were a duty fixed for it.
Indeed, after the seventh week, having learned that the Blessed One had promised Brahmā and Sakka to teach the Dhamma at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, [Brahmā] became despondent, thinking:
"Now he will lead beings beyond my domain by means of the teaching of the Dhamma."
Standing there, he thought: "Now, by some means, I shall cause him to pass into final Nibbāna; thus his desire will be frustrated, and my own desire will be fulfilled.
Having reflected thus, he approached the Blessed One and, standing to one side, requested his final Nibbāna with the words:
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now pass into final Nibbāna," and so forth. It was with reference to this that [the Buddha said]:
It is stated, “In the eighth week,” and so forth. Therein, the word “today” (ajja) is said with reference to the day of relinquishing the life-formations.
Although the Blessed One knew his intention to bind [himself], he did not disclose it; rather, rejecting the request, he made clear that it was not yet the time for his final nibbāna.
Therefore he said, “Not yet, indeed,” and so forth.
"Skilled by way of the path" means skilled through proficiency in the penetration of the Truths.
"Likewise disciplined" means disciplined by the complete eradication of the defilements through the path.

"Likewise confident" means having attained fearlessness in the Teacher’s Dispensation precisely through the attainment of the Noble Path, due to the disappearance of evil states such as views and doubt which cause timidity.

The meaning is that one attains a state of confidence. Regarding the statement "by way of the Three Piṭakas," he says this because the learning by means of which escape from the suffering of saṃsāra becomes possible is intended here as "learning" (suta) in its most excellent sense.
A collection of the three Piṭakas is *tepiṭaka*; alternatively, the three Piṭakas themselves are *tipiṭaka*, and *tipiṭaka* itself is *tepiṭaka*. Of that...
By way of that. "That very same" means precisely that which was stated as "the Three Piṭakas heard in the sense of being heard.

"Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma). "They bear it in mind" means they bear it in their hearts, keeping it from perishing—like lion's meat placed in a golden vessel—and by way of its being well-mastered and well-recited. Thus, by way of the Dhamma of the scriptures...
Having demonstrated his state of being one who has heard much and who upholds the Dhamma, he now says "Or else," and so forth, to demonstrate that same quality by way of penetration (*paṭivedha*).
"Of the noble Dhamma" means of the Dhamma of the Path and Fruition, or of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
"Consistent with the Dhamma" means a state of Dhamma that is conformable to its realization. "The appropriate practice" refers to that very Dhamma of insight (*vipassanā*).
Or, it refers to the sixfold purifications. "In accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhamma*) means the Dhamma that accords with the Dhamma of Nibbāna;

that is, the practice as previously described, and the qualities such as fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) which are appropriate to it and lead to self-effacement. "Those whose nature is to conduct themselves [accordingly]" (*caraṇasīlā*) means those whose nature is to undertake and maintain [the training].

Alternatively, "in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhammā*) refers to the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*), which has the Dhamma of the fruit of the path as its concomitant; those whose nature is to conduct themselves according to that are so called.
"One's own teacher’s doctrine" (*attano ācariyavādaṃ*) means the doctrine of one’s own teacher, the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).
Because he teaches the training in conduct to the world including the devas, the Blessed One is the "teacher" (*ācariya*); his "doctrine" (*vāda*) is the teaching of the Four Noble Truths.
"They will explain" (*ācikkhissanti*) means they will first speak [of it], and they will cause others to learn according to the method they themselves have mastered.
The meaning [of "will teach"] is that they will cause [others] to recite; the meaning is that they will correctly awaken them to the Pāḷi.
"Will establish" means they will cause them to understand; the meaning is that they will cause them to remember. "Will set forth" means they will establish by way of various modes;
the meaning is that they will make manifest. "Will reveal" means they will make it open. "Will analyze" means they will make it analyzed. "Will clarify" means...
They will make the profound clear and the obscure manifest.

Regarding the phrase "with the Dhamma" (*sahadhammena*), here the word *dhamma* is used in the sense of a cause, as in such passages as "the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma is knowledge regarding the cause. Thus it is said: "by speech that is accompanied by reason and possessed of a cause.
"With demonstration" (*sappāṭihāriya*) means with an escape (*sanissaraṇa*). Just as one's own doctrine becomes established after having refuted the doctrines of others, so too...
Having established the meaning as it was understood through reasons and examples, they will preach the Dhamma. Therefore he said, "having made it leading-outward, they will teach the Dhamma";
the meaning is that they will awaken [others] to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
And here, by the six phrases beginning with "they will proclaim," six points of meaning are shown; however, from the beginning...
With two words there are six phrasing-components (*byañjanapada*). To this extent, the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas has been shown by way of the method of commentary.
For it is said in the *Netti*: "The Sutta consists of twelve words;
all of that is both the phrasing and the meaning."
“Comprising the three trainings” means comprising the three trainings beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
“The entire holy life of the Dispensation” means the supreme conduct that constitutes the Teacher’s teaching in its entirety, without remainder. “Fully flourished” means properly increased.
“By way of the relish of jhāna” means by way of the bliss of jhāna attained by various bhikkhus. “Attained to growth” means by way of reaching a state that is sublime and excellent.
It has reached complete growth. It is like being in full bloom because the growth of the Dispensation has reached its pinnacle through the perfections of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
"By way of establishment" means by way of being established; the sense is "by way of attaining a foundation.
"Beneficial to many people" (*bāhujañña*) means by way of penetration. Therefore he said: "By way of the realization of the great multitude."

*Puthubhūtaṃ* means that which has become (*bhūtaṃ*) various (*puthu*) and broad (*puthulaṃ*), or that which has reached (*pattaṃ*) a state of being various (*puthattaṃ*). Therefore he said: "Having reached a state of broadness in every respect.
*Supakāsitaṃ* means well-proclaimed, having been made known correctly through its excellence in being good in the beginning and so forth.
"Having established mindfulness well" refers to this division of the body and so on, designated as the selfhood, as the burden of suffering, [which has been examined] by me to this extent...
Previously it was carried along, but now it must no longer be carried;

for the sake of not carrying it further, the equipment for the Noble Path has been accumulated over a very long time, and this Noble Path has been penetrated, whereby these aggregates, bases, and so forth have been thoroughly understood according to their true nature as foul and so on.
Thus, having made the fourfold mindfulness well-established in its object exactly as it is.

"Having delimited it by means of knowledge": because the welfare of oneself—which constitutes the purpose for bearing this burden of suffering known as the personal existence (*attabhāva*)—was completed at the foot of the Bodhi tree;

whereas the welfare of others—the training of those to be converted by a Buddha—had reached its culmination and was now about to be brought to completion within just three months, he therefore said: "On the full moon of Visākha."
"I shall attain final Nibbāna"—having thus delimited [the time] with Buddha-knowledge and made a determination through a portion of the Truths—he relinquished the life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*).
He relinquished the formation of life—that is, the vitality—thinking, "I will not enter the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
By that very act of relinquishment, he thought, "I will not cause the life-formation being formed by it to continue."
He released it. Therefore he said, “Therein,” and so forth.
The earthquake was great both by way of the vastness of its location and by way of the vastness of its mode of occurrence.
Therein, in order to show the greatness of the earthquake by way of the vastness of its location, it was said: “Then... [it] shook,” and that [location] is the field of its origin.

It was only the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*), not just any system whatsoever. Why was it that even when [the earth] shook during the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*), the Great Birth (*mahājāti*), and so forth, it shook only to that same extent?
It is because he first delimited that very field as his birth-field (*jātikhetta*);
and this delimitation should be understood as occurring by way of the natural law (*dhammatā*). For it was likewise for the Buddhas of the past.
The field of birth was exactly that much. For it is said: "The ten-thousandfold world system becomes silent and undisturbed...
the great ocean heaves, and the ten-thousandfold world system quakes," and so forth.
Because it causes a sixfold trembling extending as far as the limits of the water, it is called *bhiṃsana*; that which is terrifying is *bhiṃsanaka*.
He said, "It is 'fear-inducing. The term "divine drum" (*devabherī*) is merely a synonym for the sound of the divine drum (*devadundubhi*);
here, no actual drum is intended by the term "divine drum," but rather the sound of a resonance arising from the sky due to its nature as a portent.
Therefore he said, "The god," and so forth. "The god" refers to the cloud; for at that time, because of its clarity, it was [like] the sky.
Because there was no actual rain, the sound that issued forth—resembling a dry thundering—was designated as the "celestial drum" (*devadundubhi*). Therefore, it is said:
"The god thundered a dry thunder.
[The phrase] "released by the force of joy" refers to the thought: "For such a long time this burden of suffering, known as this personal existence (*attabhāva*), has been carried..."
"Now, before long, I shall lay [the burden] down"—with such joy arisen, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) released by the force of natural rapture.
In order to show that this purpose was also accomplished by him while uttering it in this way, the *Aṭṭhakathā* states "Why? and so forth.
The word *tula* is explained as "that which weighs" (*tuliyatīti tulam*), indicating that the term *tula* functions as a noun denoting the object of the action.
Thus, it is said to be "weighed" (*tulitam*). It is limited by way of its lack of great power; for it is called "limited" (*paritta*) because it is completely broken down by its opposite.
Because it suppresses its opposite, possesses a long continuity, and yields abundant fruit, it is not "weighed" and is not limited.

For those reasons by which it was previously stated without distinction that "the sublime is incomparable" (*mahaggataṃ atulaṃ*), those same reasons exist in an even more eminent degree for the formless realm (*ārūpāvacara*) compared to the fine-material realm (*rūpāvacara*);
thus, the formless realm is said to be "incomparable" (*atula*), while the other is "comparable" (*tula*). Regarding "small fruit" (*appavipāka*):
among the three types of kamma, that which has small fruit and is inferior is "comparable. Regarding "great fruit" (*bahuvipāka*): that which has great fruit and is sublime is [incomparable].
That is the incomparable (*atula*). But as for that which is intermediate here, one should divide it into two parts—the inferior and the superior—and include them within those two portions.

Having determined the relative magnitude of the result (*vipāka*) according to the method stated in the commentary on the "Inferior Triad," the state of being comparable or incomparable should be understood by way of that.
He said "origin" (*sambhava*) because it originates from this.

“Becoming the cause”: one who delights in the internal nature of certainty means one who delights in the cultivation of the objective field by way of insight (vipassanā) regarding the phenomena within one’s own continuum.

Since karma that possesses fruition—which merely gives rise to the process of rebirth—is "becoming" in the sense of having fruition, yet it is not the formative action (abhisaṅkhāra) for existence such as sensual existence (kāmabhava) and so forth, the term "becoming" is stated and then specified as "formative action of existence" (bhavasaṅkhāra) for the purpose of distinguishing it from that [mere karma].
It was said. "He cast off" (ossaji) means he abandoned [the defilements] by means of the Noble Path.

He "pierced the defilement born of self" (attasambhavaṃ kilesaṃ), which stood enveloping his very being like armor because it had arisen within himself; thus, demonstrating the casting off of karma that occurs simultaneously with the destruction of the defilements, he states the cause for both of these as:
"delighting inwardly, concentrated" (ajjhattarato samāhito).
In the first alternative, only the act of scrutinizing (*avasajjana*) was mentioned. Here, showing the manner of that scrutiny, he says “Alternatively,” and so forth.
Therein, “examining” means investigating by way of such [formulations] as “Arising is danger, non-arising is security.

Having stated “the five aggregates,” etc., in order to show in detail the meaning briefly expressed by the passage beginning with “weighing, examining,” and so forth, [he speaks] regarding the formative process of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*).
He shows the manner of disparagement by way of its actual form. With the words "Thus," etc., he shows by way of conclusion the meaning stated at the beginning of the commentary on the Udāna verses.
It should be understood that this purpose—namely, for the sake of making known his state of fearlessness—is also included.
The commentary on the Cāpāla Vagga is finished.
2. The Chapter on the Quaking of the Palace (Pāsādakampanavagga). 1–2. Commentary on the First Sutta, etc. (Pubbasuttādivaṇṇanā) 823–824.
These will be made clear further on in the tenth sutta of this Chapter on the Quaking of the Palace. [They are] the bases for the six direct knowledges (cha-abhiññā-pādaka).

They are the foundation and the basis for the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). The meaning is that, just as in the first sutta, so too in the second and third suttas, the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) that serve as the foundation for the six direct knowledges are explained.
3. Commentary on the *Chandasamādhi-sutta*.
825. The desire that serves as the basis for concentration is what is intended here; thus he says, "‘Desire’ means the desire consisting in the wish to act.
Its sense of being a basis is its sense of being a support; for it is not without depending on that desire [that concentration arises]. Thus he says:
"‘Depending on’ means having made it a support, having made it the dominant factor—this is the meaning. "Becoming exertion" means becoming preeminent; this is the state of being preeminent.
And because it occurs by accomplishing even a single fourfold function, for that very reason there is an expression in the plural;

it is called "volitional formations" (*saṅkhāra*) in the sense of being the primary volitional formation, due to its being the principal formative activity. By this scriptural passage, “If one relies upon desire...

this is called concentration through desire (*chandasamādhi*),” a compound is stated by eliding the word *adhipati* (predominance), such that concentration dominated by desire is termed “concentration through desire.”

Or, by way of showing the meaning of the word *adhipati* (predominance), concentration caused by desire, or concentration in which desire is predominant, is "concentration due to desire" (*chandasamādhi*).

By means of that, he will say: "endowed with both concentration due to desire and with the volitional formations of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*), which are volitional formations consisting of striving.
Having brought that [phrase] in, the connection [is made]. "Consisting of striving" means consisting of energy (*vīriya*). Some [say]:

They say: "The term 'exertion' (*padhāna*) is included for the purpose of excluding conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) and so forth. Alternatively, it is called a formation (*saṅkhāra*) because it forms various specific qualities;
thus, it refers to all energy (*vīriya*). In that context, the term "exertion" is included to exclude anything other than that which accomplishes the four functions.
Just as desire (*chanda*) is endowed with both concentration through desire (*chanda-samādhi*) and the formations of exertion (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*), [so too is energy].
Thus, in the case of *chandasamādhi*, it is endowed with both desire (*chanda*) and the volitional formations of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*).
The volitional formations of striving are also endowed with both desire and the concentration of desire. Therefore, the word "endowed" (*samannāgata*) should be applied to all three factors.
Consequently, because these three—desire and the others—are included within a single arising of consciousness, all those states are [present] together as one.

Having thus stated, "This is called... [etc. ...the basis of psychic power," it is shown that here the status of being a basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) is attributed only to desire and the other factors;

however, in the *Vibhaṅga*, the status of being psychic power (*iddhi*) is attributed to them, while the status of being a basis of psychic power is attributed to their associated states. To demonstrate this, he says:
"But in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*... and so forth.
Now, showing that the status of being a "basis of psychic power" (iddhipāda) is also possible for these, he said, "Moreover," and so forth.

In this context, for one who develops desire by making effort while developing it, the desire that succeeds by virtue of the previously formed volitional formations (saṅkhāra) occurring in that manner is called "psychic power" (iddhi);
the volitional formations of effort, which serve as its support, are called the "basis of psychic power" (iddhipāda). This applies to the other two as well.
The same method applies. This was stated with reference to the mere primary factor for one who is thus developing [the path];
however, showing that the sense of "success" (ijjhanattha) is common to all, he said: "The associated... they indeed succeed.

To show the bases of success (iddhipāda) without confusion, he said "Furthermore," and so forth. Therein, "desire and so forth" refers to the desire-concentration and the volitional formations of striving (padhāna-saṅkhāra).
"In the *Sesiddhipāda* [passages]" means in the cases of the basis of psychic power consisting of energy (*vīriyiddhipāda*), and so forth.
Therein, the term "endowed with the volitional formation of striving and concentration of energy" mentions energy twice. Of these, the first refers to a specific kind of concentration;

the second is the indication of the factor of endowment, namely that it is precisely the concentration dominated by energy (*vīriyādhipatisamādhi*) that constitutes "concentration of energy. For indeed, in all instances, there are only two factors of endowment.

Concentration (*samādhi*) and the volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) are present; while desire and the other factors are qualifications of concentration, the volitional formation of striving is qualified by the word "striving" itself and not by desire and the rest.
Therefore, the predominance of energy (*vīriyādhipati*) is not stated here as a qualification of the volitional formation of striving.

Furthermore, it is precisely because energy stands as a qualification of concentration that it is mentioned by the term "volitional formation of striving" as a factor of possession (*samannāgama-aṅga*).
It is not stated that there is an endowment with two types of energy (*vīriya*).

However, since concentration (*samādhi*) is distinguished by zeal (*chanda*) and the other factors, and likewise the formative effort of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*) and the remaining phenomena are associated with that very same [concentration] as being distinguished, therefore the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) are stated by way of the qualifications of concentration.
And the state of being a qualification belongs to zeal and the others by way of showing their respective supports.

Regarding the statement, “It becomes ‘the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration due to desire’... [etc.]”: here, by taking the word *pāda* (basis/foot) in the sense of a support (*nissaya*), the status of desire and the others as bases of psychic power is stated in the sense of being that which is relied upon (*upādāyattha*).

For this very reason, in the Abhidhamma, in the *Uttaracūḷabhājaniya* of the *Pañhāpucchaka*, the status of desire and the others alone as bases of psychic power is stated as: “The four bases of psychic power: the basis of psychic power consisting in desire,” and so forth.

And: although the four bases of power (*iddhipāda*) were first presented here by the formula beginning, “In this case, a bhikkhu [possesses] concentration of desire,” etc., the state of being wholesome and so forth is explained again specifically for desire and the others.
For it is precisely for the purpose of showing the basis-of-power as a means (*upāya*) that the basis-of-power as a support (*nissaya*) was shown;
otherwise, there would not be a fourfold division. This is the analysis of the meaning according to the scripture (*pāḷi*). Therein:

"Only for the purpose of showing the basis of success as a means": having made zeal and the other [factors] the primary, the chief, and the precursors, the concentration produced is "concentration dominated by zeal.
This is the demonstration of the means for attaining the success of zeal and the others;
it is precisely for that purpose that, in various places in the Canon, it is said: "For one who has become thus, the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness."

The demonstration of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) has been made because it is the aggregates beginning with feeling—specifically those distinguished by zeal (*chanda*) and so forth—that are intended.

This must be accepted in this way; otherwise, if the status of being a base of psychic power were understood solely on the basis of the aggregates associated with psychic power, they would not possess their fourfold nature, as the intended meaning is that [zeal and the rest] function as the specific causes [of distinction].
"Kecī" (some) refers to the residents of the Uttaravihāra monastery. "Anibbatto" means not produced by causes and conditions;

the intended meaning is that it is not a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva), but is a mere conceptual designation (paññatti). The construction is: "It exists for the purpose of crushing [opponents'] arguments, and it is included in the Abhidhamma as the *Uttaracūḷavāra*.
The passage beginning with "The four bases of psychic power (*iddhipādā*)" is the demonstration of the *Uttaracūḷavāra*. These, however, are the bases of psychic power found in the *Uttaracūḷavāra*.
The Elder Raṭṭhapāla, thinking, "If there is such zeal, how could they not grant permission? refrained from eating for seven days.
Having obtained his parents' consent, he went forth and, relying solely on that zeal, attained Arahantship. Thus it is said:
"The Elder Raṭṭhapāla, making zeal his primary burden, realized the supramundane Dhamma. As for the Elder Soṇa, he was the Elder Soṇa the Delicate.

For that venerable one, disregarding his own delicate nature and not relinquishing his effort even when his feet were blistered from excessive walking, took diligence as his burden and realized the supramundane Dhamma. The Elder Saṃbhūta [thought]:
"If the distinction of noble knowledge and vision should succeed for one who possesses the mind, may it succeed for me," and he took the mind as his burden.

Having done so, he produced supramundane states. Mogharāja thought, "If the cultivation of the path should succeed for one possessed of wisdom, it would succeed for me," and by making wisdom the precursor, the burden, and the chief, he attained Arahantship;
thus it is said: "Mogharāja, having made investigation his burden, produced supramundane states. Now, regarding them...

He said, "In this regard, just as... and so forth, in order to show by way of illustration the sons of ministers who had received special favor from the king, based on their excellence in attendance upon the Noble Ones, their zeal, and their mastery of counsel.
And here, the generation of desire is said to be similar to attendance because it repeatedly brings satisfaction; and because of its state of firmness, it is like energy (*vīriya*).
The similarity to a king’s favor is due to the mind being predominant in reflection; the similarity to the preparation of a mantra is due to the mind’s nature of thinking;
and the similarity to noble birth is stated for wisdom, because among wholesome states arising from wise attention, wisdom is the most excellent.
4. Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta.

826. "Of restless nature" (*uddhacca-pakati*) means having a scattered disposition; the meaning is that their minds are distracted. Because of instability and because of the state of the mind being agitated, they are said to have "agitated minds.
Because of their emptiness, they are like reeds; thus "reed" (*naḷa*) refers to conceit (*māna*). Since they have risen up like a reed, they are called "arrogant" (*unnaḷa*);
thus it is said: "'Arrogant'... [etc.]... this is what is meant. "Fickle" (*capala*) refers to the state of fickleness.
*Lolabhāvo* means one who has a lustful nature. *Murāti* means harsh speech; that is, rough speech. *Vikiṇṇavācā* means those who speak frivolously (*saṃphappalāpino*);

this is expressed by the phrase "those whose speech is unrestrained," and so forth. Because mindfulness (*sati*) has been forgotten, lost, and utterly ruined in regard to the Dhamma of practice, they are called "of muddled mindfulness" (*muṭṭhasatī*);
thus he said, "those whose mindfulness is lost. *Ubbhantacittā* means because of the absence of concentration (*samādhi*).

"With minds wandering higher and higher through restlessness" means their minds are unsettled by agitation. "With faculties unguarded" means that because they have not developed the body, their faculties are in their natural, untrained state, like those of village children.
*Nema* refers to the portion of ground marked by the footprint; one whose footprint is deep is called *gambhīranema*.
"Well-sunk," and so forth, demonstrates the firmness with which that foot is planted.
5. Commentary on the Uṇṇābha Brāhmaṇa Sutta:
827. “For the purpose of abandoning” means for the purpose of abandoning by way of non-arising.
9. Commentary on the Iddhādi Desanā Sutta.
831. The fourth jhāna that serves as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is intended here, because of the statement:
"It proceeds for the attainment of psychic power (*iddhi*). 10. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta 832.

"Having generated desire" means having generated the desire for cultivation (*bhāvanā-chanda*). "The mode of sluggishness" refers to the mind of cultivation falling into a state of depression; it is said to be the occurrence of being permeated by indolence (*kosajja*).

Thus, through the absence of confidence, there occurs a lapse into mental distraction. To show the manner of producing that encouragement which is desired by generating confidence therein, it is said:
"Having adverted to the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha," and so forth.
Because one who is distracted with regard to sensual objects of the world remains distracted again and again, it is said: "repeatedly distracted" (*anuvikkhitta*).
The "sutta-staff" (suttadaṇḍa) refers to the suttas themselves as a staff in the sense of punishing and restraining a mind that has gone astray; having threatened the mind with that sutta-staff,

it is said that the mental distraction proceeding with reference to the five strands of sensual pleasure arises again and again, hence the terms "continually distracted" (anuvikkhitto) and "continually dissipated" (anuvisaṭo).

In order to show both the purity of the subsequent state and the application of attention (*manasikāra*) to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*)—whether by way of learning (*uggaha*) or otherwise—the passage beginning with "How" was stated.

Regarding the "four places such as excessive laxity (*atilīna*)": this refers to the four states designated as excessive laxity (*atilīna*), excessive exertion (*atipaggahita*), contraction (*saṃkhitta*), and distraction (*anuvikkhitta*).
Among these, "excessive laxity" is the shrinking back without having fully entered into the cultivation of meditation; whereas having entered into it...
“Internal contraction” means narrowness; “internal compression” means excessive exertion, which is the state of over-aroused energy (*accāraddhavīriyatā*) and lack of composure.
Since one who falls into the influence of externally scattered thoughts should grasp [the object] by way of the thirty-two aspects or by way of the perception of the skeleton, he said:
“It should be understood by way of the body. Therefore he said: “From the soles of the feet upwards,” and so forth.

They are called *ākāra* (aspects) because they are scattered (*ākirīyanti*) without confusion from one another and established as distinct types; thus he said, "by which aspects" means "by which constituent parts.
It is called *liṅga* (mark) because it is marked (*liṅgīyati*) or observed; it is the shape.
It is called *nimitta* (sign) because it is fixed (*nimīyati*) by being extracted and delimited; it is the appearance. "The monk who... and so forth [refers to] the perception of light.
He masters it; that is "vision. In "in an open space" means in an uncovered courtyard. "He brings to mind the perception of light at night":

just as the detailed method was stated regarding desire (*chanda*) in the passage beginning, "Here a bhikkhu, having generated desire," this same detailed method should be applied to energy (*viriya*) and the others as well.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Shaking of the Palace is finished.
3. The Chapter on the Iron Ball. 2.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Iron Ball.
834. "By this body composed of the four great elements" means by this body produced from the four great elements, which is evident to the whole world.
However, the mind-made (manomaya) created body is evident to others according to the Blessed One’s own wish.
"Ava-māti" means he measures down; for the word *mā* preceded by *ava* also has the sense of "to be able," as in "he is capable" or "he is able."
The meaning has been stated. "Unmixed phrase" means a unique phrase, because it does not occur elsewhere.

The sinking of the body into the mind, its placement [therein], and making it dependent upon that—since these in actual fact amount to nothing other than proceeding by way of the movement of the mind, he said:
"he impels by way of the movement of the mind."

In this context, "conforming to the course of the mind" means establishing a state of identical movement between the body and the mind by means of transforming the body through the power of the mind, thinking:
"Let this body become like this mind. But how can the body, which functions slowly, conform to the course of the mind, which functions rapidly?
It does not conform in every respect. For just as [the body conforms] by way of the body...
In the transformation of the mind, the mind does not in every respect share the same course as the body.
For it can never, without halting for its own moment established by its own nature, proceed under the influence of a material phenomenon which is slow in its movement;
rather, it follows the course of the body—which is slow in its movement—through the power of resolution, thinking, "Let this mind become like this body."
As long as it continues in a continuous stream by way of conformity with the movement of the body until it reaches the desired place,

the mind is said to have been "directed" toward the movement of the body. Thus, because it has already been accomplished through the perception of ease and lightness— by means of the resolution, "May this body become like this mind"—
it does not proceed slowly, as would be the case for those who have not developed the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Just as one reaches a desired place very quickly by means of only a few mental moments without having to turn around, so too the body, when it proceeds in this way, is said to be "directed by the course of the mind";
it is not because it reaches the desired place in a single moment of consciousness.
And by taking it thus, the simile of bending and stretching out the arm is even more appropriately applied without resorting to figurative usage.

Otherwise, there would be a violation of the nature of things (*dhammatā*); nor is it possible by the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*) to alter the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) of phenomena, though it is possible to alter their state (*bhāva*).
3–10. Commentary on the Sutta on the Bhikkhus, etc.
835–842. The phrase “of two fruits” is stated with reference to the sutta that follows, meaning “beginning with the two fruits. The remainder is easily understood.
The commentary on the Ayoguḷa-vagga is finished.
The commentary on the Iddhipāda-saṃyutta is finished.
8. Anuruddha Saṃyutta 1.
Rahogata Vagga 1–2.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Solitude, etc.
899–900. Regarding "in thirty-six instances": there are nine contemplations—contemplating the nature of arising in the internal body, its passing away, both arising and passing away;
externally, its arising, its passing away, both arising and passing away; and internally and externally, its arising, its passing away, and the nature of both arising and passing away.
Likewise for feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena. Thus, it is in thirty-six instances. In the second [section]...
"In twelve places" means: in the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally; in feelings, in the mind, and in mental phenomena—thus, in these twelve places.
3. Commentary on the Sutanu Sutta.

901. “By this text” means by this text concerning the inferior triad (*hīnattika*). These states are “inferior” in the sense of being base. These states are “middling” because they exist between the inferior and the sublime. They are “sublime” because they have been brought to a state of excellence in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being self-sufficient.
4–7. Commentary on the First Kaṇḍakī Sutta, etc. (902–905).
It is called *kaṇḍakī* because it has thorns (*kaṇḍaka*); it is a *karamanda* tree. The feminine gender is used here with reference to its nature as a medicinal herb (*osadhi*).
Because of its great abundance, that forest became known as the "Kaṇḍakīvana" (Thorn Forest). "A thousand worlds" refers to a world-system of a thousand *cakkavāḷas*.
A thousand *cakkavāḷas* come within the range of a single act of attention (*ekāvajjana*), because he had performed the expansion of light (*ālokavaḍḍhana*).
9. Commentary on the Ambapālīvana Sutta.
907. *Arahattabhāvadīpakaṃ* means that which indicates the existence of the state of arahantship. Alternatively, the reading is *Arahattabhāvadīpikaṃ*.
The commentary on the *Rahogatavagga* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Chapter (*Dutiyavagga*).
909–922. *Dasabalañāṇa* means the knowledge of the tenfold power. "By way of a portion" means by way of a limited scope.

Disciples also possess knowledge corresponding to their own specific inclinations; thus, they know the *ṭhānas* (grounds) by way of time and place, as well as by way of the seven places according to their familiarity.
However, because the Perfectly Enlightened Ones possess infinite knowledge, it is entirely unobstructed in all respects.
He said, "Knowledge," beginning with the words, "But as for the omniscient Buddhas... This knowledge of the ten powers (dasabala-ñāṇa) is without limitation because its object is infinite;
it is complete in every aspect due to its lack of deficiency.
The commentary on the second chapter is finished.
The commentary on the Anuruddha Saṃyutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Jhāna Saṃyutta: 923.
The Jhāna Saṃyutta is indeed easy to understand; they say it is a mixed collection.
The commentary on the *Jhānasaṃyutta* is finished.
10. *Ānāpānasaṃyutta*. 1. The Chapter on the Single Dhamma (*Ekadhammavagga*).
1. Commentary on the Ekadhamma Sutta 977.
"In this" means in this first sutta. It has already been stated; therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method explained therein.
6. Commentary on the Ariṭṭha Sutta.
982. The word *nu* is used in the sense of an inquiry; therefore, he said "bhāvetha nu" (cultivate, surely), as it has the same meaning as *nu*.

Regarding "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*), he said "lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure," meaning the desire for objects of sense. [This refers to] the twelve bases (*āyatana*) of phenomena included within one's own and others' continuums.
By this description of the abandoning of sensual desire and the description of the removal of perceptions of aversion, [he indicates] the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*).

He speaks thus because the severance of the five lower fetters (*pañcorambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) has been declared [by the Blessed One]. "Showing insight" means showing [it] by saying, "Devote yourselves to insight.
8. Commentary on the Lamp Simile Sutta (*Padīpopama-sutta-vaṇṇanā*).
984. The citation from the Commentary, “Neither the body nor the eyes become weary,” was made [to clarify].

Having stated, “The body becomes weary and the eyes are distressed,” the passage beginning with “In the case of the meditation subject of the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna),” etc., was spoken to show where and how this occurs.
That the eyes throb and become weary, and so forth, happens when one contemplates for too long.
This has been stated having made [this point]. "In this meditation subject" means in the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna*).
"He said thus" means he said: "If a bhikkhu should wish, his body would not become weary.
"It is possible" is stated from the standpoint of the intention of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), whereas it is not accepted according to the Theravāda that follows later.

For the form of the stars, which resembles a string of pearls and so forth, being merely the mode of appearance of the sign (*nimitta*) and lasting only for a moment, cannot be removed as one can with the *kasiṇa*-signs. Therefore he said, "it simply cannot be obtained.

This was mentioned for the purpose of showing the benefit: that once concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-samādhi*) is accomplished, this quality is easily achieved. Because [the text says] "for the monk" (*yasmā bhikkhu*).
Regarding the phrase "it has not come down in this instance":

just as in the previous instance it was stated, "If a bhikkhu should desire," so too here, in the passage where it says, "Bhikkhus, when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed," the mention of a "bhikkhu" was not made;
therefore, the word "he" is not used.
9. Commentary on the Vesālī Sutta 985.
"By the expansion of the city walls and enclosures" means by the expansion of the ground through the addition of city walls and enclosures.
Like Rājagaha and Sāvatthī, this city as well... [omitted] ...has attained fullness in every respect. Regarding the phrase "in many ways," here the word *pariyāya*— [End of excerpt]

"By way of reasons" means he said, "by many reasons. The meaning is that this body—whether it be insentient or sentient, and whether it be impure in this way or impure in that way—is [described] by various kinds of reasons.

"Proceeding by way of demonstrating the aspect of foulness" means proceeding by way of seeing the aspect of foulness in every respect therein, starting from the hair and so forth, and starting from the color and so forth. "A discourse for the purpose of dispassion toward the body."
This is a discourse on generating disenchantment with one's own body and that of others. With the words "It emits urine," and so forth, he shows the repulsiveness of the body by way of contrast.
Therein, first, by means of three phrases, he shows its lack of beauty and its corelessness;
in the middle, by four phrases, its foul odor; and at the end, by one phrase, the total absence of anything attractive in it, even in the slightest degree.
The passage beginning with “Now then” (*atha kho*) and so forth shows the unattractiveness [of the body] through its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of its actual form.
The phrase “hair, body hair, and so forth,” which was stated in brief, is expressed in detail by the words “even those that...

and so on. “Expounding” (*vaṇṇento*) means expanding upon it. “In the meditation subject on the foul” (*asubhāya*) means in the matrix of the foul (*asubha-mātikā*). “Practice” (*phātikamma*) means frequent cultivation. Because it cannot be overcome by the thieves of the defilements (*kilesa*), the jhāna is called the “jewel casket of the mind” (*cittamañjūsā*). “Depending on” (*nissāya*) means making it the foundation (*pādaka*).
Others, however, say: "It is said that during that half-month there was no one who could be converted by the Buddha; therefore the Blessed One spoke thus:
'Bhikkhus, I desire,' and so forth. Here, the particle *kira* in the phrase *pare kira* indicates a lack of approval (*aruci*).
For this reason he said: "But this is merely a matter of desire."
"Intermingled with many causes": here, "cause" refers to the body's impurity, foul odor, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness.

"They did everything": ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), perceiving even what is blameworthy therein as blameless, committed every evil consisting of the threefold division of doing, causing others to do, and consenting.
Granted that mindfulness of breathing is included by the inclusion of the ten recollections, nevertheless, in that context—
It is suitable and beneficial for many among the assembled bhikkhus; therefore, it is taken up again.

For indeed, the Blessed One taught that very same meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in this sutta. Furthermore, the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is similar to the meditation subject on the foul (asubha), whereas the four formless attainments (āruppa) are unsuitable for beginners; thus, their omission here should be understood.
“Dependent upon Vesālī” means having made the city of Vesālī their alms-resort village (*gocaragāma*).
“In a mere moment” is said with reference to the fact that as soon as the words of the monks who had approached out of reverence for the Teacher and the True Dhamma were spoken, they rose up.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha, the monks remained with their ears attentively inclined to receive the message of the Blessed One upon their heads.

"By means of mindfulness that functions by way of grasping the in-breaths and out-breaths" means: by means of mindfulness (*sati*) that occurs through the act of grasping the inhalation and exhalation.
"Concentration associated with it" means: the concentration (*samādhi*) arisen together with that [mindfulness], which serves as a mutual condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).

Or, by the phrase "concentration in mindfulness of breathing," he also shows its nature as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*); for in both cases, there are also [other conditions] such as the co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and so forth.
He shows the state of being a condition by way of those seven conditions as well.
In such passages as, "My disciples, practicing rightly, develop the four foundations of mindfulness," it is called "development" (bhāvanā) in the sense of producing and increasing;
thus, showing the meaning by way of both of these, he said, "Developed means produced or increased. In that context, *bhāva* means existence (*vijjamānatā*).
"Developed" means "gone from here," the sense being that it has been produced and merely acquired. But when it has arisen and its cultivation is attained, it is "developed";

the sense is that it has reached a state of proficiency and has increased. "Cultivated repeatedly" means it has been made to occur frequently. By this, he expresses the attainment of mastery over the preliminary work of adverting and so forth.
For that which has reached mastery will occur again and again, since it can be entered into at whatever desired moment.
Therefore it was said: "repeatedly performed. Just as in such passages as, "Right here, monks, is the ascetic;

quite secluded from sensual pleasures," where the word *eva* (only/just) stated in the first clause is understood to apply to the second and subsequent clauses as well, so it is here too. Thus he said:
"In both places, the restriction (*niyama*) is to be understood by means of the word *eva*. To show the benefit obtained through this restriction in both places:
The passage beginning with “This indeed... has been stated. “The meditation subject of foulness” (asubhakammaṭṭhāna) refers to jhāna having foulness as its object.

For that [jhāna] is called “the meditation subject of foulness” because it is the practice of yoga regarding foul things, and because it serves as the cause for specific kinds of happiness for the meditator. By the word “exclusive” (kevala), the object is indicated.

He turns back. "By way of penetration" means by way of the penetration of jhāna. For jhāna, when succeeding through a specific mode of development, proceeds precisely while penetrating its own object;
and because it is penetrated according to its true nature, it is called "penetration. "Because the object is gross" means because the object is loathsome.
"Because the object is repulsive" means because the object is to be felt with disgust.
"By way of method" means by way of cause or by way of a different aspect.
"Due to the continuity of the object" is said with reference to the extreme subtlety of the object that has reached a state of being successively investigated.

A phenomenon (dhamma) occurring when the object is calm and settled is itself also calm and settled. Therefore he said: "Calm, tranquil, extinguished," meaning one whose all fevers have been extinguished.

The meaning is as follows. The continuity of the states that take that as their object (tadārammaṇa) due to the continuity of the object is to be understood by means of the reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) cognitions which have supramundane states as their objects.

It is "unfading" (asecanaka) because there is no addition (secanam) whatsoever that brings about its state of being peaceful and sublime. Because it is unfading, it is "unsurpassed" (anāsittaka); because it is unsurpassed—
Thus it is uninterrupted, unmixed with preliminary work (*parikamma*) and so forth. For that very reason, it is distinct, being entirely separate. It is unique and uncommon.

All of this is stated to show the state of peace (*santabhāva*) by its own intrinsic nature; or else, "preliminary work" refers to the process ending with the production of the sign (*nimitta*) through the preparation of the *kasiṇa* and so on, and the intention here is that such [work] does not exist in this case.
For at that time, because the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) lacks flavor, it would be non-existent and unexalted.

Or, the construction is: "In access concentration (upacāra), there is no 'peace' (santatā) here. Just as in the moment of access concentration there is peace for others through the disappearance of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth, and through the manifestation of the [jhāna] factors (aṅga), such is not the case for this [access concentration]. But this [access concentration], being endowed with the initial [factors]...
is "exalted" (paṇīta). Thus is the construction. "Some" (keci)... *Note: The ellipsis (... indicates an omitted portion of the original text.*
"Residents of the northern monastery. "Unsprinkled" (*anāsittaka*) means not sprinkled with a pouring of water. Therefore he said, "rich in essence" (*ojavanta*);
the meaning is "resembling that which is rich in essence. "Sweet" (*madhura*) means desirable.

"Conducive to the attainment of mental pleasure" should be understood by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas, or by way of all jhānas because they lead to a state of happiness through the peaceful nature of equanimity (*upekkhā*). [It is also understood] by way of the body being touched by the sublime matter produced by jhāna.
However, it should be understood as leading to the attainment of bodily pleasure, and that indeed occurs at the time of emerging from jhāna.
In this interpretation, the locative case in "at every moment of absorption" (appitappitakkhaṇe) should be seen as expressing the cause.
"Unsuppressed" means not driven out or abandoned from one's own mental continuum by means of jhāna. "Born of unskillfulness" refers to unskillfulness...
It is called ignorance; [the defilements] arise from that. For all evil states have ignorance as their precursor.

"In an instant" means in the very moment of its own occurrence. "Causes to disappear": here, "disappearing" means destruction; however, since that is intended here as having meditation (jhāna) as its agent, it is the abandoning of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), which is why he says "he suppresses."
“Vūpasameti” means he pacifies specifically. Since specific pacification is indeed thorough pacification, he says, “he thoroughly pacifies.
Because the development of jhāna for one following the Dispensation is for the most part conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), he says, “because it is conducive to penetration.
This concentration, which serves as the foundation for the Noble Path, increases gradually...
"He has, as it were, entered into the state of the Noble Path," thus he said, "gradually attaining growth in the Noble Path.
This meaning, however, is correctly applicable by way of the contemplations on fading away (*virāga*), cessation (*nirodha*), and relinquishment (*paṭinissagga*). The rest is easily understood.
10. Commentary on the Kimila Sutta.
986. "The Elder" refers to the Elder Ānanda. "This teaching" refers to the teaching set forth beginning with, "How indeed was Kimila made clear?
"In a certain part of the body" means in a certain portion of the material body (rūpakāya).

"In this way" means that just as a bhikkhu who is recollecting in-and-out breathing becomes one who contemplates the body in the body, so too should the meaning be understood in all sections, beginning with "one who contemplates feelings," and so forth.

"Desanāsīsanti" means the basis of the teaching. Since feeling was stated by way of the basis of attention (*manasikāra*), he points to all of that in its true nature by way of another basis. With the words "Just as... and so forth, he shows the illustration for that.
"In the two terms for mental formations" refers to the pair of terms: "experiencing the mental formation, he tranquilizes the mental formation."

"Even though this is so": even if feeling (*vedanā*) has been stated by way of the phrase "mental formation consisting of attention to rapture" (*pīti-manasikāra-citta-saṅkhāra*), even so, this aforementioned feeling does not become an object (*ārammaṇa*). And since the contemplation (*anupassanā*) has feeling as its object, therefore the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*) is not tenable.
If it is asked: "If that is so, how is it that in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and other texts it is said, 'feeling feels'? [the answer follows].
He said: “In the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna and other [suttas],” and so forth.

Therein, “the basis for pleasure and so on” means that feeling feels by taking as its object the visible forms, sounds, and so forth, which have become the basis for the arising of pleasure and so on;
it is not a person who feels, because a person does not exist at all. It is merely a conventional expression based upon and dependent on the occurrence of feeling, such as “a person feels a feeling.”
It exists. Thus, here too, there is an occurrence [of mindfulness] directed toward the inhalations and exhalations as feeling;
and with the heading of "attention occurring in that manner," it is said: "At that time, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings.
"With reference to that" means with reference to that state of being the object of feeling. "Of the initial words" refers to this objection stated as: "Contemplation of feelings is not applicable."
"He enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture" means that he enters the first and second jhānas, which are associated with rapture, in succession.
"Of him" (tassa) is used in the genitive case in the sense of the agent, in view of its dependence on the word "sound" (sadda) [from the preceding context].

"At the moment of attainment" (samāpattikkhaṇe) means at the moment of entering [the jhāna]. "By the acquisition of jhāna" (jhānapaṭilābhena) means by being endowed with jhāna. "From the object" (ārammaṇato).
By way of the object, the joy included within the jhāna that has that as its object is experienced; what is meant is that because the object is experienced, [the joy] is experienced.

Just as, for example, by one wandering in search of a snake, when its lair is experienced, the snake itself is also experienced, because it is easy to capture it through the power of spells and medicinal herbs.

Thus, when the object that serves as the basis for rapture has been clearly discerned, that rapture itself becomes clearly discerned, because it is easy to grasp it both by way of its specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*) and its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).
"At the moment of insight" (*vipassanakkhaṇe*) means at the moment of seeing the object by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanāpaññā*) which has attained a state of sharpness and clarity.
"By the penetration of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇappaṭivedhena*) refers to the specific characteristic of rapture.
And by means of penetrating the general characteristic.
For when the specific and general characteristics of rapture are known, that [rapture] itself becomes known exactly as it is. Therefore he said: "Rapture is experienced through non-delusion.
Now, in order to clarify this meaning by means of the scripture itself, he said: "For it is said," and so forth. Therein, "by way of long inhalation" means...
By way of the long inhalation as its object. The connection is: "for one who understands, that rapture is clearly experienced.

"Understanding the unification and non-distraction of the mind" means understanding, by means of the wisdom associated with it, the unification of the mind—which is included within the jhāna and receives the name "non-distraction"—just as [one understands] by way of the object.
Rapture is clearly experienced; in this way, the mental states associated with it are also clearly experienced by way of the object.

"Mindfulness is established": through the long inhalation, the mindfulness associated with the jhāna is established upon that object, and by way of the object, it is said to be established in the jhāna as well. By means of that mindfulness... [thus].
Because that object is well-penetrated by means of that mindfulness established [within] and by that aforementioned knowledge, that rapture is experienced through the influence of that object.
The meaning in the phrases "by way of long out-breaths," etc., should also be understood according to this same method.
Therefore it was said: "In this very same manner, the remaining terms are also to be understood according to their meaning."
Regarding the passage beginning with "Just as," this is the summary of the meaning:

Just as joy and the other factors are experienced from the perspective of the object through the attainment of jhāna—since they do not occur without it—in the same way, through the attainment of attention (manasikāra) termed "feeling" (vedanā), which is associated with and included within that jhāna, feeling is experienced from the perspective of the object, just as the sun is [revealed] by the rising of dawn; for without that [attention], there is no feeling.

Because it does not proceed [in that way]. Therefore, since feeling has been well-penetrated through its pre-eminent manifestation according to the method already stated, he refutes the previous objection by saying, "Therefore, this is well-stated.
Regarding "the object," he refers to the sign of the in-breath and out-breath. Indeed, he is one who contemplates the mind precisely because of his non-delusion.

Because of the mind’s being clearly experienced. Therefore he said, “Therefore,” and so forth. By the phrase “by way of the mind’s being clearly experienced,” the word “and so forth” includes the other three contemplations of mind as well.
“He” refers to the bhikkhu devoted to the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*). “That abandonment” refers to the knowledge that abandons. “By means of wisdom” (*paññāya*)...
Having seen [the aggregates] through another kind of insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) as impermanent, dispassionate, and so forth, one maintains equanimity toward both types.
This "tetrad" refers to the tetrad described by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so on. Regarding that contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*), he says, "It abandons;
thus it is 'abandoning,'" meaning that the knowledge which performs the act of abandoning is intended [by the term]. [The phrase] "succession of insight" (*vipassanā-paramparā*)...

He speaks of insight (vipassanā) in its successive order. "He looks on with equanimity at the mind that has entered the path" means that he looks on with equanimity at the developing consciousness that has correctly entered the path by means of the middle way of practice, through refraining from both exertion and suppression.
"Appearance as one" [occurs] because, by not overstepping the middle course of serenity (samatha), it leaps forward into that state.
Through the state of single flavor among the faculties, by way of cultivating equanimity toward them, it manifests as entirely one-pointed without distinction;
therefore, one looks on with equanimity, thinking that nothing further needs to be done there. "Therein" means in such looking on with equanimity.
There is also equanimity toward the co-nascent factors, because one looks on at the mode of their occurrence.
Because it is said, "having seen with wisdom," equanimity toward the object is intended here. The construction is:
not only is one equanimous toward states such as the hindrances, but rather, having seen covetousness and so forth with wisdom, one becomes equanimous.
To show the place of origin of the defilement, which is comparable to a heap of dust, [it says] "like a crossroads" for the six...
Thus it is said: "the bases. The body and so forth are the four foundations of mindfulness as objects. Regarding the phrase "in the four objects":
the four foundations of mindfulness that occur in the four objects, beginning with the body, are so called because they strike down the defilement which stands in the place of a heap of dust.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Single Dhamma is finished.
2. Second Chapter: 1–2.
Commentary on the *Icchānaṅgala Sutta* and others. 987–988.
The passage beginning with "Why? is commenced in order to clarify the reason for teaching the meditative abidings (*vihāra*) and attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Eva-vākāra" means the word *eva* and the word *vā*. Because they are exclusively peaceful, due to the state of having exclusively peaceful mental attention.

Although it is already established by the very term "trainee" (*sekkha*) that there exists something for them to train in, since the designation "trainee" is also applied to those who are devoid of what is to be trained in, they are stated here as distinguished from such non-trainees by the phrase "that which is to be trained in. For the purpose of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

Although there is nothing further to be trained in, they are called "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa) because, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, there is no longer any need for training such as that in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
However, because the Buddhas have completely and perfectly finalized their training in every respect, it is not said of them, "I am training.
The meditative absorption on mindfulness of breathing and the attainment of fruition are the dwellings of the Tathāgata.

"In a place where there is a confluence" means where a mixture or a coming together has occurred. Where these great rivers converge...

Regarding the phrase "established in the wholesome," he shows what that absolute establishment in the wholesome is.
“He is established in skill regarding the path,” it is said; the intention is that he is skilled in the lower paths. Therefore, it says, “he develops the path.

The noble fruit itself is the essence of the Dhamma. It is called the destruction of defilements (*kilesakkhaya*) because defilements are destroyed therein; it is Nibbāna, and he delights in that destruction of defilements.
4. Commentary on the First Discourse on Great Wealth (Paṭhamamahaddhanasutta-vaṇṇanā) 1040.
"The wealth of the Noble Ones" (*ariyadhana*) means the wealth belonging to the Noble Ones, the Buddhas; some say it refers to Nibbāna.

Furthermore, it is called "Noble Wealth" (*ariyadhana*) because it is noble in the sense of being purified, and it is wealth in the sense of being cherished as wealth. "By that noble wealth" means by that noble wealth. "By the enjoyment of that very [wealth]" means by the enjoyment of the noble wealth.

1048. "Having brought together" means those very faculties and so forth by which, when cultivated, the path of stream-entry is attained;

"That [tradition] has been told as a lineage" means that it was explained as a persistence based solely on the textual tradition (*tantra*), without regard for any particular person to be trained.
3. Commentary on the Dhammadinna Sutta 1049.
"Among seven persons" means among the seven lay followers (upāsaka) who are being praised. Regarding the terms "profound" and so forth:

"profound in the Dhamma" means profound in the course of the textual recitation (*pāḷigati*). And thus the *Salla Sutta* has already been explained above: "Bhikkhus, I say that volition (*cetanā*)..."
This refers to the *Cetanā-sutta*, which begins with the words, "I say that action is intention," and so forth.

Its profundity should be understood through the method presented in the *Paṭṭhāna*—namely, "arising together with intention" (*cetanāsahajāta*) and "occurring at different times" (*nānākkhaṇika*)—and through the method found in the Suttas, such as "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), and so forth.
Furthermore, because it elucidates both Nibbāna and the Noble Path, it illuminates the supramundane meaning contained within the *Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta*.
By such statements as, “In the past I was devoured by form; now I am being devoured,” the fact that the five aggregates are the devourers and the person is the object to be devoured is clarified;
thus, through this discourse on being devoured (*khajjanīya-paryāya*), the absence of a sentient being and the absence of a soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*) are specifically illustrated.
Therefore it is said: “The *Khajjanika-sutta* and others illustrate the emptiness of a sentient being (*sattasuññatā*). “Having attained, we shall dwell... (*upasampajja viharissāma*).
Those who correctly fulfill the practice taught in those suttas are said to "enter upon and abide in" them.

In this context, the word "not" (*na*) in the phrase "it is not so" (*na kho netaṃ*) is merely a phonetic link between syllables, like the letter *m* in the word "mutually" (*aññamaññaṃ*); it has no meaning of its own.

1050. Regarding "Na kho panetaṃ" (But this is not...): he said "na kho amhehi" and so forth, explaining that the meaning of "no" is "not by us. Regarding "assasanti":

one whose death is certain, and since his life is subject to death, it is said "maraṇapaṭibaddho" (bound to death). Regarding "adhimuccehi": [it refers to] adhimutti (resolute confidence).
“Arise! But because that aspiration of the mind is a placing [of the mind], he said, “Place [it]! Regarding “in the qualities to be acquired”: this refers to the preliminary qualities.
There is no measure because they are infinite and immeasurable. There is no differentiation because liberation is without diversity. 9.

"From one-pointedness of mind" (*cittekaggatāya*) is an ablative construction in relation to the word "declining" (*parihāyanti*).

(*samāhito, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ passati*).

"...understands," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of the passage beginning with "for thus because... is to be understood. For indeed, by means of the words "for thus because...

Those belonging to the Dispensation (*sāsana*) are intended [here], because outsiders lack the realization of the truths (*saccābhisamaya*).
