10. Commentary on the *Tiracchānakathā-sutta*. 1080.
It is called "emancipation" (*niyyāna*) because one goes out from it; thus, it refers to both the path to heaven and the path to liberation.
"Leading out" (niyyānika) means being engaged in that departure; it is "leading out" because it exists here [in this context].

Alternatively, having shortened the vowel *ī* and changed the letter *y* to *k*, it is "leading out" because it leads away from the defilement of verbal misconduct (*vacī-duccarita-saṅkilesa*). It is the abstention from idle chatter together with volition (*cetanā*).
Because it is the opposite of that, it is "not leading out" (*aniyyānika*); the state of being so is "non-leading-out-ness" (*aniyyānikatta*). "Become like an animal" (*tiracchānabhūta*)...

"Consisting of concealment" (*tirokaraṇabhūtaṃ*). "Cultivating the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānabhāveti*) means cultivating the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths associated with impermanence (*aniccatā*).
"Meaningful" (*sātthakaṃ*) means connected with welfare because it is based on giving, virtue, and so forth.
"Street" (*visikhā*) refers to a residential area. And by the mention of a "street," just as in the case of mentioning a village and so forth, those who dwell therein are specifically indicated.

It is included [in the category of worldly talk], as in the expression “the village has arrived,” and so forth. Therefore he said, “brave and capable. By using the term “water-pot” as a designation, water-carriers (kumbhadāsī) are meant;
thus he said, “the talk of water-carriers. That by which the world is described in terms of its arising, persistence, dissolution, and so on, according to its true nature, is called *lokakkhāyikā*.
Thus, it includes the talk concerning existence and non-existence (*itibhavābhavakathā*), which occurs in the form: “In this way there is existence; in that way there is non-existence.”
The commentary on the Chapter on Concentration is finished.
2. The Chapter on Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion.

1081. To explain in detail the meaning briefly stated as "it is called Isipatana because it is the place where sages (ṛṣis) fell and rose, or sank and leaped," the passage beginning with "For here... was spoken. Regarding the word "addressed" (āmantesi):

since this address was for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, it is appropriate to first set forth the Teacher’s previous conduct in brief, starting from his attainment [of enlightenment]; thus [the text says]: "At the feet of Dīpaṅkara..."
The passage beginning with “starting from the time he made his resolution” is commenced. Therein, “having broken the power of Māra” means having shattered both Māra and the power of Māra.
Alternatively, it means having shattered the two-fold power of Māra, namely the internal and the external.

In the phrase “These two, monks, are extremes,” the word *anta* (extreme) signifies a division or part, as in such expressions as “knowledge of the past limit” (*pubbante ñāṇaṃ*) and “knowledge of the future limit” (*aparante ñāṇaṃ*).
He said: “Monks, there are these two portions. “Simultaneously with the utterance” means at the very moment of speaking.

By the power of the Buddha, it stood spread out. The Brahmās who had assembled were those whose roots of merit were fully ripened and who had performed their duties for the sake of the full realization of truth.
“The fetter of a householder” means the bond of a householder. “Having cut” means having removed. “Not to be used” means not to be indulged in.

"Of sensual pleasure consisting of defilements" means of pleasure associated with the objects of defilement (*kilesakāma*). "Devotion" means experience. "Belonging to village-dwellers" means it is the property of village-dwellers because it is to be cultivated by them.
"Of oneself" refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*). It is called "self" (*atta*) because the conceit "I am" (*ahaṃmāna*) is placed therein;
thus, it is the personal existence. "Causing suffering" means the production of suffering. "By those that kill the self" means by those that harm the self. "For the sake of peace" (*upasamāya*).

The subsiding of the defilements (*kilesavūpasama*) is intended; it is a statement for the accomplishment of that purpose, thus he said, "for the sake of the subsiding of the defilements. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.

It is called "threefold-turning" (*tiparivaṭṭa*) because it has three turnings by way of the knowledge of the truths (*saccañāṇa*) and so forth; it is "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*). Therefore he said, "knowledge of the truths," and so on.

"Knowledge according to reality" (*yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ*) refers to penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedhañāṇa*). And regarding the functions to be performed by that very knowledge within those same truths, such as the penetration of full understanding (*pariññā*), etc.
Some say that the knowledge of knowing is "prior to penetration"; others say it is "subsequent. Likewise for the knowledge of having done.
"Twelve aspects" means the division into twelve kinds of modes. "In other places" means in other suttas.
Both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching are called the "Wheel of Dhamma," because in those instances the function of knowledge is considered primary.
It has been said. Furthermore, the collection of phenomena such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and so forth is called the "Wheel of Dhamma" (dhammacakka) in the sense of its proceeding.
Alternatively, "wheel" (cakka) means command; because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is both the Dhamma and the wheel, thus "Dhamma-wheel.

Or, it is the wheel by way of the Dhamma—that is, by way of the principle (ñāya)—thus it is also the "Dhamma-wheel. As it was said: "It sets the Dhamma in motion and it is a wheel, therefore it is the Dhamma-wheel; and it is a wheel..."

"It sets the Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma; it proceeds by means of the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma; it proceeds through the practice of the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma"—and so forth.
"Both" refers to both penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and teaching knowledge (*desanā-ñāṇa*).

"This" refers to those two together. "By this teaching" means by the Blessed One who was revealing [it] through this Sutta, [referring to] that which is designated as the aforementioned pair of knowledges.
"It is called 'set in motion' because the function of setting it in motion was not yet completed.
"It was established" means that the Elder Koṇḍañña was known to have been established in the fruit of stream-entry.
It is called "set in motion" because, from the time the teaching of Kassapa Buddha disappeared until the arising of this Buddha, it had never previously been set in motion during all that time.
Furthermore, his attainment of the higher path has already vanished.
"In a single stroke" means in a single moment designated as a stroke (*pahāra*). For a third part of the day is called a stroke.
However, it is stated in the Canon: "at that very instant, at that very moment, at that very second. This is merely a specific designation for the duration of a stroke.

"The radiance of omniscient knowledge" (sabbaññutaññāṇobhāsa) should be understood as a temperature-originated (utusamuṭṭhāna) light that arises dependent upon the mind through the power of omniscient knowledge.

Because an exceedingly sublime joy and gladness arose in the Blessed One both at the commencement and at the conclusion of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma—just as it did at the beginning—therefore it was said: "Of this exalted utterance (udāna)," and so forth.
9. Commentary on the Saṅkāsana Sutta 1089.

They are called *vaṇṇā* (syllables) because they are described (*vaṇṇīyanti*) in the explanation of meaning. By way of synonym, they are called *akkharā* (phonemes) because they are articulated (*akkhaṇato*).

They are called *byañjanā* (consonants) because they manifest (*byañjenti*) the meaning. Furthermore, since the designation *sara* (vowel) applies to *a* and so forth, while the designation *byañjana* (consonant) applies to *ka* and so forth.
In both cases, the designation "phoneme" (*vaṇṇa*) applies; therefore it was said: "Or, phonemes are a portion [of words], namely what are called syllables (*byañjana*).

However, in the *Netti*, the designation "syllable" (*byañjana*) applies to a sentence. It should be understood that by the inclusion of the term "syllable" here, the grammatical forms (*ākāra*), etymological explanations (*nirutti*), and formal descriptions (*niddesa*) are also included.
"Indication" (*saṅkāsanā*) means the making known of the meaning part by part. Therefore he said: "The case-endings (*vibhattiyo*)."
And here, by the very mention of "making known" (*saṅkāsanaggaḥaṇa*), "explanation" (*pakāsanā*) is also stated.

For the case endings (*vibhattiyo*) explain [the meaning] through the statement of the sense (*atthavacana*); since the designations of reasons (*kāraṇapaññattiyo*) are already expressed by them, the words of the sense are thereby also grasped.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga-vaṇṇanā* and the *Netti-aṭṭhakathā*.
It is to be understood. "In every aspect" means by way of the aspects of distinguishing between similar and dissimilar [factors] and so forth.
"Of color and the rest" refers to the color and other qualities that occur in that detailed exposition. "Therefore" means because there is no end to color and the rest.
"He said thus" means he said: "The colors, phonemes, and explanations are immeasurable."
10. Commentary on the *Tathasutta* 1090.
"In the sense of not abandoning its own nature" means that it possesses suchness (*tathasabhāva*) because it never relinquishes its own nature of suffering (*dukkhasabhāva*).
Therefore he said: "For suffering is indeed called 'suffering'. "Of its nature" means of the nature of suffering. "By way of non-futility" means...
“Non-deceptiveness” (*avañjhatāya*). “Not false” (*avitathaṃ*) means it is not otherwise than what it is. Therefore he said: “For suffering does not become non-suffering.
“By not undergoing another state” (*aññabhāvānupagamena*) means that because it does not undergo another nature—such as the nature of the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth—it is not false;
thus, being not otherwise, it is “non-otherwise” (*anaññathaṃ*). Therefore he said: “For not,” and so forth.

1112–3. *Mariyādapāsāṇa* means a large rock resembling the boundary wall of Mount Gijjhakūṭa.

*Upāsana* means attending upon a teacher; it is the craft of archery, so named because it must be attended upon day by day by a pupil through the process of training. "Transgressing the arrow" refers to the shaft.
They are shot. To make the meaning of the term *poṅkhānupoṅkha* clear, it is said: "having shot one arrow," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "another [arrow] following the *poṅkha*":
here, "another" refers to the third arrow. To show what is meant by "following the *poṅkha*," it is said:
"what is called 'following the *poṅkha*' is the [arrival] of the second *poṅkha*. For that [third arrow] is by means of the third...
It is pierced by the arrow. Furthermore, the phrase "again, another" (*puna aparaṃ tassa poṅkha*) is stated to show that there was no failure [of the arrow] even in successive repetitions.
"Difficult to overcome" (*durabhisambhavataraṃ*) means more difficult to master or surpass. "Hair" (*vālaṃ*) means a lock of hair.
"Having split into seven parts" (*sattadhā bhinditvā*) means having torn it apart seven times. "One part of that" (*tassa ekaṃ bhedaṃ*) refers to one portion of that hair.
"Taking one portion known as a hair-fiber (*aṃsu*)," means taking a single strand of hair.
"Tying it in the middle of a vātiṅgaṇa fruit" means tying it at the central part of the *vātiṅgaṇa* fruit. "Another portion" refers to another hair-fiber.
"Tying it at the tip" means [tying it] so that the tip of that hair-fiber reaches the very point of the fruit's stalk, even by the measure of a louse-egg or a grain of rice.
"Remaining after being cast out" means remaining after having been bound in this way. "The size of a bull" means standing at a distance of twenty *hatthas*.
"With the tip of a hair tied to an arrow" means that with the tip of the hair tied to the arrow, one would pierce the tip of the hair used for tying the *vātiṅgaṇa* fruit.
8. Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Hole and the Yoke (Chiggaḷayugasutta)
"Occasional arising" (*adhiccuppatti*) means that which arises according to one's own desire. "Through a gap" (*chiggaḷena*) means by way of a gap.

"Above the gap" (*chiggaḷupari*) means above the gap of the lower pair. "Through the gap of that which has ascended" (*āruḷhassa chiggaḷena*) means through the opening of both [the upper and lower pairs].
"Like the insertion of a neck" (*gīvappavesanaṃ viya*) refers to [the neck] being situated one above the other precisely through the opening of the four pairs.
The insertion of a tortoise’s neck through the opening of a yoke-halter is a possibility occurring only by extreme chance;
even more difficult than that is the attainment of human birth, and even more difficult than that is the attainment of the Noble Path. Demonstrating this, he said:
“The penetration of the Four Truths is a possibility occurring by an exceedingly extreme chance.”

8. Commentary on the *Bījagāma Sutta* 1148. Regarding the passage beginning with “root-seed” (*mūlabīja*), a root itself is the seed, thus it is a “root-seed”; or, that which has a root-seed as its [source] is also called a “root-seed. Therein, by the former [definition], the “seed-division” (*bījagāma*) is stated, taking it as “a collection of seeds”; by the second, the “living-division” (*bhūtagāma*). This twofold division is as follows: [The text continues: ...the first is the seed-division, and the second is the living-division. Both of these are of two kinds. The seed-division is of two kinds: that which is propagated from seeds and that which is propagated from slips. The living-division is of two kinds: that which is propagated from roots and that which is propagated from joints. Of these, the seed-division is propagated from seeds, while the living-division is propagated from roots and joints. Furthermore, the seed-division is propagated from seeds, while the living-division is propagated from roots, joints, and cuttings. Thus, both are twofold. The seed-division is twofold: that which is propagated from seeds and that which is propagated from slips. The living-division is twofold: that which is propagated from roots and that which is propagated from joints. Among these, the seed-division is propagated from seeds, while the living-division is propagated from roots and joints. Moreover, the seed-division is propagated from seeds, while the living-division is propagated from roots, joints, and cuttings. Thus, both are twofold. The seed-division is twofold: that which is propagated from seeds and that which is propagated from slips. The living-division is twofold: that which is propagated from roots and that which is propagated from joints. The meaning of "seed" (*bīja*) should be understood through the method of common designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*), or by the principle of single-remainder (*ekasesanaya*) as "root-seed and root-seed [is] seed.
This same method applies to the remaining types as well. "Corm-seed" (*phaḷubīja*) refers to a bulbous seed.

The word "seed" is conventionally established for a hard, solid fruit capable of sprouting, because it serves as the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when combined with external conditions.

Because it occurs in some instances, such as the root, for the sake of establishing that specific meaning, it is stated as "seed-seed" (*bījabīja*)—distinguished by the word "seed" (*bīja*) alone—in order to exclude those other instances, just as one says "matter-matter" (*rūparūpa*) or "suffering-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*).
"Of blue grass, trees, and so forth" refers both to fresh grass and to fresh trees and the like. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), medicinal herbs, creepers, and the like are included.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on Eating at the Wrong Time (Vikālabhojana-sutta) 1149.

From the rising of the sun until midday is the time for eating that has been habitually practiced by the Buddhas and other Noble Ones; any time other than that is the "wrong time" (*vikāla*). Therefore, it is said: "Eating at the wrong time means eating after the proper time has passed. 10.

1151. In brief, because the Blessed One’s teaching—as set forth in the manner beginning with “The non-doing of all evil” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.90;

thus he said, “Because it is not in conformity with the teaching. This applies to that which is performed by oneself, by others, or instigated by others.
It was already included by the sound of dancing itself, as well as by the sounds of singing and instrumental music; thus he said, "by way of dancing, causing others to dance, and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), he includes singing, causing others to sing, playing instruments, causing others to play instruments, and the like. And here, by the method of "the remainder of the dissimilar" (virūpekasesanaya), hearing is also included within seeing.
Or [it may be understood] because each of the five [senses] has the intrinsic nature of perceiving its respective object.
Because the act of hearing cognitions also possesses the quality of seeing in a summarized sense, it is described simply as "seeing.
Since the hearing of songs that are not frivolous is sometimes permissible, he says: "and frivolous sights.

Commentary on the Discourse on High Beds (Uccāsayanasutta). 1152.
*Uccā* is another word with the same meaning as the word *ucca*. A bed (*sayana*) is so called because one lies (*seti*) upon it; thus, it is a high bed (*uccāsayana*).
Since high beds and large beds are rejected as being unsuitable for a recluse, it is said: "exceeding the proper measure, with an unworthy covering.

Here, seats such as the *āsandi* (stool) and so forth are included by the term "bed" (*sayana*) itself. However, because when the physical basis (the bed) is rejected, the activity based upon it is also necessarily rejected, it is stated simply as "high beds and large beds.
In terms of meaning, however, this refers to sitting and lying down that constitute the enjoyment of those [beds].

It should be understood that abstinence is what is shown here. Alternatively, by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*), this designation is made for the sense of "high and luxurious beds and seats" as "high and luxurious beds and seats," just as in the expression: "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.
Or else, because the act of reclining is preceded by the act of sitting, by the mention of "reclining" (*sayana*), the "sitting" (*āsana*) is also included.

The connection [is as follows]: Precisely because it possesses qualities that bring about specific wisdom (*paññā*), it was stated at the very beginning of this work, even in the introduction to the book, that it is "for the generation of the various kinds of wisdom.
"The essence of the Great Commentary" means the essence of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
The term "only fifty-nine" includes the word "mere" (*matta*) because it is slightly less than sixty.
"The essence of the *Mūlaṭṭhakathā*" means that the very essence of the previously mentioned Great Commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* has been stated again by way of conclusion.
Alternatively, "the essence of the *Mūlaṭṭhakathā*" refers to the essential meaning within the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
By this, he shows: "Having taken the essential meaning of the Great Commentary on the *Saṃyutta*, while composing this *Sāratthappakāsinī*..."

"In the root commentaries (*mūlaṭṭhakathā*) of the other great schools (*sesamahānikāya*) as well, [the author] composed [this work] by taking the essential meaning that is capable of being separated [from them]," so it is said.
Furthermore, the phrase "of those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra" (*mahāvihārādhivāsīnam*) should be connected with both the preceding and following words, as in:
"proclaiming the system of those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra" and "taking the essence from the root commentary of those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra. By this...

"By means of merit: 'May the whole world be happy'—he dedicates his own merit for the attainment of ultimate happiness by the world including the devas, thinking: 'May the entire world of beings, categorized according to the planes such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth, be made happy by the bliss of Nibbāna associated with the realization of the threefold enlightenment, each according to their capacity."
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya*.
